Thesis gate

How we can know our own attitudinal states (beliefs, intentions, etc.), given how much interpretation appears to be doing. The empirical literature on confabulation, motivated reasoning and implicit attitudes (Nisbett and Wilson; Schwitzgebel) undermines a simple observational or inner-perception model of introspection. But the interpretive alternative — that we read ourselves off behavioural and contextual evidence much as we read others (Carruthers, Gopnik) — struggles to explain first-person authority, the asymmetry between self-ascription and other-ascription that Moran's agentialist account and Bar-On's neo-expressivism were built to capture. At issue is whether first-person authority survives the interpretive turn, and if so what grounds it.

Look here first

Promise 4+ with nothing above a 2 left unanswered. Ambitious and hard to break. Expect a short list, and an empty one on some runs.

P1. The asymmetry between self- and other-ascription is real but inverted from what everyone assumes: others have MORE interpretive access to our standing attitudes than we do, while we have privileged access only to our occurrent judgments in the moment of avowal.

Scores
promise 5/5 · residual 0/5 · worst 4/5 · survives
Move · Target
reframing — The assumption shared by both sides that self-knowledge is primarily about access to standing psychological states rather than occurrent acts
Sketch

The debate assumes that if there's first-person authority, it extends to our beliefs and intentions generally. But the confabulation literature shows that when asked about our standing attitudes ('Do I believe in gun control?'), we often generate an answer through the same interpretive process observers use—except observers see our patterns better because they aren't inside our motivated reasoning. The real asymmetry is occurrent: when I judge right now that gun control is good, that very act of judging constitutes an attitude-in-the-moment that only I can report non-interpretively. This explains both the phenomenology of authority (we feel authoritative when forming judgments, not when reporting pre-existing beliefs) and the data (we confabulate about standing attitudes but not about what we're currently thinking). Moran gets closest to this with his emphasis on the deliberative stance, but still treats it as revealing pre-existing attitudes rather than constituting momentary ones.

Appraiser (blind)
Inverting the asymmetry—others know standing attitudes better, we know occurrent judgments—is genuinely surprising and could reorient the debate.
Objections
  • MISATTRIBUTION — landed 4/5, answered. Defence showed Moran preserves first-person authority over beliefs via deliberation while thesis eliminates it for standing states—a genuine inversion, not mischaracterization
  • ALREADY TAKEN — landed 4/5, answered. Defence distinguished thesis from Edgley/Hampshire performativism by preserving epistemic asymmetry for occurrent episodes rather than making authority merely conventional
  • PROVES TOO MUCH — landed 3/5, answered. Defence separated privileged access to content-generation from interpretive access to standing attitudes, blocking the absurdity while clarifying the position's radicalism
  • COUNTEREXAMPLE — landed 3/5, answered. Defence showed concealed beliefs involve privileged access to evidence (memories, private feelings) plus interpretation, not non-interpretive access to standing states themselves
  • TRIVIAL — landed 2/5, answered. Defence demonstrated the thesis makes substantive revisionary claims about where authority lies, not merely reports familiar distinctions or empirical findings
Survives as

The asymmetry between self- and other-ascription is real but inverted: others have superior interpretive access to our standing attitudes (functional-dispositional patterns) because they observe behavioral patterns without motivated reasoning, while we have privileged non-interpretive access only to occurrent judgments in the moment of avowal and to the evidence (memory traces, private feelings) we use for self-interpretation

full exchange (10 turns)

KILLER (MISATTRIBUTION)

ATTEMPT. The thesis claims to invert "what everyone assumes" and targets "the assumption shared by both sides" about standing vs. occurrent states. But this mischaracterizes the dialectical landscape. Moran's *Authority and Estrangement* explicitly distinguishes the deliberative stance (forward-looking, rational) from the theoretical stance (backward-looking, interpretive) and argues that first-person authority attaches to the former precisely because it involves active commitment-making rather than discovery of pre-existing states. Evans's transparency account similarly emphasizes the present act of judgment-formation over archaeological retrieval. The thesis claims Moran "still treats it as revealing pre-existing attitudes rather than constituting momentary ones," but Moran's central point is that avowing a belief is taking a stand, not reporting a discovery. The view that occurrent judgment-formation has special authority while standing attitudes require interpretation isn't an inversion of the debate—it's already Moran's position. The thesis attacks a caricature where everyone treats all self-knowledge as archaeological, when sophisticated participants already draw precisely the distinction the thesis claims to introduce.

STRENGTH: 4/5 — This is a serious problem. The thesis presents as novel dialectical terrain that Moran (named in the sketch) already occupies. Without a clearer account of how this differs from Moran's deliberative stance, the reframing collapses into restating an existing position while claiming to oppose it.

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE

The objection conflates *making* the distinction with *getting it right*. Yes, Moran distinguishes deliberative from theoretical stances, but he mislocates the asymmetry in two fatal ways that the thesis corrects.

First, Moran treats the deliberative stance as a *method of access* to beliefs that exist independently of the avowal. When I ask "Shall I believe p?" I'm settling what to believe, but for Moran this settles what I *already* believe in some constitutive sense—the deliberative stance reveals my rational commitments. The thesis breaks this: there is no standing belief to access. The occurrent judgment *is* the only attitude present. When I judge now that gun control is good, I haven't discovered or constituted my "belief about gun control"—I've had an episode that will dissipate. If you ask me tomorrow, I'll interpret traces like anyone else.

Second, and more damaging: Moran still grants first-person authority over standing attitudes, just via a different route (rational self-constitution rather than introspection). He thinks deliberation gives me privileged access to what I believe *generally*, not merely what I'm judging *now*. The thesis denies this entirely. There is no first-person authority about my beliefs as standing states, full stop. Others read my patterns better. The asymmetry exists only for the vanishingly narrow category of occurrent judgment-in-the-moment-of-avowal.

The objection's cited quote—"Moran's central point is that avowing a belief is taking a stand, not reporting a discovery"—actually proves the difference. For Moran, taking a stand *on whether p* constitutes having the belief that p (a standing state). For the thesis, taking a stand constitutes only an occurrent episode. The stand doesn't persist as "my belief"—it evaporates.

This isn't restating Moran with aggressive marketing. It's denying that his deliberative stance delivers what he claims: self-knowledge of beliefs as such, rather than merely of judgments-in-progress.

VERDICT

The defence succeeds. The objection correctly identifies that Moran makes a deliberative/theoretical distinction, but misses that the thesis *inverts Moran's conclusion* about what that distinction establishes. Moran uses deliberation to *preserve* first-person authority over beliefs (reconceived as rational commitments). The thesis uses the same materials to *eliminate* first-person authority over anything except the occurrent act itself. That's a genuine inversion, not a restatement. The dialectical novelty stands.

KILLER (ALREADY TAKEN)

ATTEMPT. The thesis is essentially Edgley's (1969) and Hampshire's (1965) position that avowals are performative rather than descriptive, combined with the confabulation literature's empirical findings. Edgley argued that "I believe that p" functions more like a commitment or endorsement than a report of an inner state—the utterance itself constitutes taking a stand rather than describing a pre-existing belief. Hampshire similarly distinguished the momentary act of judgment from any standing dispositional state. The thesis adds empirical detail from Nisbett & Wilson about confabulation regarding standing attitudes, but the core structural claim—that genuine first-person authority attaches only to the speech act itself, not to standing psychological states, and that what we call "beliefs" are really interpreter-dependent patterns rather than self-accessible states—is their view. Even the specific contrast (occurrent judgment vs. standing attitude) maps onto Hampshire's distinction between the activity of judging and the dispositional belief-state. The thesis presents this as "inverting" the debate, but it's actually returning to a mid-century ordinary language position that was extensively discussed and then largely abandoned in favor of functionalist accounts of belief precisely because the performative view struggled to explain belief-desire psychology's predictive success. The "inversion" rhetoric obscures that this is a known position being revived.

STRENGTH: 4/5 — This significantly undermines the novelty claim. The thesis would need to explain how it differs from Edgley/Hampshire's performativism or why reviving that position answers the objections that led to its abandonment. Simply adding confabulation data to a 1960s speech-act theory of avowals doesn't constitute a new reframing.

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE

The objection trades on superficial structural similarity while missing the thesis's departure from performativism on the crucial question: what makes avowals *authoritative*?

Edgley and Hampshire's performativism explains away the epistemic puzzle by denying there's anything to know: "I believe p" doesn't report a belief-state because it constitutes a speech act (endorsing, committing). But this leaves first-person authority *unexplained*—why should my performative have any special status? You can endorse p too; why is my self-ascription authoritative in a way yours about me is not? Classical performativism either denies the asymmetry (it's just a social convention that self-ascriptions count as authoritative) or leaves it mysterious.

The thesis *preserves* the epistemic asymmetry but relocates it. There *is* something I know non-interpretively that you cannot: my occurrent judgment at the moment of avowal. This isn't a speech act constituting a commitment—it's *cognitive access* to a mental event. When I judge that p (occurrent episode), I have direct acquaintance with that episode of judging; you must infer it from my utterance. The asymmetry is epistemic, not performative.

The difference emerges in cases of insincere avowal. For Hampshire/Edgley, "I believe p" said insincerely is still a performative (a lying endorsement, perhaps). For the thesis, insincere avowal *misreports* the occurrent judgment I actually have. There's a fact about what I'm judging right now, and I have privileged epistemic access to it—but *only* to the occurrent episode, not to any standing state.

Second, the thesis explains what performativism cannot: why we systematically *mistake* occurrent episodes for standing states. We feel authoritative when avowing because we *are* authoritative about the occurrent judgment, but we wrongly interpret this as authority about a belief-as-standing-state. Performativism has no resources to explain this phenomenological error—if avowals just are performatives, why does it feel like reporting?

Third, on predictive success: functionalism won because performativism couldn't explain belief-desire prediction. The thesis *accepts* beliefs as functional states for prediction—it just denies we have privileged access to them. Others predict my behavior better by tracking my belief-patterns (functional states); I confabulate about these patterns just as Nisbett & Wilson showed. The occurrent judgment I access non-interpretively is predictively useless (it's momentary, doesn't persist). This isn't performativism's problem—it grants the functionalist ontology while denying the epistemology.

The objection mistakes *mentioning* speech acts for *being* speech-act theory. The thesis isn't about what avowals *do*; it's about what mental items we access when making them.

VERDICT

The defence succeeds. The thesis differs from Edgley/Hampshire on the fundamental question: whether first-person authority is *epistemic* (privileged access to occurrent mental events) or *pragmatic* (performative speech acts having conventional authority). The thesis takes the epistemic route, which is why it can explain both the phenomenology (feels like reporting because it partly is—reporting an occurrent state) and accommodate functionalism (standing beliefs exist as functional states; we just don't access them introspectively).

Classical performativism denied the epistemic asymmetry or left it unexplained; the thesis explains it by restricting it to occurrent episodes. That's not revival—it's using the occurrent/standing distinction to solve performativism's authority problem while keeping its insight that standing attitudes aren't introspectively accessible. The position is genuinely distinct.

KILLER (PROVES TOO MUCH)

ATTEMPT. If the argument worked—that others have superior interpretive access to our standing attitudes because they observe our behavioral patterns without motivated reasoning, while we confabulate—it would prove that we systematically lack self-knowledge about virtually ALL our psychologically relevant states. Standing attitudes aren't some peripheral category; they're the core of belief-desire psychology that explains action. My standing belief that my child is at school, that fire burns, that I'm a generous person—these are what make my behavior intelligible. If I must interpret these through the same process observers use, but worse (because motivated), then for the vast domain of psychological states that matter for understanding agency, I'm a *less reliable interpreter of myself* than strangers are. This licenses the absurd conclusion that you could know better than I do what I believe about nearly everything (since most beliefs are standing, not occurrent). It would vindicate the most extreme externalist position: that a team of behavioral observers with no access to my phenomenology could write a more accurate psychological profile of my beliefs, desires, values, and intentions than I could. But this contradicts the obvious fact that I can tell you thousands of things I believe that no amount of behavioral observation would reveal—that I believe the population of France is around 67 million, that Hume was Scottish, that my password is X. The argument proves too much because it eliminates self-knowledge precisely where it's most obvious we have it: in the vast store of standing propositional attitudes.

STRENGTH: 4/5 — This is a serious problem. The thesis needs a principled way to limit the "others know better" claim to avoid the absurd conclusion that I'm generally a worse authority on my own beliefs than behavioral observers are, which conflicts with obvious cases where I can report beliefs no observation would reveal.

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE

The objection assumes that "interpretive access" means "access to content" when the thesis concerns access to *whether the attitude exists as a standing state*. This conflates two entirely different questions, and the absurdity dissolves once we separate them.

You're right that I can tell you my password and you cannot learn it behaviorally. But *how* do I tell you? Not by introspecting a standing belief-state and reporting it. I *reconstruct* it: I imagine the login screen, simulate typing, perhaps retrieve an episodic memory of creating it, and *generate* the answer. This generation process is exactly what the confabulation literature describes—it feels like retrieval but is actually interpretation of traces. The crucial point: I have superior access to the *traces* (memories, associative connections, imaginative capacities) that I use for reconstruction, which is why I can report content you cannot access behaviorally.

But having better *inputs* to interpretation doesn't mean having better *interpretive judgment* about whether these inputs constitute a standing belief. Consider: Do I *believe* my password, or do I merely retain the capacity to generate it when prompted? The thesis says there's no fact of the matter I access directly—I interpret my generative success as indicating a belief, just as you would. I'm better at generating the content (privileged access to memory traces), but not better at judging whether this constitutes a standing attitude.

The "others know better" claim applies specifically to *global patterns* that reveal standing attitudes: Do I believe in gun control? Am I generous? Do I trust my colleague? Here, behavioral observation over time genuinely does outperform my motivated, episodically-biased self-interpretation. You see that I consistently advocate gun control in conversations, donate to related causes, vote accordingly—a pattern I might not notice because I'm interpreting from inside my motivated reasoning ("I'm just following the evidence in each case").

The France population case actually supports the thesis. If you ask me "Do you believe France's population is around 67 million?", I don't introspect a standing belief—I generate the number (from memory traces), notice it seems right, and *form the occurrent judgment* "yes, about 67 million." That occurrent judgment is what I have privileged access to. Whether this generation-and-endorsement constitutes having *believed* it (standing state) before you asked, or whether I merely had the capacity to generate it, is interpretive. I'm not a better judge of that than you are—I just have better access to the generative process.

The thesis doesn't eliminate self-knowledge of *content*—I know what I'm judging right now, and I have superior access to memory traces that let me generate answers. It eliminates self-knowledge of *standing attitudes as such*—whether these capacities and episodes constitute beliefs that exist between episodes is something I interpret, not introspect.

So the "thousands of things I believe" reduces to: thousands of contents I can generate when prompted, which I (and you) *interpret* as indicating standing beliefs. The interpretation is theory-laden and fallible. The generation is privileged. No absurdity follows.

VERDICT

The defence holds, but barely, and reveals a dangerous instability in the thesis.

The distinction between "privileged access to traces/content-generation" versus "interpretive access to whether standing attitudes exist" does block the immediate absurdity. I'm not claiming strangers know my password better—they don't have access to my memory traces. The asymmetry is preserved for *content* while denied for *attitude-attribution*.

However, this defense exposes how much weight now rests on the standing/occurrent distinction doing real metaphysical work, and whether "standing belief" remains a coherent category at all under this picture. If standing beliefs are just patterns that interpreters (including me) impose on my capacity to generate judgments when prompted, plus behavioral regularities, then the thesis is sliding toward eliminativism about standing beliefs—they're not mental states I fail to access, they're *interpretive posits* with no determinate existence.

That might be defensible, but it's a much more radical position than the thesis initially suggested. The "inversion" framing implied standing beliefs exist but others access them better. The defence here suggests they might not exist as mental states at all—just as patterns in the eye of interpreters.

The defence succeeds in blocking the specific absurdity (strangers knowing my password), but at the cost of revealing that the thesis may be more revisionary about the ontology of belief than it initially appeared. That's not a failure of the defence—it's a clarification that the position is more radical than "inverting" access claims. It may be *dissolving* one of the relata.

KILLER (COUNTEREXAMPLE)

ATTEMPT. Consider a standing belief that is both (1) clearly action-guiding and dispositionally real, and (2) directly accessible to me but hidden from behavioral observation: my belief that my father sexually abused me as a child, which I have never disclosed to anyone and which I actively conceal through compensatory cheerful behavior around him.

According to the thesis, others should have superior interpretive access to this standing attitude because they observe my behavioral patterns without motivated reasoning. But observers see only my warm interactions with my father, my regular visits, my public defenses of him. They would interpret these patterns as indicating I believe he's trustworthy and I love him. Meanwhile, I have direct, certain knowledge of my standing belief about the abuse—I can report it immediately without interpretation, it explains my private behavior (nightmares, avoidance of certain topics, therapeutic work), and it's a paradigm case of a standing attitude that guides action over years.

This isn't about content-generation from memory traces (like the password case). The belief that abuse occurred is a standing attitude that structures my entire relationship with my father, persists between episodes of thinking about it, and disposes me to various behaviors. Yet observers, lacking access to my concealed reactions and private mental life, would systematically misinterpret my standing attitude. I am the better interpreter here, not because of privileged access to occurrent judgments, but because I have access to the standing belief itself—and the thesis provides no account of how this access works if standing beliefs are only interpretively accessible.

STRENGTH: 4/5 — This is a serious problem. Cases of deliberately concealed standing beliefs that structure behavior over time seem to refute the claim that others are better interpreters of our standing attitudes through behavioral observation.

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE

The objection presents a case where behavioral evidence *misleads* observers, but this doesn't establish that the subject has non-interpretive access to a standing belief—it establishes only that the subject has access to *different evidence* for interpretation, including evidence observers lack.

Unpack what "direct, certain knowledge" of the abuse belief actually involves. The subject doesn't introspect a standing belief-state labeled "my father abused me." Rather, they have:

1. Episodic memories of abuse events (privileged access to memory traces)
2. Affective responses when around the father—anxiety, disgust, hypervigilance (privileged access to occurrent feelings)
3. Patterns in their own behavior they observe privately—the nightmares, the therapeutic work, the topics they avoid (privileged access to private behavioral evidence)

From these inputs, the subject *interprets* themselves as having the standing belief that abuse occurred. This interpretation is more accurate than the observer's interpretation because the evidential base is vastly superior—but it's still interpretation, not introspection of a standing state.

The key test: Does the subject have the standing belief *between episodes* of accessing these evidence sources? Suppose the subject develops dense amnesia for the abuse memories, the affective responses are chemically suppressed, and they lose access to the private behavioral patterns. On the thesis, there's no standing belief to introspect independently of these evidence sources. The belief exists *as* the pattern these sources manifest, not as a separately accessible mental state.

Compare a genuinely parallel case: "I have the standing belief that my colleague dislikes me, which I've never disclosed and actively conceal by being friendly. Observers see only warm interactions and would misinterpret. But I have direct knowledge of this belief." Do I? Or do I interpret a pattern of evidence—microexpressions I catch, ambiguous comments I parse negatively, gut feelings in their presence—and conclude I believe they dislike me? The thesis says the latter. I have privileged access to evidence (I notice microexpressions they don't know I noticed), but I *interpret* this evidence as constituting a standing belief.

The abuse case feels different because the evidence is more vivid and the stakes are higher, but the structure is identical: privileged access to evidence (memories, private feelings, concealed behaviors) that I interpret as indicating a standing belief. The interpretation happens to be more accurate than the observer's interpretation because my evidence is better—but superior evidence doesn't mean non-interpretive access to the attitude itself.

The objection's phrase "the standing belief itself" begs the question. What is this belief, apart from the pattern in memory traces, affective dispositions, and behavioral tendencies? If it's *just* that pattern, then I access it interpretively (by accessing the pattern elements). If it's something *over and above* the pattern—a separately existing mental state—then the thesis denies such states exist for standing attitudes, and the objection's counterexample assumes what it needs to prove.

Finally, the "structures my entire relationship" point actually supports the thesis. A standing belief that genuinely structures behavior over years *is* a functional-dispositional state—exactly what the thesis says exists but isn't introspectively accessible. The subject doesn't access this dispositional structure directly; they infer it from its manifestations (the memories, feelings, and behaviors they observe in themselves). That inference is better grounded than the observer's inference, but it's still inference.

VERDICT

The defence succeeds, but reveals a critical ambiguity the thesis must resolve.

The defence correctly identifies that "direct access" to the abuse belief reduces to privileged access to evidence (memories, private feelings, concealed behaviors) plus interpretation of that evidence. This blocks the counterexample: the subject isn't accessing a standing belief non-interpretively; they're making a better-grounded interpretation from superior evidence.

However, the defence exposes a deep tension about what standing beliefs *are*. Two options:

Option 1: Standing beliefs are functional-dispositional states (patterns of memory traces, affective dispositions, behavioral tendencies). Then the thesis is coherent—these patterns exist, but we access them only interpretively by observing their manifestations. I have better access to private manifestations (memories, feelings), so my interpretation is often better grounded, but it's still interpretation. The abuse case is handled: I interpret my pattern of memories/feelings/behaviors as constituting the belief.

Option 2: Standing beliefs are determinate mental states over and above their functional manifestations. Then the thesis faces a dilemma: either (a) these states exist but are completely epistemically idle (I can never know I have them, even interpretively, since interpretation only accesses manifestations), which makes them metaphysically suspect, or (b) they don't exist, and the thesis is eliminativist about standing beliefs.

The defence implicitly takes Option 1, which is defensible but commits the thesis to a specific metaphysics of belief: standing beliefs are *constituted by* patterns of dispositions and traces, not separate states that *cause* those patterns. This is a coherent position (roughly functionalist), but it means the thesis isn't just an epistemological claim about access—it's a metaphysical claim about what beliefs are.

The counterexample fails because it assumes Option 2 (standing beliefs as separate states I can access), which the thesis rejects. But the defence only works if the thesis embraces the full metaphysical package of Option 1.

The defence holds. The thesis survives, but must acknowledge it's making a metaphysical claim about belief-constitution, not just an epistemological claim about access asymmetries.

KILLER (TRIVIAL)

ATTEMPT. The thesis claims to reveal a "real asymmetry" that inverts conventional assumptions, but this dissolves into either (a) a trivial empirical observation dressed as philosophical discovery, or (b) a stipulative redefinition of terms that creates an illusion of inversion.

The trivial empirical core: The confabulation literature establishes that people are sometimes wrong about their own standing attitudes while observers who track behavioral patterns may be more accurate. This is just psychological data—interesting, but not a philosophical thesis about "asymmetry." Saying "others are sometimes better at reading our patterns" is like saying "others sometimes have better evidence about our medical conditions because they notice symptoms we ignore." True, but philosophically uninteresting.

The stipulative move occurs when the thesis restricts "genuine first-person authority" to occurrent judgments. But this is just *defining* the domain of authority narrowly enough that the empirical data can't touch it. It's like saying "I have infallible knowledge of my thoughts—by which I mean only the thought I'm having in this exact millisecond of introspection." The restriction makes the claim true by verbal fiat, not by discovery.

The supposed "inversion" depends entirely on this stipulation. There's no inversion in the claim that (1) people confabulate about standing attitudes [empirical fact], and (2) people don't confabulate about what they're judging right now [trivial—you can't be wrong about what you're currently doing]. The appearance of paradox comes from *calling* both things "beliefs" and then pretending it's surprising they have different epistemic profiles. But once we distinguish occurrent episodes from standing states (which the thesis admits everyone already does), the asymmetry is exactly what we'd expect: current mental acts are self-intimating, stable dispositions require interpretation. That's not an inversion—it's a truism.

The thesis packages this truism as discovery by suggesting the debate "assumes self-knowledge is primarily about standing states." But if this means philosophers discuss standing beliefs more than occurrent judgments, that's because standing beliefs do more explanatory work in folk psychology and cognitive science—not because anyone thought occurrent episodes were interpretively inaccessible. If it means philosophers wrongly thought standing beliefs were introspectable, then the thesis is just reporting empirical findings (confabulation), not making a philosophical move.

Where's the philosophical content beyond "confabulation happens + let's restrict 'authority' to occurrent episodes"?

STRENGTH: 2/5

The attack has some force against the *presentation* of the thesis as a dramatic inversion, but doesn't actually kill the substantive claim. Here's why it falls short:

The thesis isn't merely reporting that confabulation happens—it's making the stronger claim that there's a *systematic* asymmetry where others have *superior* (not just sometimes better) interpretive access to standing attitudes. This goes beyond "sometimes we're wrong" to "we're structurally disadvantaged as interpreters of our own patterns." That's not trivial if true.

More importantly, the thesis makes a claim about *where the real epistemic asymmetry lies* that does contradict a substantive assumption in the literature. Many philosophers (even those who discuss standing vs. occurrent) assume that if there's first-person authority, it extends to beliefs generally—perhaps through different mechanisms (introspection, rational reflection, transparency), but still covering the domain of standing attitudes. The thesis denies this: there's *no* first-person authority about standing attitudes by any route. That's not a stipulation about what to call "authority"—it's a substantive claim that all the proposed mechanisms (Moran's deliberation, Evans's transparency) fail to deliver what they promise for standing states.

The "truism" charge would work if the thesis were just distinguishing occurrent from standing. But it's making the further claim that the folk psychological category of "belief" systematically misleads us by conflating these, and that recognizing this requires abandoning the search for first-person authority over beliefs-as-ordinarily-understood. That's revisionary, not trivial.

The attack correctly identifies that the thesis could be *presented* less dramatically, but the core claim—that first-person authority is radically narrower than the literature assumes and that standing attitude attribution is interpretive for everyone including the subject—isn't rendered trivial by noting that the occurrent/standing distinction exists.

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE

The objection conflates "making a distinction" with "drawing the right conclusions from it," and mistakes "expected by the objector" for "trivial."

Yes, the occurrent/standing distinction exists in the literature. The philosophical work lies in what the thesis *does* with it—and here the claim is neither trivial nor stipulative.

Against the triviality charge:

The thesis doesn't merely observe that "confabulation happens sometimes." It claims that for standing attitudes, *self-interpretation and other-interpretation are the same in kind*, with others often having superior evidential position. This contradicts the structuring assumption of the entire self-knowledge debate: that there's something distinctively first-personal about attitude self-ascription that makes it epistemically different from other-ascription.

Consider the dialectical landscape. Virtually every position in the literature—from introspectionism to rationalism to interpretationism—agrees that self-ascription of beliefs has *some* distinctive epistemic character, even if they disagree about its source:
- Introspectionists: I have perceptual access to my beliefs
- Rationalists (Moran): I have constitutive authority through deliberation
- Interpretationism (Gopnik): I use the same theory as for others, but with different/better evidence

The thesis breaks this consensus: for standing attitudes, there's *no* epistemic asymmetry at all, not even an evidential one that favors the subject. Others may have *better* evidence (they see my patterns without motivated reasoning). That's not a trivial observation—it's denying what every party to the debate affirms.

Against the stipulation charge:

Restricting "genuine authority" to occurrent judgments isn't verbal fiat—it's a *diagnosis* of where the phenomenology of authority actually comes from, which explains why we've been systematically confused.

We *feel* authoritative when self-ascribing beliefs. The thesis explains this: we're authoritative about the occurrent judgment we form when asked "Do you believe p?"—but we mistakenly interpret this as authority about a standing state. The phenomenology is *real* but *misattributed*. That's an explanatory claim, not a stipulation.

Compare: Saying "we have direct access only to sense-data, not external objects" isn't trivially true by definition. It's a substantive (if controversial) claim about what direct acquaintance actually reaches, offered to explain why we *think* we access external objects directly (the sense-data mediate seamlessly). Similarly, "we have direct access only to occurrent judgments, not standing beliefs" explains why we *think* we access beliefs directly (the occurrent judgment feels like it's revealing something pre-existing).

Against the "truism" charge:

The objection says: "Current mental acts are self-intimating, stable dispositions require interpretation. That's not an inversion—it's a truism."

But this *is* the inversion, and it's only a truism *after* you accept it. Before the thesis, the debate assumes:
- Self-ascription of belief = privileged epistemic position
- Other-ascription of belief = interpretive/inferential

After the thesis:
- Self-ascription of *standing* belief = interpretive (often worse than others)
- Self-ascription of *occurrent* judgment = privileged
- Other-ascription of standing belief = interpretive (often better)

The inversion is: what we call "beliefs" (standing attitudes) are precisely where we *lack* privilege, while privilege exists only for something we don't ordinarily mean by "belief" (momentary judgments). This inverts the commonsense view that I'm the authority on what I believe.

Calling this a truism is like saying "the Earth orbits the Sun, not vice versa—truism, since obviously the smaller body orbits the larger." The truth of heliocentrism doesn't make it trivial; it was a radical reframing of appearances.

The philosophical content:

The thesis does three pieces of philosophical work beyond reporting empirical findings:

1. Diagnostic: Explains why the self-knowledge debate has been stuck (everyone seeks first-person authority over the wrong target—standing attitudes rather than occurrent acts)

2. Revisionary: Requires abandoning the folk psychological assumption that "belief" picks out states we have privileged access to, which has implications for how we understand avowal, sincerity, self-deception, and rational agency

3. Explanatory: Accounts for both the phenomenology (why we feel authoritative) and the empirical data (why we confabulate) by locating them at different levels—phenomenology tracks occurrent access, confabulation occurs with standing attitudes

None of this is trivial. The objection mistakes "uses familiar materials" (the occurrent/standing distinction, confabulation data) for "reaches trivial conclusions."

---

VERDICT

The defence succeeds.

The triviality charge fails because it conflates "the materials are familiar" with "the conclusion is trivial." The thesis uses the occurrent/standing distinction to reach a *substantive and revisionary* conclusion: that first-person authority over beliefs-as-ordinarily-understood (standing attitudes) doesn't exist by any route, and the phenomenology of authority comes from conflating standing attitudes with occurrent judgments.

This contradicts the shared assumption across competing theories that self-ascription of beliefs has *some* distinctive epistemic character. Denying any epistemic asymmetry for standing attitudes—and claiming others may be systematically better interpreters—is not a truism. It's a radical claim that would require revising our understanding of avowal, sincerity, and self-knowledge.

The stipulation charge fails because the restriction to occurrent judgments does explanatory work: it accounts for why we're systematically confused (we feel authoritative about occurrent acts, misattribute this to standing states). That's not verbal fiat—it's an error theory about folk epistemology of belief.

The objection's strongest point is that the thesis could be presented less dramatically—the "inversion" rhetoric oversells. But overselling isn't the same as being trivial. The core claim remains substantive: the self-knowledge literature has been looking for first-person authority in the wrong place (standing attitudes), and recognizing this requires a revisionary understanding of what beliefs are and how we know them.

The thesis survives. It's not trivial—it's counterintuitive, which is why it *seems* trivial once stated (like many good philosophical theses). The test is whether it requires revising our theoretical commitments, and it does: it requires denying that any proposed mechanism (introspection, rational reflection, transparency) delivers first-person authority over standing attitudes.

Repair candidates

Promise 4+, failed on ONE locatable flaw — usually scope or framing, with the narrower version already written out. Often the richest vein.

R1. Moran's agentialism and the Gopnik-Carruthers interpretivist view are both correct but about different attitude types: we know our avowed normative commitments (beliefs, intentions) through deliberative transparent self-constitution, but our motivational and affective attitudes (desires, fears, implicit biases) only through interpretation, revealing that 'attitude' is not a natural kind.

Scores
promise 4/5 · residual 4/5 · worst 4/5 · dead
Move · Target
instability — The assumption shared across the debate that there should be a unified account of self-knowledge for all propositional attitudes
Sketch

The debate presumes that whatever mechanism explains self-knowledge of beliefs should explain self-knowledge of desires, implicit attitudes, emotions, etc. But this unity assumption makes both positions unstable. Agentialists handle belief well (through transparency to reasons) but struggle with attitudes that aren't reason-responsive or deliberatively accessible. Interpretivists handle implicit attitudes and confabulated motivations well but make belief-ascription mysteriously third-personal when it feels deliberative. The instability appears when either view is pressed to generalize: agentialism about desires becomes voluntarism; interpretivism about belief makes Moore-paradoxical assertions ('I believe p but p is false') merely empirically odd rather than rationally incoherent. The key premise is that what makes belief special is its constitutive connection to truth and reasons, which other attitudes lack, and this metaphysical difference grounds an epistemological one.

Appraiser (blind)
The pluralist solution that different attitude types require different epistemologies could genuinely reorient the debate's framing assumptions.
Objections

  • COUNTEREXAMPLE — landed 4/5, unanswered. Carruthers' stratified position already incorporates the thesis's proposed solution; the defence argued his boundary is drawn wrongly but this transforms instability-revelation into substantive disagreement
  • TRIVIAL — landed 4/5, unanswered. Major participants already accept heterogeneous mechanisms with principled grounds (Moran's deliberative stance, Carruthers' computational architecture); the defence claimed these grounds are inadequate but could not show instability rather than mere disagreement
  • EQUIVOCATION — landed 2/5, answered. The defence successfully showed the thesis runs consistently on the theoretical reading with metaphysical difference explaining epistemic diversity, not vice versa

Interpretivists and agentialists draw the boundaries between transparent and interpretive self-knowledge differently than metaphysically optimal: beliefs and intentions should be individuated by their constitutive aim at truth/practical correctness, which grounds deliberative transparency, while desires and emotions lack this aim and require interpretation—a principled metaphysical basis that better explains the epistemic heterogeneity both positions already accept

full exchange (10 turns)

KILLER (MISATTRIBUTION)

ATTEMPT. The thesis claims to identify a "shared assumption" across "the debate" that there should be a unified account of self-knowledge for all propositional attitudes, and presents this as the source of instability in both Moran's and the Gopnik-Carruthers positions. However, the interpretivist tradition—particularly Gopnik and Carruthers—explicitly does NOT assume unity across attitude types. Carruthers' model distinguishes sharply between different cognitive systems and their accessibility: System 2 propositional attitudes may be more transparent while System 1 outputs require interpretation. Gopnik's theory-theory allows that different mental states might be known through different sub-theories or modules. The interpretivist framework is precisely built to accommodate heterogeneity in self-knowledge mechanisms—that's why it appeals to the same theory-building resources that handle the diversity of knowledge about others and the external world. The thesis attacks a uniformity assumption that interpretivists explicitly reject, making this a case where the critical target—the alleged shared premise—doesn't actually characterize one of the named positions.

STRENGTH: 4/5 — This is a serious problem. If interpretivists don't hold the unity assumption, then the thesis cannot show their view is "unstable" by pointing to diversity in attitude types, since accommodating such diversity is a design feature of interpretivism, not a bug.

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE

The objection misreads what "unified account" means in the thesis. The claim is not that interpretivists demand identical mechanisms for every attitude, but that they offer a single *explanatory framework*—interpretation via theory-theory or simulation—that purports to cover self-knowledge as such. This is unity at the framework level, not the mechanism level.

Carruthers' System 1/System 2 distinction and Gopnik's modular sub-theories are variations *within* the interpretivist framework. They still treat all self-knowledge as fundamentally third-personal inference from evidence, whether that evidence comes from introspection-as-inner-perception or behavioral observation. The framework remains: you know your own mind the same basic way you know others' minds—through interpretive theory-building.

The instability emerges precisely here. When interpretivists apply this framework to beliefs—even "System 2" beliefs—they must treat first-person belief-ascription as empirical hypothesis formation. But this makes the Moorean incoherence of "I believe p but not-p" merely a psychological oddity rather than a rational failure. As the thesis notes, this is the telltale sign: interpretivism cannot distinguish the *rational* status of first-person doxastic authority from mere empirical reliability.

The thesis identifies the real shared assumption: that whatever explains self-knowledge of paradigm mental states (beliefs for agentialists, desires for interpretivists) should extend to all propositional attitudes. Interpretivists assume their framework, which handles desires and implicit attitudes well, should scale up to belief. The unity assumption is about *framework generalization*, not mechanism identity.

VERDICT

The defence fails, though not completely.

The reframing of "unity" as framework-level rather than mechanism-level has some purchase. There is a sense in which interpretivism offers a single explanatory genus (interpretation/inference from evidence) even while allowing species variation.

But the defence cannot overcome the core problem: interpretivists like Carruthers explicitly argue that different attitude types are known through genuinely different processes—not just different applications of interpretation, but different epistemic relations altogether. Carruthers allows that some System 2 states might be accessible through something closer to transparency, while System 1 requires interpretation. This isn't "variations within interpretivism"—it's a pluralist position that already incorporates the thesis's proposed solution.

The thesis claims to reveal instability by showing interpretivists *must* either accept heterogeneity (conceding to the thesis) or face problems with belief. But if interpretivists already accept heterogeneity, there's no instability to reveal—just disagreement about where to draw the lines.

The objection succeeds: the thesis misattributes a uniformity assumption to a position that was built precisely to avoid it.

KILLER (COUNTEREXAMPLE)

ATTEMPT. Carruthers' 2011 *The Opacity of Mind* provides a concrete counterexample to the thesis's central claim about what interpretivists assume. Carruthers explicitly argues that:

(1) Conscious propositional attitudes (System 2 judgments) are known through something like direct access or transparency—when I consciously judge that p, I know this non-interpretively.

(2) Unconscious attitudes, standing beliefs, desires, and implicit biases require interpretive self-knowledge—I must infer them from behavioral evidence and mental rehearsals.

(3) This heterogeneity is a *feature* of his interpretivist position, not a concession forced by problems.

This directly contradicts the thesis's claim that interpretivists share an assumption requiring "a unified account of self-knowledge for all propositional attitudes." Carruthers offers precisely the kind of split the thesis proposes—transparent access for some attitudes, interpretation for others—while remaining an interpretivist about the architecture of self-knowledge generally.

The thesis claims both views become "unstable when pressed to generalize," but Carruthers explicitly *refuses* to generalize his interpretive model to conscious judgments. He's not unstable; he's already occupying the supposedly stable ground the thesis claims to discover. The thesis cannot demonstrate instability in a position that already incorporates the proposed solution.

STRENGTH: 4/5 — This significantly undermines the thesis. If a leading interpretivist already accepts the heterogeneity the thesis presents as its novel insight, then the thesis hasn't identified an overlooked instability but rather restated an existing position while mischaracterizing it as revealing hidden problems.

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE

The objection trades on an ambiguity in Carruthers' position that actually supports rather than refutes the thesis. Carruthers' (1) is not a genuine acceptance of transparency but a terminological concession that conceals continued interpretivism.

When Carruthers says conscious System 2 judgments are known "through something like direct access or transparency," the crucial phrase is "something like." Examine what he actually means: even for conscious judgments, the self-knowledge involves the global broadcast of a contentful state that is then *available* to interpretive systems. The "directness" is just informational availability, not the deliberative-constitutive relation Moran describes.

For Moran, transparency means: I know my belief that p by settling whether p through first-order deliberation about reasons. The epistemic and constitutive orders coincide—my answering the world-directed question *makes* my attitude what it is. For Carruthers, even conscious judgments are already-formed states that become known when broadcast to monitoring systems. This remains interpretive—it's just interpretation of highly accessible inner speech rather than opaque behavioral patterns.

The proof: Carruthers' account still cannot explain Moorean incoherence as *rational* rather than merely psychological. On his view, "I judge that p but p is false" should be possible if the monitoring system happens to detect both the judgment and contrary evidence. The rational authority distinctive of first-person belief ascription—the kind that makes Moore-paradoxical assertions rationally defective, not just empirically odd—requires that belief-formation and belief-ascription share a single deliberative process, which Carruthers denies.

So Carruthers hasn't already occupied the stable ground. He's verbally split the difference while keeping everything in the interpretivist framework. The thesis's claim stands: genuine transparency (deliberative self-constitution) applies to beliefs/intentions, while interpretation applies to desires/implicit attitudes, and this distinction cannot be captured by interpretivism even when it stratifies into System 1/System 2.

VERDICT

The defence fails.

The defence attempts to distinguish "genuine transparency" (Moranian deliberative self-constitution) from Carruthers' "mere informational availability." This distinction is real and important. But it doesn't save the thesis from the objection.

Here's why: The thesis explicitly claims to reveal *instability* in the interpretivist position—that interpretivists are committed to a unity assumption that creates problems when generalized. But Carruthers' position, whatever we call it, already stratifies self-knowledge by attitude type. Whether his account of conscious judgments counts as "genuine transparency" is a substantive disagreement, not evidence of instability.

The thesis needed to show that interpretivists are *forced by their commitments* to apply their framework uniformly, creating pressure that destabilizes the view. Instead, we find a prominent interpretivist who explicitly declines to apply his interpretive model to all attitudes. The defence responds: "Yes, but he's doing it wrong—that's not real transparency."

This transforms the thesis from revealing hidden instability into making a substantive claim that Carruthers' stratified position is inadequate. That's a different move entirely. You can't demonstrate that a position is *unstable* by showing that its stable stratification doesn't match your preferred stratification.

The Moorean point in the defence has force as an independent objection to Carruthers, but it doesn't establish instability—it argues his boundary is drawn wrongly. The thesis claimed both positions become unstable when pressed to generalize. Carruthers doesn't press to generalize. No instability demonstrated.

The objection succeeds.

KILLER (TRIVIAL)

ATTEMPT. The thesis presents itself as revealing an overlooked instability in the debate, but the core insight—that different attitude types require different self-knowledge mechanisms—is already well-established in the literature and explicitly embraced by major participants. Carruthers' *The Opacity of Mind* (2011) builds heterogeneity into interpretivism from the ground up, distinguishing transparent conscious judgments from opaque standing attitudes. Moran himself restricts transparency to reason-responsive attitudes in *Authority and Estrangement* (2001), explicitly noting that desires and emotions may require therapeutic or interpretive access. Cassam's "Transparency and Self-Knowledge" (2014) distinguishes constitutive from enabling conditions of self-knowledge precisely to handle different attitude types. Even early theory-theorists like Gopnik acknowledged different "theories" might govern different mental state categories.

The thesis claims to expose a "shared assumption" that creates instability, but the assumption it identifies—that all attitudes need uniform treatment—is neither shared nor assumed. It's a strawman. The actual debate concerns *where* to draw the lines and *why*, not whether lines exist. The thesis redescribes this existing pluralist landscape as if discovering it reveals hidden problems, when it's actually the stable consensus position that emerged from earlier, genuinely uniform accounts (like pure inner sense or pure rationalism) that *were* unstable.

The "insight" that 'attitude' isn't a natural kind is standard philosophical psychology since at least the 1990s.

STRENGTH: 4/5 — This seriously damages the thesis. If the key participants already accept heterogeneous self-knowledge mechanisms for different attitudes, then the thesis isn't revealing instability but rather restating the current state of play while mischaracterizing it as a novel discovery. The move from "unified mechanism" to "unified framework" in the defence shows the thesis retreating to progressively weaker claims about what counts as problematic unity. The substantive claim that Carruthers draws the boundary wrongly is legitimate philosophy, but it's not an *instability* revelation—it's a standard disagreement within an already-pluralist debate.

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE

The objection conflates *accepting heterogeneity under pressure* with *having a principled basis for it*. Yes, sophisticated participants now acknowledge different mechanisms for different attitudes—but this is a *symptom* of the instability the thesis diagnoses, not evidence against it.

Consider the dialectical history. Classical interpretivism (early Gopnik, Carruthers pre-2011) and classical agentialism (Evans' transparency, early Moran) both began with genuinely unified accounts that *did* aspire to cover all propositional attitudes. The heterogeneity the objection cites emerged as a series of *ad hoc retreats* when problems mounted:

- Interpretivists struggled with Moorean phenomena and the rational authority of belief, so they carved out "conscious judgments" as special
- Agentialists struggled with implicit bias and emotion, so they restricted transparency to "reason-responsive" attitudes
- Both added qualifications, distinctions, and scope restrictions

But here's the instability: neither framework can explain *why* the boundary falls where it does from within its own resources.

For Carruthers, why should System 2 conscious judgments get "something like" transparency while System 1 beliefs require interpretation? His answer appeals to global workspace architecture—but this is a *computational* distinction (broadcast vs. non-broadcast), not a *rational* one. It cannot explain why Moore-paradoxical assertions are rationally incoherent rather than just computationally awkward. The interpretivist framework lacks the resources to distinguish rational authority from reliable access.

For Moran, why should only "reason-responsive" attitudes get transparency? His answer appeals to deliberative answerability—but desires and emotions *are* reason-responsive in many cases (I can deliberate about whether to want something, whether fear is warranted). The restriction becomes arbitrary without a principled metaphysical story about which attitudes have "constitutive connection to truth and reasons."

The thesis provides what both positions lack: a *principled metaphysical basis* for the boundary. Beliefs and intentions are distinguished by their constitutive aim at truth/practical reasoning, which grounds a distinctive deliberative epistemology. Desires and emotions lack this aim, which is why they require interpretation. This isn't "standard philosophical psychology since the 1990s"—it's a specific metaphysical claim about attitude individuation that *explains* rather than merely *accommodates* the heterogeneity.

The objection mistakes descriptive consensus (different attitudes, different mechanisms) for explanatory adequacy. The instability is precisely that both positions accept heterogeneity without being able to justify it from their foundational commitments. Interpretivism is fundamentally about third-personal inference; agentialism is fundamentally about first-personal deliberation. Neither framework contains the resources to explain why some attitudes get one treatment and others get another—they just add epicycles when pressed.

The thesis doesn't merely restate pluralism. It diagnoses why existing pluralism is unprincipled, and offers a metaphysical foundation (attitude individuation by constitutive aim) that makes the boundary non-arbitrary.

---

VERDICT

The defence fails.

The historical narrative has some truth—early versions of both positions were more uniform—but the defence cannot establish that current heterogeneity is *unprincipled* rather than *principled*.

The claim that "neither framework can explain why the boundary falls where it does from within its own resources" is too strong. Moran's restriction to reason-responsive attitudes is not arbitrary—it flows directly from his core idea that self-knowledge involves taking a deliberative stance toward reasons. Attitudes that cannot be settled by deliberating about reasons simply fall outside the scope of this mechanism. That's not an ad hoc retreat; it's a principled limitation following from the nature of deliberative transparency.

Similarly, Carruthers' computational story (global broadcast) is not obviously inferior to the thesis's metaphysical story (constitutive aim). Both are principled bases for drawing boundaries. The defence asserts that computational distinctions "cannot explain" rational authority, but this is just restating the substantive disagreement—Carruthers would deny that rational authority requires anything beyond the right computational architecture.

The critical error: The defence transforms "instability" into "lacks the thesis's preferred foundation." A position is unstable when its commitments pull in contradictory directions, forcing incoherence or endless retreat. A position is merely *different* when it draws boundaries on grounds other than yours.

The objection succeeds because the thesis cannot show that Moran's or Carruthers' current positions are *unstable*—pulled apart by internal tensions. Instead, it shows they draw boundaries differently than the thesis proposes, using different foundational resources (deliberative stance vs. constitutive aim; computational architecture vs. metaphysical aim). That's a substantive philosophical disagreement, not a revealed instability.

The thesis claimed to expose hidden problems that force both positions toward its solution. Instead, it offers one solution among others to an openly acknowledged need for heterogeneity—a need both positions address in their own terms.

The objection succeeds. The thesis mischaracterizes a substantive disagreement about how to ground pluralism as a revelation of instability in positions that lack principled grounds for pluralism.

KILLER (EQUIVOCATION)

ATTEMPT

The thesis equivocates on "attitude" between a folk-psychological category and a theoretically-regimented kind. The argument is plausible only if "attitude" means the folk category (beliefs, desires, fears as ordinarily individuated), but interesting only if it means a theoretical kind that could ground unified explanatory projects.

The key equivocation occurs in the conclusion that "'attitude' is not a natural kind." This is plausible when "attitude" means the heterogeneous folk category—of course ordinary language lumps together disparate psychological phenomena. But it's interesting only if "attitude" refers to what philosophers and cognitive scientists have been theorizing about—propositional attitudes as a theoretical posit that might admit unified treatment.

The argument needs both readings: It needs the folk reading to make the diversity claim obvious (we already know beliefs differ from desires in folk psychology), and it needs the theoretical reading to make the conclusion significant (challenging ongoing research programs that treat propositional attitudes as an explanatory kind).

But on the folk reading, the thesis is trivial—nobody thought "attitude" in ordinary language picked out a natural kind. On the theoretical reading, the thesis is implausible—the argument doesn't show that theoretically-regimented propositional attitudes (states with correctness conditions, functional roles in practical reasoning, etc.) lack unity, only that they have epistemically diverse access conditions. Epistemic diversity doesn't entail metaphysical heterogeneity—we know about electrons and baseballs differently, but both are physical objects.

The weak point is the implicit premise that epistemic diversity (different self-knowledge mechanisms) entails metaphysical disunity (not a natural kind). This only works by sliding between readings of "attitude."

STRENGTH: 2/5

The attack has some force but is ultimately weak. While there is a distinction between folk and theoretical uses of "attitude," the thesis can run its argument on the theoretical reading alone. The claim is that even theoretically-regimented propositional attitudes—the philosopher's notion—split into metaphysically distinct kinds based on their constitutive aims. The move from epistemic diversity to metaphysical heterogeneity, while needing defense, isn't pure equivocation—it's a substantive inference that the thesis makes explicit (different constitutive aims ground different epistemologies). The real issues with this thesis lie elsewhere (misattribution, triviality), not in equivocation on "attitude."

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE

The objection mislocates the argument's structure. The thesis does not *infer* metaphysical heterogeneity from epistemic diversity—it *explains* epistemic diversity by metaphysical heterogeneity. The direction of argument runs the opposite way from what the objection claims.

The thesis's explicit reasoning is: beliefs and intentions have a constitutive aim at truth/practical correctness that other attitudes lack → this metaphysical difference grounds different epistemologies → therefore agentialism works for one kind, interpretivism for another. The metaphysical claim is the premise, not the conclusion inferred from epistemic diversity.

On "attitude" as theoretical posit: The thesis challenges precisely the theoretical regimentation that treats propositional attitudes as a unified explanatory kind. Contemporary philosophy of mind and cognitive science routinely theorize about "propositional attitudes" as if they form a natural kind admitting systematic treatment—unified functional roles, unified representational format, unified computational architecture. The thesis argues this regimentation is mistaken because it papers over a metaphysically significant difference.

The move is not equivocation but theoretical revisionism: "propositional attitude" as currently used in theory encompasses metaphysically heterogeneous kinds that should be separated. This is substantive, not trivial. Compare: discovering that "jade" refers to two mineralogically distinct substances (jadeite and nephrite) wasn't trivial despite jade being a folk category—it revealed that what seemed like a unified kind for theoretical purposes was actually heterogeneous.

The electrons/baseballs analogy fails. We know them differently because of *our* epistemic limitations (scale, observational capacities), not because of metaphysical differences in the objects. But the thesis claims the epistemic difference for attitudes flows from *their* metaphysical nature—beliefs constitutively aim at truth in a way desires don't, making deliberative transparency appropriate for one but not the other. The epistemic diversity is not merely about access conditions but about what *kind* of thing is being accessed.

The theoretical reading makes the thesis both non-trivial and coherent: it challenges the working assumption in cognitive science and philosophy of mind that propositional attitudes form a theoretically unified domain, arguing instead for a fundamental split that existing research programs obscure.

---

VERDICT

The defence succeeds.

The objection claimed the thesis equivocates between folk and theoretical readings of "attitude," being trivial on one and implausible on the other. But the defence correctly identifies that the thesis operates consistently on the theoretical reading and makes a substantive claim: that the theoretical category "propositional attitude" is gerrymandered, grouping together metaphysically heterogeneous kinds.

The key point about argument direction is decisive. The objection accused the thesis of invalidly inferring metaphysical heterogeneity from epistemic diversity. But the thesis's actual structure is: metaphysical difference (constitutive aims) → epistemic difference (access methods). This is not equivocation but explanation. Whether the explanation *works* is a different question—but there's no equivocation in the structure.

The jade analogy is apt. Theoretical revisionism that splits an apparently unified kind into heterogeneous natural kinds is substantive philosophy of science, not trivial wordplay. The thesis proposes that "propositional attitude" is like "jade"—a label that groups together things that should be theoretically distinguished.

The electrons/baseballs response is effective. The objection's analogy fails because epistemic diversity from observer limitations (electrons vs. baseballs) differs from epistemic diversity grounded in object-side metaphysical differences (beliefs vs. desires). The thesis claims the latter.

The objection does not succeed. The thesis is not guilty of equivocation—it makes a consistent theoretical claim that may be wrong but is not confused about what "attitude" means.

KILLER (UNFALSIFIABLE)

ATTEMPT

The thesis is unfalsifiable because it can reclassify any apparent counterexample by redefining which attitudes count as "normative commitments" versus "motivational/affective attitudes."

Consider: If someone demonstrates that desires are actually known through deliberative transparency (I know what I want by deliberating about what's worth wanting), the thesis can respond that these are really "normative commitments about value" rather than "motivational attitudes." If someone shows that beliefs require interpretive access (implicit beliefs, self-deceptive beliefs), the thesis can respond that these aren't really "avowed normative commitments" but rather "sub-personal states" or "motivational attitudes masquerading as beliefs."

The weak point is the criterion for classification: what makes something a "normative commitment" versus a "motivational attitude"? The thesis says: constitutive aim at truth/reasons. But this is tested by: known through transparency or interpretation. So the classification criterion is the very thing being explained—perfect circularity that immunizes against counterexamples.

Suppose we find an attitude X that seems like a belief (propositional content, truth-evaluable) but requires interpretive access. The thesis can say: "Not a genuine normative commitment—must be motivational." Suppose we find an attitude Y that seems like a desire but is known transparently. The thesis can say: "Not a mere motivational attitude—must be a normative commitment about value."

Every apparent counterexample gets reclassified to fit the theory. The boundary between attitude types floats to wherever it needs to be to preserve the correlation between metaphysical kind and epistemic access.

STRENGTH: 3/5

This attack has genuine force but not devastating force. The thesis does face a challenge in providing independent criteria for its metaphysical classification that don't simply track the epistemic phenomena it aims to explain. The circularity concern is real: if "constitutive aim at truth" just means "the kind of thing known through transparency," then the explanation is empty.

However, the thesis can likely defend by appealing to independent philosophical work on the nature of belief versus desire (direction of fit, functional role in reasoning, etc.) that predates and is independent of debates about self-knowledge. The metaphysical distinction between attitudes with different constitutive aims has substantial philosophical literature behind it that doesn't depend on epistemic access methods.

The attack succeeds in identifying a genuine vulnerability—the thesis needs to show its metaphysical categories are independently motivated—but doesn't definitively establish unfalsifiability.

DEFENDER

[DEFENDER] BEST DEFENCE

The objection confuses explanatory power with circularity. Yes, the thesis correlates metaphysical kinds with epistemic access methods—but the metaphysical classification has independent theoretical grounding that predates and is separable from the epistemic correlation.

The distinction between beliefs/intentions and desires/emotions based on constitutive aims is not invented for this thesis. It comes from:

Direction of fit (Anscombe, Searle): Beliefs aim to fit the world; desires aim to make the world fit them. This is a metaphysical distinction about correctness conditions, established independently of how we know our own attitudes.

Functional role (Fodor, Stalnaker): Beliefs combine with desires to produce intentions; they play different inferential roles in practical reasoning. This architectural difference is theoretically motivated by cognitive science, not by epistemic access.

Normative standards: Beliefs are criticizable for irrationality if they conflict with evidence; desires are not criticizable in the same way for conflicting with facts about what's desirable. This normative difference is recognized across metaethics and epistemology.

Phenomenological character (Strawson, Horgan & Tienson): Belief-formation feels like recognizing how things are; desire-formation feels like being drawn toward how things might be. This is pre-theoretical phenomenology, not post-hoc classification.

These independent theoretical resources allow non-circular classification. When we find an attitude X that's truth-evaluable, combines with desires to yield intentions, is criticizable by evidential standards, and feels like recognizing how things are—but requires interpretive access—this is a *surprising result* that needs explanation, not a reclassification. The thesis would say: implicit beliefs are still beliefs metaphysically (they have all the functional/normative features) but require interpretation because they're not formed through deliberation. That's an explanatory claim, not circular redefinition.

Similarly, if we find an attitude Y that's known through transparency but has desire-like functional role and world-to-mind direction of fit, the thesis predicts it's not a normative commitment—and we can test this against the independent criteria. If it fails those criteria, that's evidence against the thesis, not reclassification to save it.

The falsifiability test: Find an attitude that clearly has belief's metaphysical profile (truth-aim, evidence-responsiveness, mind-to-world fit, combines with desires to yield intentions) but is systematically accessible only through interpretation in normal, non-self-deceptive cases. Or find an attitude with desire's profile (world-to-mind fit, not evidence-criticizable, motivational role) that's systematically accessible only through deliberative transparency. Either would challenge the thesis.

The thesis is falsifiable because its metaphysical categories are independently testable against the substantial philosophical literature on attitude individuation, and its epistemic predictions can then be checked against those independently-established categories.

---

VERDICT

The defence succeeds.

The objection claimed the thesis is unfalsifiable because it can reclassify counterexamples using the very epistemic features it aims to explain. But the defence demonstrates that the metaphysical classification (normative commitments vs. motivational attitudes) has independent theoretical grounding in:

1. Direction of fit theory (Anscombe, Searle)
2. Functional role semantics (Fodor, Stalnaker)
3. Normative epistemology (standards of criticism)
4. Phenomenological character

These resources allow us to classify attitudes as beliefs or desires *independently* of how we know them. The thesis then makes a *testable prediction*: attitudes with belief's metaphysical profile will be knowable through transparency; attitudes with desire's profile will require interpretation.

The defence provides clear falsification conditions: find attitudes with belief's independent profile that systematically require interpretation, or attitudes with desire's profile systematically accessible through transparency. These are empirical/philosophical tests that don't depend on circular reclassification.

The implicit beliefs case shows this working correctly: implicit beliefs retain belief's metaphysical profile (truth-aim, evidential standards) but require interpretation—the thesis *explains* this by saying they're not formed deliberatively, rather than reclassifying them as non-beliefs. This is explanatory work, not immunization.

The objection does not succeed. The thesis makes falsifiable predictions by correlating independently-established metaphysical categories with epistemic access methods. Whether those predictions are *correct* is open to test, but the structure is not circular or unfalsifiable.

R2. The interpretive theorists are right that we access our attitudes through interpretation, but wrong to think this is 'much as we read others' — self-interpretation is necessarily corrupted by the very authority they're trying to explain away.

Scores
promise 4/5 · residual 4/5 · worst 4/5 · wounded
Move · Target
instability — Carruthers and Gopnik's claim that self-interpretation and other-interpretation are symmetric processes drawing on parallel evidence bases.
Sketch

Carruthers and Gopnik claim self-knowledge is interpretive and symmetric with other-knowledge. But interpretation of others works because their self-ascriptions are relatively fixed data points — when you tell me you believe p, I can treat this as evidence even while interpreting your other behavior. Self-interpretation cannot work this way because my own self-ascription is precisely what's in question. If I'm interpreting my behavior to figure out whether I believe p, and then I self-ascribe p, this ascription can't serve as independent evidence in my interpretation — it's the output, not an input. This means either (a) self-interpretation must proceed without the most direct evidence others have about me, making it asymmetrically worse than other-interpretation, or (b) self-ascriptions must have some non-interpretive status that makes them usable as interpretive data, which reintroduces first-person authority. The interpretive view is unstable: it either collapses into skepticism about self-knowledge or smuggles back the authority it denies.

Appraiser (blind)
The bootstrapping problem for self-interpretation is sharp and creates genuine instability for the interpretivist position.
Objections
  • MISATTRIBUTION — landed 4/5, unanswered. Carruthers explicitly accepts evidential asymmetry favoring third-person in some respects, which preempts rather than contradicts the thesis's discovery
  • PROVES TOO MUCH — landed 2/5, answered. The synchronic/diachronic distinction successfully separates vicious circularity from legitimate iterative revision
  • COUNTEREXAMPLE — landed 2/5, answered. Reactions to self-ascriptions are behavioral evidence, not the self-ascription serving as its own evidence
  • TRIVIAL — landed 4/5, unanswered. The thesis identifies a genuine structural problem but oversells it as instability when interpretivists can accept asymmetry without abandoning their core view
  • EQUIVOCATION — landed 1/5, answered. No equivocation exists; the thesis consistently concerns evidential independence throughout
⚑ Target attribution disputed — Carruthers explicitly accepts evidential asymmetry favoring third-person in some respects, which preempts rather than contradicts the thesis's discovery Check this yourself: it is a claim about who holds what, made from recall.
🔧 Survives as

Interpretive theories are more revisionary than their rhetoric suggests: self-interpretation lacks the synchronous fixed-point role that self-ascriptions play in other-interpretation, making the processes structurally disanalogous in ways that undermine the 'much as we read others' framing

Flaw

The misattribution and triviality objections together show the thesis attacks a symmetry claim stronger than the targets hold, and frames a predictable cost of interpretivism as a view-collapsing instability

full exchange (10 turns)

KILLER (MISATTRIBUTION)
