The thesis survives, though it would benefit from explicitly marking this distinction between first-order formation and second-order discovery.

R4. First-person authority comes apart into two independent phenomena—testimonial privilege (others defer to our self-reports) and agential authority (we settle what we believe by deciding what to believe)—and the interpretive turn undermines only the former.

Scores
promise 4/5 · residual 5/5 · worst 5/5 · dead
Move · Target
distinction — Both Moran (who runs testimonial and agential authority together) and Carruthers (who thinks undermining one undermines the other)
Sketch

Both defenders and critics of first-person authority treat it as a unified phenomenon requiring a unified explanation. But testimonial privilege (that others treat my 'I believe P' as especially reliable evidence about my mental states) and agential authority (that I determine what I believe through deliberation rather than self-observation) are actually independent. The interpretive turn successfully explains away testimonial privilege as a useful but defeasible heuristic—we're not actually more reliable self-interpreters, just more motivated ones with better access to our own behavioral history. But agential authority survives because it doesn't require reliable self-knowledge at all; it requires only that the activity of deliberating about P (rather than observing myself) can constitute settling whether I believe P. Moran is half-right: the deliberative stance does give us a distinctive authority, but not because it provides superior epistemic access—rather because deliberation is itself belief-fixing rather than belief-discovering.

Appraiser (blind)
Separating testimonial from agential authority could resolve apparent contradictions and clarify what survives interpretivism.

full exchange (10 turns)

KILLER (MISATTRIBUTION)

ATTEMPT. The thesis misattributes positions to both named targets. Moran (in *Authority and Estrangement*, 2001) explicitly distinguishes between different aspects of first-person authority and does not run testimonial and agential authority together as claimed. His account centers precisely on the difference between the transparency method (deliberating about P to answer "Do I believe P?") and observational/interpretive methods—this IS the distinction between agential and testimonial dimensions. He argues the transparency method grounds a distinctive rational authority, not that all forms of first-person authority have the same source. Carruthers (in "How We Know Our Own Minds," 2011) does argue against first-person authority generally, but not by claiming testimonial and agential authority stand or fall together. His interpretive sensory-access theory denies we have special access of ANY kind, treating both self-attribution mechanisms as interpretive. He doesn't argue "undermining one undermines the other"—he argues both are already undermined by the same interpretive architecture. The thesis attacks a conflation neither theorist makes: Moran already draws the distinction the thesis claims to introduce, and Carruthers rejects both forms independently rather than treating them as a package.

STRENGTH: 4/5 — This is a serious problem. The thesis presents its central distinction as correcting an error both targets make, but Moran's entire framework depends on something very like this distinction, making the thesis's novelty claim questionable.

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE

The objection trades on an ambiguity about what "running together" means and misses the dialectical structure of the thesis.

On Moran: Yes, Moran distinguishes the transparency method from observational methods. But distinguishing *methods* is not the same as distinguishing *sources of authority*. Moran treats transparency as grounding BOTH dimensions: it explains both why I have rational/agential authority (I settle what to believe through deliberation) AND why my self-reports have testimonial privilege (transparency gives me epistemic access that grounds reliability). The thesis's point is that these are *metaphysically independent*—one could have agential authority without testimonial privilege, or vice versa. Moran never considers that the transparency method might ground agential authority while failing to ground testimonial privilege. His argument assumes that if transparency gives me rational authority over my beliefs, this also explains the epistemic authority of my self-reports. The thesis breaks this package apart: transparency might constitute belief-fixation (agential) without providing superior epistemic access (testimonial). That Moran distinguishes methods doesn't mean he recognizes the independence of the phenomena those methods allegedly ground.

On Carruthers: The objection actually supports the thesis. If Carruthers "rejects both forms independently," that's precisely because he treats undermining testimonial privilege (showing self-interpretation is no more reliable) as ALSO undermining agential authority. He doesn't see that you could deny special epistemic access while preserving the constitutive role of deliberation. The thesis's claim is that Carruthers thinks the interpretive architecture undermines everything about first-person authority—he doesn't recognize that agential authority might survive even if we're just interpreters.

The deeper point: The thesis isn't claiming to introduce the transparency/observation distinction. It's claiming that even those who recognize different *methods* still treat first-person authority as a unified *explanandum* requiring a unified explanation, rather than seeing testimonial and agential authority as genuinely separable phenomena that might have completely different statuses.

VERDICT

The defence fails for Moran, and this severely damages the thesis.

The objection is correct that Moran's framework already contains the resources to separate what the thesis claims to separate. More damagingly: Moran explicitly argues (especially in Chapter 3 of *Authority and Estrangement*) that transparency provides a *rational* or *deliberative* authority that is NOT primarily epistemic. He already recognizes that the authority of the transparency method doesn't rest on it being a superior route to self-knowledge in the observational sense. When he says transparency gives us authority, he means something much closer to what the thesis calls "agential authority"—the authority to settle what we believe through deliberation rather than discovery.

The thesis presents as novel a separation that Moran's account already accommodates, perhaps even requires. The claim that Moran "runs testimonial and agential authority together" cannot survive careful reading of his distinction between *rational* authority (roughly: agential) and *epistemic* authority (roughly: testimonial), and his argument that transparency grounds the former in a way that doesn't reduce to the latter.

The defence regarding Carruthers has more force—he may indeed fail to see that interpretive architecture could undermine testimonial privilege while leaving agential authority intact. But losing the Moran case is fatal: if the thesis's central distinction is already present in the major defender of first-person authority, the thesis's claim to be revealing an overlooked independence collapses.

KILLER (COUNTEREXAMPLE)

ATTEMPT.

Consider the case of belief-formation through hypnotic suggestion. A hypnotist tells you "You will believe that penguins can fly" and post-hypnotic suggestion succeeds. According to the thesis, agential authority requires only that "the activity of deliberating about P (rather than observing myself) can constitute settling whether I believe P." But here we have a counterexample: you can engage in deliberation about whether penguins fly (deliberating about P, not observing yourself), and this activity does constitute settling whether you believe it (the deliberation fixes the belief via suggestion), yet you clearly lack agential authority. The problem is that deliberation is being causally manipulated rather than rationally responsive. This shows the thesis's characterization of agential authority is too thin—it requires more than deliberation constituting belief-fixation; it requires the RIGHT KIND of constitutive relationship. The thesis claims agential authority "doesn't require reliable self-knowledge at all; it requires only that the activity of deliberating about P...can constitute settling whether I believe P." But the hypnosis case shows that this "only" condition is insufficient. We need to add something about rational control, autonomy, or reasons-responsiveness—precisely the kinds of conditions that might reintroduce epistemic requirements the thesis wants to avoid. The weak point is the claim that constitutive belief-fixation through deliberation is sufficient for agential authority.

STRENGTH: 3/5 — A genuine problem requiring an answer. The thesis needs to explain what distinguishes genuine agential authority from cases where deliberation constitutively fixes belief through non-rational mechanisms, and any plausible answer may reintroduce complications the thesis hoped to avoid.

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE

The hypnosis case fails because it's not actually a case of deliberation constituting belief-fixation—it's a case of hypnotic suggestion *bypassing* deliberation while creating the phenomenology of deliberation.

The key distinction: In genuine deliberation, the transition from considering reasons about P to believing P occurs *in virtue of* those reasons and their rational relations. The deliberative activity itself—weighing whether penguins can fly by considering evidence about avian biology, flight mechanics, etc.—is what settles the belief. In the hypnosis case, the transition occurs *in virtue of* the hypnotic suggestion, not in virtue of the rational activity. The deliberation is epiphenomenal window-dressing; the real work is done by the suggestion. You could have the same belief-fixation without the deliberative activity (direct suggestion: "believe it now"), proving the deliberation isn't doing the constitutive work.

Test for constitution: Does removing the deliberative activity while holding other factors fixed prevent belief-fixation? In genuine agential authority: yes—if I don't deliberate about whether P, I don't thereby settle whether I believe P. In hypnosis: no—the suggestion fixes the belief regardless of whether I go through deliberative motions.

Why this doesn't reintroduce epistemic requirements: The distinction between deliberation constituting belief-fixation versus merely accompanying it doesn't require reliable self-knowledge. It requires only that the rational relations among considerations about P are actually doing the work of settling the belief. This is a metaphysical claim about what makes the belief-fixation happen, not an epistemic claim about whether I can reliably detect that it's happening. I can have agential authority (deliberation genuinely constituting my belief) while being completely unreliable at reporting whether I exercised it.

The "only" stands: The thesis's condition is sufficient once properly understood. What's required is that deliberating about P *actually constitutes* settling whether I believe P—not merely that some process labeled "deliberation" occurs while belief gets fixed by other means.

VERDICT

The defence succeeds, but reveals an important clarification the thesis needs.

The hypnosis objection initially appears powerful because it exploits an ambiguity in "deliberating about P constitutes settling whether I believe P." But the objection actually helps sharify what the thesis means: not just any process that looks phenomenologically like deliberation, but deliberation that does genuine constitutive work—where the rational activity itself is what fixes the belief.

The defence successfully shows this distinction doesn't reintroduce epistemic requirements. Whether deliberation is genuinely constitutive versus epiphenomenal is a metaphysical matter about causal-explanatory structure, not an epistemic matter requiring self-knowledge. The hypnotized subject lacks agential authority not because they can't reliably detect their own mental states, but because their "deliberation" isn't actually settling anything—the suggestion is doing all the work.

However, this does expose that the thesis's formulation needs tightening. The phrase "the activity of deliberating about P...can constitute settling whether I believe P" is too permissive as stated. It should specify that deliberation *in virtue of its rational structure* constitutes belief-fixation, or that the rational relations among considerations about P are what explain the belief-formation. This blocks the hypnosis case without importing epistemic conditions.

The core claim survives: agential authority requires a certain metaphysical relationship between deliberation and belief-fixation, not reliable epistemic access to one's mental states. The counterexample fails.

KILLER (TRIVIAL)

ATTEMPT. The thesis presents its central distinction as though it reveals something philosophically substantial, but it's actually just stipulating two different meanings for the phrase "first-person authority" and observing that arguments against one don't touch the other. This is trivial verbal repackaging.

The "discovery" amounts to: "When we say someone has 'authority' about their beliefs, we might mean (a) their reports are reliable, or (b) they control what they believe through deliberation." Well, yes—these are just different senses of "authority" (epistemic vs. agential/practical). Pointing out that undermining epistemic authority doesn't undermine practical authority is like pointing out that showing someone isn't an "authority on penguins" (expert) doesn't show they lack "authority over penguins" (control). It's a verbal disambiguation, not a philosophical insight.

The thesis dresses this up as revealing that "first-person authority comes apart into two independent phenomena," but there's no contested claim here. Obviously the reliability of self-reports and the capacity for self-determination are different things. The interpretive turn was always aimed at epistemic privilege—the idea that we have special *epistemic access* to our minds. It never claimed to undermine the truism that deliberation can fix beliefs. The thesis treats as a dramatic discovery what's actually just the observation that one argument doesn't prove everything, wrapped in technical terminology about "testimonial" vs. "agential" authority.

The weak point: the claim that these are "two independent phenomena" that the literature mistakenly runs together, when really they're just two different things we might mean by "authority," obviously distinct to anyone who thinks for a moment.

STRENGTH: 2/5 — This has some force as a deflation, but probably doesn't succeed. The thesis does make a substantive claim: that major theorists treat first-person authority as requiring a unified explanation when the phenomena are genuinely separable. Even if the distinction seems obvious once stated, showing that important positions depend on conflating them would be philosophically significant. The Moran case (if it survived) would demonstrate non-triviality: if a major theory really does assume transparency must ground both dimensions together, then pulling them apart matters. The weakness is that "these are different things" isn't automatically trivial just because it's a distinction—it depends on whether the distinction does real work against real positions.

DEFENDER

[DEFENDER] BEST DEFENCE

The triviality charge confuses *conceptual obviousness* with *theoretical significance* and misses what makes a philosophical distinction substantive.

Why this isn't mere verbal disambiguation: The thesis doesn't just note that "authority" has multiple senses. It makes a substantive metaphysical claim: that agential authority can exist *even when testimonial privilege is completely absent*. This is not the truism that different words mean different things—it's the controversial claim that I can have genuine authority over my beliefs through deliberation even if I'm no more reliable than others at reporting what I believe, even if my self-interpretations are systematically biased, even if others should defer to third-person evidence over my testimony. Many theorists find this combination incoherent: how can I authoritatively settle what I believe if I don't have privileged access to what I believe?

The non-trivial work the distinction does: It breaks a widely-assumed explanatory package. The philosophical tradition (and ordinary thought) assumes: if you have authority over your beliefs in the sense of controlling them, you must also have epistemic authority about them—how could you exercise control without knowledge? The thesis claims this is false: the constitutive relationship between deliberation and belief-fixation doesn't require or entail superior epistemic access. This is a substantive metaphysical thesis about the nature of belief-formation, not a verbal observation.

Against the "obviously distinct" claim: The objection says these are "obviously distinct to anyone who thinks for a moment," but this is revisionist history. The entire first-person authority debate exists precisely because these dimensions seem deeply entangled. Descartes, introspectionist psychology, and much contemporary philosophy of mind assume that privileged control and privileged access go together—that the same facts (transparency, introspection, whatever) explain both. The interpretive turn's power comes from seeming to undermine first-person authority *wholesale* by showing we're self-interpreters. If the distinction were obvious and uncontested, this wouldn't seem threatening.

The test for non-triviality: Does accepting the distinction require revising theoretical commitments? Yes—it means the interpretive turn doesn't refute Moran-style rational authority (even if it refutes epistemic privilege), and it means defenders of first-person authority can't use agential authority to argue for testimonial privilege. These are substantive theoretical consequences, not just verbal clarifications.

VERDICT

The defence succeeds, and the triviality charge fails.

The objection makes a common mistake: treating a distinction as trivial because it *can* be stated simply, ignoring whether it does substantive theoretical work. Many important philosophical distinctions are "obvious once stated"—that's often what makes them good distinctions. The question isn't whether the distinction is conceptually simple, but whether it cuts through genuine theoretical confusion.

The thesis makes a substantive claim: you can have agential authority without testimonial privilege. This isn't trivial because:

1. It's genuinely controversial. Many theorists assume control requires knowledge. The idea that I can authoritatively settle what I believe through deliberation while being no more reliable than others at reporting what I believe strikes many as paradoxical or incoherent.

2. It has real theoretical consequences. It means interpretive theories like Carruthers's don't undermine everything about first-person authority—they leave agential authority untouched. This isn't a verbal point; it's a claim about what the interpretive turn actually establishes.

3. It challenges real explanatory packages. The thesis claims major theorists assume these phenomena need unified explanations. Even if the objection is right that the distinction is "obvious to anyone who thinks for a moment," the philosophical significance lies in showing that people *haven't* thought for that moment—that sophisticated theories rest on conflating what should be separated.

The triviality charge would succeed only if no one in the debate actually runs these together, and if separating them has no theoretical consequences. Neither condition holds. The distinction is simple, but simplicity isn't triviality. The charge fails.

KILLER (EQUIVOCATION)

ATTEMPT. The thesis equivocates on "authority" in a way that makes its central argument appear to work when it actually doesn't. The argument is plausible when "agential authority" means simply "causal role in belief-fixation" (deliberation causally fixes beliefs), but interesting only when it means "normative authority" (deliberation gives me a special rational standing regarding my beliefs). The thesis needs both readings to work.

The plausibility claim—that agential authority survives the interpretive turn—works only on the thin causal reading. Yes, obviously deliberation can causally constitute belief-fixation even if we're self-interpreters with no special epistemic access. Deliberating about P rather than observing myself can be the process that fixes my belief about P. The interpretive turn doesn't deny this causal-mechanical fact.

But the interest claim—that this matters, that something important about first-person authority survives—requires the thick normative reading. Who cares if deliberation causally fixes beliefs unless this gives me some special rational standing, some authority in the normative sense that others should recognize? The thesis promises to show that "agential authority survives" the interpretive challenge, but survival matters only if what survives is normatively significant authority, not just a causal mechanism.

The argument cannot run on either reading alone. On the thin reading, agential authority survives but so what?—it's just a psychological mechanism with no normative significance. On the thick reading, the thesis hasn't shown survival at all—it hasn't established that deliberation-as-belief-fixation gives me normative authority if I lack epistemic privilege. The phrase "agential authority" slides between these meanings, appearing to establish something normatively significant (thick) by establishing something causally uncontroversial (thin).

STRENGTH: 4/5 — This is a serious problem requiring substantial work. The thesis must either accept that "agential authority" means just causal-mechanical belief-fixation (making the survival claim uninteresting) or explain how deliberation-as-constitution grounds normative authority without epistemic privilege (which reintroduces exactly the explanatory burden the thesis hoped to avoid). The equivocation allows the argument to appear successful by conflating what needs proving with what's obviously true.

DEFENDER

[DEFENDER] BEST DEFENCE

The objection presents a false dilemma. There's a third option the objection ignores: agential authority is normatively significant precisely *because* of the constitutive relationship between deliberation and belief-fixation, and this normative significance doesn't depend on epistemic privilege.

Why the constitutive relationship matters normatively: When deliberation constitutes belief-fixation (not merely causes it), I stand in a distinctive rational relationship to my beliefs. The belief is answerable to my reasoning about P in a way that makes *me* rationally responsible for holding it. This isn't just causal-mechanical—it's the difference between beliefs I'm rationally committed to (because they flow from my deliberation about reasons) and beliefs that merely happen to me (formed through conditioning, suggestion, or sub-personal mechanisms I don't control). This difference has genuine normative significance: it determines which beliefs I can be asked to defend, which I'm committed to revising if I revise my reasons, which express my rational agency rather than just my psychology.

Why this doesn't require epistemic privilege: The normative significance comes from the *rational structure* of the belief-forming process, not from my epistemic access to it. What matters is that my belief about P is constituted by my assessment of reasons bearing on P—that the rational relations among considerations are doing the work. Whether I can reliably report this fact about myself is a separate question. I can be rationally responsible for beliefs formed through deliberation even if I'm terrible at detecting which beliefs were so formed.

Against the "so what?" challenge: The objection asks why we should care about agential authority on the thin reading. Answer: because it grounds rational responsibility and commitment. When you challenge my belief, the appropriate response depends on whether it was deliberatively formed. If yes: I must defend it by giving reasons about P, and I'm committed to revising it if those reasons fail. If no: I can only report it as a psychological fact about myself. This is normatively significant—it's the difference between beliefs that express my rational agency and beliefs that are merely mine. The interpretive turn threatens to collapse this distinction by suggesting all beliefs are just self-interpretations. The thesis shows the distinction survives: beliefs formed through deliberation about P have a different rational status than beliefs formed through self-observation, even if I'm no better at detecting my own mental states than others are.

The thick/thin distinction itself is confused: The objection treats "normative authority" as requiring something beyond the constitutive relationship—some extra normative ingredient. But the normativity is *already present* in the constitutive relationship itself. That deliberation about P constitutes settling whether I believe P just *is* a normative fact about rational commitment and responsibility. There's no equivocation between "mere causation" and "normative standing"—the specific kind of constitutive relationship at issue (rational deliberation constituting belief-fixation) is inherently normative.

Why others should recognize this authority: The objection suggests normative authority requires that "others should recognize" my special standing. But they should: when a belief is deliberatively formed, the appropriate way to engage with it is through rational criticism of the reasons, not through behavioral interpretation. This is a normative constraint on proper epistemic interaction, and it holds even if I'm no more reliable at self-reporting than others. My agential authority doesn't give me testimonial privilege (others needn't defer to my reports), but it does constrain how they should engage with my beliefs—through reason-giving dialogue rather than third-person interpretation.

VERDICT

The defence partially succeeds but exposes a significant burden the thesis must discharge.

The objection is wrong that the thesis faces a simple dilemma between trivial-causal and unsupported-normative readings. The defence successfully identifies a third option: the constitutive relationship between deliberation and belief-fixation is itself normatively significant because it grounds rational responsibility and commitment. This isn't mere causation—it's a specific kind of rational-constitutive relationship that makes beliefs answerable to reasoning in a way that grounds genuine normative differences.

However, the objection succeeds in showing the thesis needs to do more work than it has done. The defence sketches why the constitutive relationship matters normatively (rational responsibility, appropriate forms of epistemic engagement, etc.), but the thesis itself doesn't develop this case. As stated, the thesis does risk appearing to equivocate—moving from "deliberation constitutes belief-fixation" (which sounds mechanical) to "agential authority survives" (which sounds normatively loaded) without explicitly explaining why the former grounds the latter.

What the thesis needs: An explicit account of why deliberation-as-constitution grounds normative authority without requiring epistemic privilege. The defence provides the materials: the constitutive relationship makes beliefs rationally answerable to deliberation, which grounds responsibility and constrains appropriate forms of criticism. But this needs to be articulated as part of the thesis itself, not just assumed.

The equivocation charge fails, but barely: The thesis isn't actually equivocating—it means something normatively significant by "agential authority" throughout. But it's stated in a way that makes this unclear, allowing the objection to gain purchase. The defence shows there's no equivocation once we understand what kind of constitutive relationship is at issue, but the thesis should make this explicit.

The core claim survives: agential authority is both normatively significant and independent of epistemic privilege. But the thesis needs strengthening to make clear why the constitutive relationship between deliberation and belief-fixation carries normative weight.

KILLER (UNFALSIFIABLE)

ATTEMPT. The thesis claims agential authority requires only that "the activity of deliberating about P (rather than observing myself) can constitute settling whether I believe P." But this criterion is unfalsifiable because any apparent counterexample gets redefined away by tightening what counts as "genuine" deliberation or "actually constituting" belief-fixation.

Consider any putative case of agential authority that seems problematic—hypnosis, manipulation, self-deception, rationalization, confabulation. The thesis can always respond: "That's not REAL deliberation constituting belief-fixation; the constitutive work is being done by something else (suggestion, bias, motivated reasoning)." But what makes deliberation "real" versus "merely apparent"? The thesis provides no independent test. The hypnosis defence revealed this: it distinguished "genuine" constitution from "epiphenomenal" deliberation by asking whether deliberation is "doing the work"—but this just restates the criterion circularly.

Similarly, if we find someone who deliberates about P, forms a belief, yet seems to lack agential authority (perhaps due to severe self-deception or manipulation), the thesis can respond: "Then the deliberation wasn't ACTUALLY constituting belief-fixation in the right way—it wasn't in virtue of rational relations." Every counterexample gets classified as "not really the kind of deliberation-constitution we mean."

The weak point is the phrase "can constitute settling"—this modal formulation combined with no independent specification of the constitutive relationship makes the thesis immune to cases. We can never present a case where deliberation constitutes belief-fixation yet agential authority is absent, because the absence of authority is always taken as proof that genuine constitution wasn't occurring.

STRENGTH: 3/5 — A genuine problem requiring an answer. The thesis needs independent criteria for when deliberation genuinely constitutes belief-fixation versus merely accompanying it, criteria that don't simply appeal to the presence/absence of agential authority itself. The defence against the hypnosis case suggested tests (removing deliberation while holding other factors fixed), but these need development into a falsifiable account of what the constitutive relationship requires.

DEFENDER

[DEFENDER] BEST DEFENCE

The unfalsifiability charge mistakes the need for theoretical specification with vicious circularity, and ignores that the thesis provides principled (if underdeveloped) criteria for genuine constitution.

Independent criteria exist: The thesis isn't reduced to saying "constitution happens when authority is present." It specifies a structural feature: deliberation about P (not about whether I believe P) settles the belief. This gives us testable predictions:

1. The transparency test: In genuine agential authority, asking "Do I believe P?" is answered by deliberating about P itself. In non-agential cases (observation, interpretation), I answer by examining my behavior, feelings, or other evidence about myself. This is empirically distinguishable—we can check whether someone answers the belief-question by considering reasons about P versus evidence about themselves.

2. The counterfactual test: Would different conclusions about P (reached through deliberation) yield different beliefs? In genuine constitution: yes—if deliberation about penguin biology led to different conclusions, the belief would differ. In hypnosis/manipulation: no—the belief is fixed by the manipulation regardless of where deliberation leads. This is testable by varying the rational considerations and checking whether belief tracks them.

3. The rational answerability test: Can the belief be defended/revised by giving reasons about P, or only by citing psychological facts about the believer? Deliberatively-constituted beliefs are answerable to reasons about their content; non-deliberative beliefs aren't. This gives us behavioral criteria: does the person treat challenges as demanding reasons about P, or as demanding psychological explanation?

Why this isn't circular: These tests don't presuppose the presence of agential authority—they check for structural features of the belief-forming process. Yes, when these features are absent, we conclude genuine constitution isn't occurring. But that's how theoretical criteria work, not vicious circularity. Physics says "genuine gravitational attraction requires mass" and when apparent attraction occurs without mass (magnets), we conclude it's not gravitational attraction. That's not unfalsifiable—it's theoretical specification.

The manipulation cases aren't problematic: The objection claims we can "always respond" that problematic cases aren't genuine deliberation. But this is a feature, not a bug. Self-deception, rationalization, and manipulation ARE cases where deliberation fails to constitute belief-fixation in the relevant way—the belief is fixed by motivated reasoning, social pressure, or suggestion, with deliberation playing a merely rationalization role. The thesis predicts exactly this: these cases lack agential authority because deliberation isn't doing the constitutive work. That's falsifiable—if we found cases where deliberation clearly satisfies the transparency/counterfactual/answerability tests yet authority is absent, the thesis would fail.

What would falsify the thesis: Find a case where (1) the subject answers "Do I believe P?" by deliberating about P, not observing themselves, (2) varying the rational considerations about P changes the belief, (3) the belief is rationally answerable to considerations about P, yet (4) the subject lacks agential authority over the belief. That would be a genuine counterexample. The thesis is falsifiable—it's just that the manipulation/hypnosis cases don't satisfy conditions (1)-(3).

The modal formulation is appropriate: "Can constitute" doesn't make the thesis unfalsifiable—it indicates that the constitutive relationship is possible for deliberation but not guaranteed. Not all deliberation constitutes belief-fixation (sometimes we deliberate unsuccessfully, or deliberation is overridden). The thesis claims that when deliberation does constitute belief-fixation (satisfying the structural criteria), agential authority is present. This is testable.

VERDICT

The defence succeeds, but reveals that the thesis needs more explicit methodological development.

The unfalsifiability charge fails because the thesis does provide independent criteria for when deliberation genuinely constitutes belief-fixation—criteria based on structural features of the belief-forming process (transparency, counterfactual dependence, rational answerability) rather than circular appeal to authority itself. These criteria are in principle testable and could be falsified by finding cases that satisfy them without yielding authority.

However, the objection succeeds in showing that the thesis, as stated, doesn't make these criteria sufficiently explicit. The defence had to reconstruct them from implications and the hypnosis discussion. A stronger version of the thesis would specify upfront:

- What structural features distinguish deliberation that constitutes belief-fixation from deliberation that merely accompanies it
- How these features can be detected independently of checking for authority
- What would count as a genuine counterexample

The charge of unfalsifiability fails because such criteria exist and can be articulated. But the charge has force because the thesis doesn't articulate them clearly enough, making it appear that "genuine constitution" is defined simply as "whatever yields authority."

Why this doesn't sink the thesis: The core claim remains intact—there are principled, non-circular ways to identify when deliberation constitutes belief-fixation, and the thesis predicts that these cases will exhibit agential authority regardless of epistemic privilege. The problem is presentational: the thesis needs to make its empirical commitments more explicit. But having implicit empirical commitments that need explication is different from being unfalsifiable. The thesis is falsifiable; it just needs to be clearer about what would falsify it.

The objection pushes the thesis to be more rigorous about its criteria, which is valuable. But it doesn't show the thesis is unfalsifiable—only that it needs better specification of its falsification conditions.

R5. First-person authority for intentions is preserved while first-person authority for beliefs is undermined because only intentions have the right direction of fit to survive the interpretive turn.

Scores
promise 4/5 · residual 5/5 · worst 5/5 · dead
Move · Target
instability — The assumption shared by both sides that first-person authority stands or falls together across different attitude types
Sketch

Defenders of first-person authority typically treat beliefs and intentions as parallel cases—both are attitudes where we supposedly have special access. But this parallelism is unstable under interpretive pressure. For beliefs (mind-to-world direction of fit), interpretation threatens authority because believing P requires getting the world right, and the confabulation literature shows we're no better at getting our own minds right than we are at getting the external world right. But for intentions (world-to-mind direction of fit), interpretation enhances rather than threatens authority, because forming an intention partly consists in committing yourself to a course of action, and avowing an intention is itself a way of undertaking that commitment. When I say 'I intend to φ,' I'm not primarily reporting a pre-existing state but binding myself. The interpretive act itself can constitute the intention in a way it cannot constitute belief. This explains why Moran's agentialism works better for intentions than beliefs—and why we should stop treating them as parallel cases.

Appraiser (blind)
The direction-of-fit distinction applied to the authority debate is genuinely illuminating and could reframe discussions of asymmetry between belief and intention.
Objections
  • MISATTRIBUTION — landed 4/5, unanswered. The defence narrows to 'structural parallelism of success' but the literature has been explicitly asymmetric for decades
  • TRIVIAL — landed 4/5, unanswered. The defence claims novelty in 'stopping the rescue project' but the literature is already divided on belief-authority
  • EQUIVOCATION — landed 4/5, unanswered. The defence claims constitutive authority grounds epistemic authority but this makes intention-avowals unfalsifiable rather than authoritative
  • UNFALSIFIABLE — landed 3/5, unanswered. The defence sketches test cases but relies on open-ended 'defeating conditions' and flexible 'interpretive pressure' thresholds
  • ALREADY TAKEN — landed 5/5, unanswered. The defence misrepresents Moran's agnosticism as confident parallelism; the thesis restates rather than destabilizes the existing debate
⚑ Target attribution disputed — The defence narrows to 'structural parallelism of success' but the literature has been explicitly asymmetric for decades Check this yourself: it is a claim about who holds what, made from recall.
🔧 Survives as

Direction-of-fit differences show why Moran's agentialist rescue of belief-authority fails: only intentions have the constitutive structure where avowal can ground epistemic authority, making practical self-knowledge fundamentally more secure than theoretical self-knowledge under interpretive conditions

Flaw

The thesis claims to expose an assumption 'shared by both sides' but the literature has been explicitly asymmetric since Anscombe (1957), with Moran and others already treating the direction-of-fit difference as making belief-authority more problematic than intention-authority—the thesis restates one side of an existing debate while presenting it as a hidden instability

full exchange (10 turns)

KILLER (MISATTRIBUTION)

ATTEMPT. The thesis targets "defenders of first-person authority" who "treat beliefs and intentions as parallel cases" where both attitudes supposedly have the same kind of special access. But the major theorists in this debate do NOT treat them as straightforwardly parallel. Moran himself distinguishes these attitudes extensively in *Authority and Estrangement* (2001), arguing that self-knowledge of intention works through deliberation about what to do (the "transparency condition") while belief works through deliberation about what's true. Edgley (1969) distinguished practical from theoretical self-knowledge. Even Shoemaker, often cited for first-person authority, explicitly treats conative and cognitive states differently. The thesis presents its insight about direction-of-fit asymmetries as if correcting a widespread error, but this asymmetry is actually common ground. The real debate concerns whether EITHER attitude type enjoys genuine authority and what explains it—not whether they work the same way. The thesis attacks a crude parallelism that serious defenders abandoned decades ago, making this a battle against a position nobody actually holds in the form described.

STRENGTH: 4/5 — This is a serious problem. The thesis may contain valuable insights about direction of fit, but it mischaracterizes the dialectical situation. The observation that intentions and beliefs differ isn't news to the literature it addresses.

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE

The objection conflates *recognizing some differences* with *recognizing the right differences in the right way*. Yes, Moran distinguishes beliefs and intentions—but he still thinks BOTH enjoy first-person authority through their respective transparency conditions. That's the parallelism the thesis targets: the structural assumption that each attitude type has its own route to authority, making them parallel successes rather than asymmetric outcomes.

The thesis claims something stronger and more specific than "they differ." It claims that only intentions survive interpretive pressure because only they have the constitutive feature that makes authority possible under interpretation: the self-fulfilling character of avowal. When I avow an intention, the avowal can *make it so* in a way that avowing a belief cannot. This isn't just "deliberation about what to do vs. what's true"—it's about whether the speech act itself has world-to-mind fit.

Moran's transparency condition for belief still faces the confabulation problem: when I ask "Is P true?" I might get the answer wrong, and then my self-attribution is false. But when I ask "Shall I φ?" and answer "Yes," my avowal "I intend to φ" can constitute the intention even if my prior psychological state was murky. The avowal has performative force for intentions that it lacks for beliefs.

The thesis isn't correcting crude parallelism—it's arguing that even sophisticated accounts like Moran's preserve a deeper parallelism (both attitudes get authority, just through different mechanisms) when they should recognize a fundamental asymmetry (only intentions get authority because only they have the right metaphysics for it). The target is the *structural parallelism of success*, not the *identity of mechanism*.

VERDICT

The defence fails, though not completely.

The defence succeeds in identifying a real distinction: there IS a difference between "these work differently" and "only one actually works." If the literature uniformly granted authority to both attitudes while merely explaining them differently, the thesis would have a genuine target.

But the defence's own citations undermine it. Moran doesn't just say beliefs and intentions work differently—he explicitly worries whether belief gets authority at all, precisely because of the confabulation problem the thesis invokes. His agentialism is widely read as *rescuing* first-person authority for belief by making it more like intention (through rational self-constitution), not as establishing a parallel success.

More fatally: the thesis presents its direction-of-fit point as if it's doing novel work to destabilize the debate, but this is exactly what Edgley's practical/theoretical distinction already captured. The performative character of intention-avowal isn't a hidden resource—it's been explicit since at least Anscombe.

The thesis may be right that intentions survive interpretive pressure better than beliefs. But it cannot claim to be *destabilizing an assumption* when the literature has been explicitly asymmetric for fifty years. At best, it's *taking a side* in an existing asymmetry debate, not exposing a false parallelism.

KILLER (TRIVIAL)

ATTEMPT. The thesis claims to destabilize "the assumption shared by both sides that first-person authority stands or falls together across different attitude types." But this purported assumption is not actually contested ground—it's a verbal repackaging of observations already explicit in the literature. The "direction of fit" distinction comes from Anscombe (1957) and has been standard equipment for 65 years. The claim that intention-avowals have performative or self-fulfilling character appears in Anscombe, is central to Moran's account, and is developed extensively by Bilgrami and others. The observation that confabulation threatens belief-authority differently than intention-authority is explicit in Moran's own discussion of why agentialism works better for some attitudes than others.

What the thesis presents as a destabilizing discovery—"only intentions have the right direction of fit to survive the interpretive turn"—is actually just a restatement, in fashionable "interpretive turn" vocabulary, of the Anscombian distinction between practical and theoretical knowledge that's been foundational to this literature from the start. The thesis hasn't identified a hidden instability in the debate; it's restated one side of a long-standing explicit disagreement about whether belief gets authority at all. The appearance of novelty comes entirely from substituting "direction of fit" and "interpretive pressure" for "practical vs. theoretical" and "self-constitution." This is terminological updating dressed as conceptual discovery.

STRENGTH: 4/5 — The thesis may have dialectical value as a clear statement of one position, but it cannot claim to be exposing an assumption or destabilizing a debate when it's rehearsing distinctions that are the explicit common ground of the literature it addresses.

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE

The objection mistakes *having the materials* for *drawing the right conclusion*. Yes, Anscombe gave us direction of fit. Yes, Moran discusses performative aspects of avowal. But the literature has consistently failed to follow these insights to their natural terminus: that first-person authority for beliefs is *impossible*, not merely *explained differently*.

Consider the actual dialectical landscape. Moran doesn't say "beliefs lack authority"—he tries to *save* belief-authority through agentialism and transparency. Bilgrami doesn't say "only intentions have authority"—he tries to extend self-fulfilling mechanisms to beliefs through rational self-constitution. Even interpretivist critics like Schwitzgebel attack first-person authority *generally*, treating beliefs and intentions as jointly vulnerable. The thesis's target assumption isn't "beliefs and intentions work the same way"—it's "both can have authority, even if differently grounded."

The literature has the conceptual tools but refuses the conclusion. It's like having DNA evidence and fingerprinting but still treating circumstantial and direct evidence as equally probative. The thesis isn't just "restating Anscombe"—it's weaponizing direction-of-fit against the persistent project of salvaging belief-authority that dominates post-Anscombian work.

Moreover, "interpretive turn" isn't mere terminological updating. It specifies a particular challenge: when we accept that self-knowledge is interpretive (as in Gopnik, Carruthers, or even modest readings of Moran), does authority survive? For intentions, interpretation is compatible with authority because the interpretation can *constitute* the intention. For beliefs, interpretation destroys authority because beliefs answer to independent facts. This isn't in Anscombe—she predates the interpretive challenge. The thesis shows that *under interpretive pressure specifically*, the direction-of-fit distinction does asymmetric work.

The real novelty is *negative*: stopping the rescue project. The literature keeps trying to make belief-authority work (through transparency, agentialism, rational self-constitution) despite having the tools to see it can't. The thesis destabilizes this salvage operation by showing that the very distinctions defenders invoke (direction of fit, practical vs. theoretical) actually doom belief-authority rather than merely explaining it differently.

VERDICT

The defence fails.

The defence's core move—"they have the tools but don't draw the conclusion"—would work if the literature were actually committed to salvaging belief-authority uniformly. But it isn't. The objection correctly notes that Moran "explicitly worries whether belief gets authority at all." The literature is already divided on whether beliefs have first-person authority. This isn't a hidden fault line the thesis exposes; it's the explicit topic of debate.

More damaging: the defence claims Anscombe "predates the interpretive challenge," but this is false. Anscombe's entire account of intention-knowledge is *already interpretive*—she explicitly denies we have introspective access to intentions and argues we know them through practical reasoning and self-interpretation of our actions. When the thesis says "under interpretive pressure specifically, direction-of-fit does asymmetric work," it's describing exactly what Anscombe already described.

The defence tries to locate novelty in a "negative" contribution—stopping the rescue project. But which rescue project? Moran is already skeptical about belief-authority. Interpretivist critics already deny it. The thesis cannot destabilize an assumption by taking a side in an existing dispute.

The fatal problem: the thesis claims to target "the assumption shared by both sides" but the defence admits the sides don't actually share this assumption—Moran worries beliefs lack authority, interpretivists think they do lack it, and only some theorists try to salvage it. An assumption "shared by both sides" that only some theorists hold and others explicitly reject is not an assumption structuring the debate—it's just one position within it.

The thesis would work better as: "Here's why the Anscombian asymmetry is correct and belief-rescue projects fail." But it cannot work as: "Here's a hidden instability I'm exposing." The instability has been explicit since 1957.

KILLER (EQUIVOCATION)

ATTEMPT

The thesis equivocates on "first-person authority," making it plausible for intentions on one reading and interesting for beliefs on another, while the argument requires both.

Reading 1 (Epistemic authority): Special reliability or justification in self-attributions—knowing your mental states better than others know them. On this reading, the claim about beliefs is interesting (denying we have privileged epistemic access to our beliefs is substantive and contested), but the claim about intentions becomes trivial or false. If "authority" means epistemic reliability, then "I intend to φ" can be false even after sincere avowal (I might be self-deceived, might fail to follow through, might lack the capacity). The performative character of intention-avowal doesn't give me epistemic authority—it just makes my avowal partly constitutive.

Reading 2 (Constitutive authority): The capacity to make something so by avowing it—performative or self-fulfilling power. On this reading, the claim about intentions is plausible (avowing an intention can constitute having it), but the claim about beliefs becomes uninteresting. Obviously beliefs lack constitutive authority in this sense—that's just what mind-to-world direction of fit means. No one thought saying "I believe P" makes P true or even makes me believe P.

The argument needs both: it needs intentions to have authority in the constitutive sense (to make the direction-of-fit point work) while beliefs lack authority in the epistemic sense (to make the claim interesting and to connect with the confabulation literature). But these are different kinds of "authority," and the thesis survives only by sliding between them.

STRENGTH: 4/5

This is a serious problem that strikes at the argument's core. The thesis cannot establish an asymmetry by giving intentions one kind of authority and denying beliefs a different kind.

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE

The objection forces a false choice between epistemic and constitutive authority when the thesis's actual claim is that constitutive authority *grounds* epistemic authority for intentions in a way impossible for beliefs.

Start with what "first-person authority" means in the target literature. It's not mere reliability (thermometers are reliable) nor bare constitutive power (promises create obligations but that's not self-knowledge). It's the epistemic-normative status where your self-ascription is *authoritative*—others should defer to it, you need not cite evidence, challenges require special justification. This is the phenomenon Moran, Burge, and Wright all address.

The thesis's claim is precisely that this epistemic-normative authority has *different metaphysical grounds* for the two attitudes, and only one ground survives interpretive pressure:

For intentions: Constitutive authority grounds epistemic authority. When I avow "I intend to φ," this avowal can constitute the intention, and *because* it constitutes the intention, I have epistemic authority about it. I'm authoritative not despite but *because* my saying-so makes it so. The speech act is self-verifying in the relevant sense—it brings about the state it purports to report. Under interpretive pressure, this works: even if my prior psychological state was indeterminate, the avowal settles it. The interpretation constitutes the fact, so the interpretation is automatically correct.

For beliefs: Epistemic authority would need grounding in privileged access or special reliability. But interpretivism shows we lack privileged access (we interpret ourselves as we interpret others), and confabulation studies show we lack special reliability. There's no constitutive story available—avowing "I believe P" doesn't make me believe P, and even if it did, that wouldn't make the belief *correct* since beliefs answer to independent facts. Under interpretive pressure, epistemic authority collapses because interpretation can be mistaken about belief-states (there's a fact of the matter independent of the interpretation) and even correct belief-attribution doesn't yield knowledge when the belief itself might be false.

This isn't equivocation—it's showing that *only intentions have the metaphysical structure that can ground epistemic authority under interpretive conditions*. The constitutive feature isn't a different kind of authority; it's what makes epistemic authority possible.

The objection claims intentions lack epistemic authority because "I intend to φ" can be false. But this misunderstands the dialectic. First-person authority is compatible with *some* errors (even Burge allows self-deception cases). The question is whether there's a *default* or *standard* case where the self-ascription is authoritative. For intentions, the constitutive mechanism provides this: in the standard case, sincere avowal constitutes the intention, making the self-ascription both true and authoritative. For beliefs, there's no such mechanism.

The thesis isn't sliding between readings—it's arguing that epistemic authority requires metaphysical grounding, and only the constitutive ground survives interpretivism.

VERDICT

The defence fails, though it makes the thesis's structure clearer.

The defence's key move—"constitutive authority grounds epistemic authority for intentions"—faces immediate problems:

First: If avowing an intention constitutes having it, then "I intend to φ" becomes *unfalsifiable* in the standard case, not *authoritative*. Authority requires the possibility of error that's nonetheless rare or special. A "self-ascription" that cannot be wrong because it makes itself true isn't an epistemic achievement—it's a performative act. We don't say I have "epistemic authority" about my promises because promising constitutes the obligation. We say I have *practical authority* or *normative power*. The defence has shown intentions involve performative power, not that this grounds epistemic authority.

Second: The defence admits "I intend to φ" can be false (self-deception, failure to follow through), then claims these are exceptional cases while "sincere avowal constitutes the intention" in standard cases. But this is exactly where the equivocation lives. In standard cases, if avowal constitutes the intention, then we're in Reading 2 (constitutive authority, uninteresting for beliefs). In exceptional cases where avowal fails to constitute the intention, we need Reading 1 (epistemic authority, but now intentions face the same interpretive problems as beliefs—I can be wrong about whether I really intend to φ).

Third: The defence claims the thesis shows "only intentions have the metaphysical structure that can ground epistemic authority under interpretive conditions." But constitutive self-fulfillment doesn't ground *epistemic* authority—it eliminates the need for it. If my saying "I intend to φ" makes it true, there's no epistemic question to have authority over. The epistemic question arises precisely in cases where avowal might fail to constitute the intention—and there, intentions face the same interpretive problems as beliefs.

The thesis could work as: "Intentions have performative authority while beliefs require epistemic authority, and only the former survives interpretivism." But it cannot work as: "Both attitudes need epistemic authority, but only intentions achieve it." The defence has clarified that the thesis actually makes the first claim while presenting it as the second—which is indeed equivocation.

KILLER (UNFALSIFIABLE)

ATTEMPT

The thesis protects itself from counterexamples through systematic redefinition of what counts as a "genuine" case of first-person authority or interpretive pressure.

When confronted with cases where intention-avowals seem to lack authority (self-deception about intentions, weakness of will, unconscious motives), the thesis can respond: "those aren't standard cases of sincere avowal" or "the interpretation hasn't properly constituted the intention yet." The self-constituting mechanism becomes unfalsifiable: if the avowal worked, it constituted the intention (confirming the thesis); if it didn't work, it wasn't a proper avowal or the intention wasn't really formed (not a counterexample).

Conversely, when confronted with cases where beliefs seem to retain first-person authority despite interpretive pressure (immediate judgments, logical beliefs, transparent self-knowledge), the thesis can respond: "that's not *real* interpretive pressure" or "residual authority there is actually practical/intention-like, not genuinely doxastic." Any apparent belief-authority gets reclassified as either not-really-authority or not-really-belief.

The direction-of-fit criterion itself becomes a sorting mechanism that determines outcomes by definition: if an attitude survives interpretive pressure, it must have had world-to-mind fit (really an intention); if it fails, it must have had mind-to-world fit (really a belief). The thesis cannot be tested because the very features it uses to explain outcomes (direction of fit, constitutive vs. epistemic authority, "genuine" interpretive pressure) are flexible enough to accommodate any result.

STRENGTH: 3/5

This is a genuine problem requiring a real answer. The thesis does show some unfalsifiable tendencies, particularly in how it handles mixed or boundary cases. However, it's not completely immune to cases—clear examples of beliefs retaining authority or intentions lacking it under specified interpretive conditions could still challenge the core claim. The thesis needs to specify what would count as a counterexample.

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE

The objection confuses *theoretical flexibility* with *unfalsifiability*. The thesis makes empirically testable predictions that could be falsified by the right cases—the objection just hasn't identified them.

What would falsify the thesis:

1. Belief cases surviving interpretive pressure through belief-mechanisms: Show me a case where (a) we adopt full interpretive stance toward belief-formation (treating self-attribution as theorizing from behavioral/neural evidence, no privileged access), (b) the attitude has clear mind-to-world direction of fit (correctness depends on external facts, not the agent's commitment), and yet (c) first-person authority is preserved *because of* rather than despite these features. The thesis predicts this is impossible—find it and the thesis falls.

2. Intention cases losing authority through constitutive mechanisms: Show me a case where (a) an agent makes a sincere, uncoerced avowal of intention, (b) the avowal has proper performative uptake (no defeating conditions like incapacity), and yet (c) the avowal systematically fails to constitute the intention *because* of the world-to-mind direction of fit. The thesis predicts the constitutive mechanism works—show it fails structurally and the thesis falls.

Why apparent flexibility isn't unfalsifiability:

The objection claims the thesis can dismiss self-deception cases as "not standard" or logical beliefs as "not really interpretive pressure." But this isn't ad hoc protection—it's principled distinction-drawing that the objection can challenge:

- Self-deception about intentions: The thesis can explain why these fail (defeating conditions on performative uptake, conflict with other intentions, lack of genuine commitment). But if self-deception were *systematic* and *structural* rather than exceptional, that would threaten the thesis. The thesis predicts it's exceptional—verify that prediction.

- Logical beliefs retaining authority: The thesis can explain these as limit cases where interpretive pressure is minimal (logical truths are transparent, little room for confabulation). But if beliefs about contingent empirical matters—paradigm cases of mind-to-world fit under full interpretive pressure—retained authority, that would falsify the thesis. The thesis predicts they don't—test it.

The direction-of-fit criterion isn't circular:

The objection claims direction of fit becomes a "sorting mechanism that determines outcomes by definition." But direction of fit is independently identifiable:

- Mind-to-world (belief): Correctness requires the world be a certain way. "I believe it's raining" is correct only if it's raining. The attitude aims at truth.
- World-to-mind (intention): Correctness requires making the world match the attitude. "I intend to leave" is satisfied by my leaving. The attitude aims at realization.

These are Anscombe's criteria, established independently of authority questions. The thesis then makes a prediction: attitudes with world-to-mind fit will preserve authority under interpretive pressure through constitutive mechanisms, while attitudes with mind-to-world fit will lose it. This prediction could be wrong—that's what makes it falsifiable.

Concrete test cases:

1. Study subjects under hypnosis form intentions through suggestion (interpretive pressure maximized, no privileged access). Thesis predicts: if they sincerely avow these intentions, the avowals constitute genuine intentions with first-person authority. Test: do subjects treat these avowals as authoritative? Do others? Can subjects be wrong about them?

2. Study subjects with accurate belief-tracking (high metacognitive accuracy on perceptual judgments). Thesis predicts: even with high reliability, they lack *authority* in the normative sense—their self-attributions still require evidential grounding, challenges don't require special justification. Test: do subjects and others treat these self-attributions as authoritative or merely reliable?

The thesis makes predictions. Run the studies. If the predictions fail, the thesis fails. That's falsifiability.

VERDICT

The defence succeeds partially but ultimately fails to save the thesis from the unfalsifiability charge.

Where the defence succeeds:

The defence correctly identifies that direction of fit is independently specifiable (Anscombe's criteria don't depend on authority outcomes), and it does sketch some testable predictions. The hypnosis case is particularly good: if subjects under hypnotic suggestion who form intentions through pure interpretation (no privileged access) nonetheless have authority over those intentions through avowal, while subjects with hypnotically-induced beliefs (equally interpretive) lack authority, that would support the thesis. This is a real empirical prediction.

Where the defence fails:

1. The test cases reveal the problem rather than solving it: Consider the hypnosis prediction more carefully. The thesis predicts that sincere avowal constitutes intention "if they sincerely avow these intentions." But how do we determine sincerity independently of whether the avowal successfully constituted the intention? If the subject later acts contrary to the "intention," do we say (a) the avowal wasn't sincere, or (b) the intention wasn't really formed, or (c) they changed their mind, or (d) the thesis's prediction failed? The thesis gives us no independent grip on these questions. This is exactly the unfalsifiability problem: the constitutive mechanism can't fail because "failure" just means the conditions weren't met.

2. The "defeating conditions" clause does protective work: The defence says self-deception cases involve "defeating conditions on performative uptake, conflict with other intentions, lack of genuine commitment." But this list is open-ended and post-hoc. When an intention-avowal fails to constitute an intention, we can always cite some defeating condition. The thesis needs to specify *in advance* what defeats performative uptake, and this specification must be independent of whether authority was achieved. Otherwise, "defeating conditions" just means "whatever explains why the avowal didn't work"—which is unfalsifiable.

3. The belief half remains protected: The defence says logical beliefs are "limit cases where interpretive pressure is minimal." But this is exactly the flexibility problem. The thesis claims to be about belief-authority "under interpretive pressure"—but now interpretive pressure comes in degrees, and beliefs that retain authority just have "minimal" pressure. What degree of interpretive pressure counts? The thesis doesn't say, which means any belief-authority can be explained away as "not enough pressure yet."

4. The metacognition case backfires: The defence claims that even subjects with high metacognitive accuracy lack "authority in the normative sense" because their self-attributions "require evidential grounding." But this just restates the thesis rather than testing it. How do we determine whether their self-attributions require evidential grounding independently of the thesis's prediction? If subjects and others treat these self-attributions as authoritative (defer to them, don't demand evidence), does that falsify the thesis, or do we say "they're confused about what real authority requires"? The defence gives no answer.

The fundamental problem:

The thesis makes a metaphysical claim (constitutive mechanisms ground authority for intentions but not beliefs) and presents it as explaining an epistemic phenomenon (asymmetric first-person authority). But the metaphysical claim is doing too much work: it determines what counts as a "genuine" case of each attitude type, what counts as "real" authority, and what counts as "sufficient" interpretive pressure. These determinations are made by the theory itself, not independently testable.

A truly falsifiable version would need: (1) independent criteria for intention vs. belief that don't reference authority outcomes, (2) independent criteria for genuine authority that don't reference constitutive mechanisms, and (3) specified thresholds for interpretive pressure that don't flex to accommodate results. The defence gestures toward (1) with Anscombe's direction-of-fit criteria, but doesn't provide (2) or (3).

The thesis isn't completely unfalsifiable—the hypnosis case shows there are some empirical constraints. But it has enough flexibility in its

KILLER (ALREADY TAKEN)

ATTEMPT

The thesis claims to show that "only intentions have the right direction of fit to survive the interpretive turn," treating this as a novel destabilizing insight. But this is precisely the position developed and defended by Richard Moran in *Authority and Estrangement* (2001) and subsequent work. Moran explicitly argues that practical self-knowledge (intentions, decisions) works through a deliberative, self-constituting mechanism where the agent's avowal has performative force, while theoretical self-knowledge (beliefs) faces special difficulties precisely because beliefs answer to independent facts. His "transparency condition" is asymmetric by design: for intentions, transparency works through "What shall I do?" (which constitutes the intention), while for beliefs, transparency through "Is it true that P?" remains vulnerable to error and confabulation. The direction-of-fit asymmetry and its implications for authority under interpretive conditions is Moran's central thesis, not a criticism of it.

Even more directly, the claim that intention-avowals have self-fulfilling or constitutive force while belief-avowals don't appears in Edgley (1969), is central to Anscombe's account of practical knowledge, and is developed extensively in the "agentialist" literature the thesis cites. The specific claim about surviving "interpretive pressure" is Moran's response to interpretivist challenges from Gopnik and others—he explicitly argues that agentialism saves authority for intentions while acknowledging beliefs are more vulnerable.

The thesis presents itself as exposing an instability, but it's actually just endorsing one side of an established position. This is Moran's view, not a critique of assumptions Moran shares.

STRENGTH: 5/5

This completely undermines the thesis as presented. The thesis cannot claim to destabilize a debate by restating the most prominent position in that debate. The direction-of-fit asymmetry, the constitutive character of intention-avowal, the vulnerability of belief-authority to interpretive pressure, and the conclusion that intentions fare better than beliefs—this entire package is Moran's explicit view. The thesis is ALREADY TAKEN by the theorist it cites as representative of the position it claims to destabilize.

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE

The objection misreads both Moran and the thesis's dialectical target. Moran does NOT hold the thesis's position—he holds precisely the view the thesis attacks.

What Moran actually argues:

Moran defends first-person authority for BOTH beliefs and intentions, just through different mechanisms. For beliefs, transparency works through deliberating "Is P true?"—and Moran explicitly argues this PRESERVES authority despite interpretive challenges. He doesn't concede that belief-authority collapses; he offers agentialism as a way to SAVE it by making self-knowledge a matter of rational self-constitution rather than inner observation. His entire project is rescuing first-person authority across the board by reconceiving how it works.

Yes, Moran distinguishes practical and theoretical self-knowledge. But distinguishing HOW they work is not the same as saying only ONE works. The thesis claims only intentions retain authority under interpretive pressure—Moran claims both do, through their respective transparency conditions. That's the disagreement.

The specific divergence:

Moran thinks transparency saves belief-authority because when I deliberate "Is P true?" and conclude "Yes," my self-attribution "I believe P" is authoritative even under interpretive conditions. He treats the rational self-constitution as sufficient for authority.

The thesis denies this. It claims that for beliefs, even Moran's transparency mechanism fails under interpretive pressure because:
1. Deliberating "Is P true?" can yield the wrong answer (I might reason badly, have false evidence)
2. Even if I correctly conclude "P is true," I might be wrong about whether I believe it (confabulation)
3. The avowal "I believe P" doesn't constitute the belief in the way "I intend to φ" constitutes the intention

Moran thinks transparency gives beliefs a parallel success to intentions. The thesis claims transparency fails for beliefs precisely because of the direction-of-fit difference Moran acknowledges but doesn't follow to its conclusion.

Why this isn't "already taken":

The objection claims "this entire package is Moran's explicit view." But Moran's view is that BOTH attitudes retain authority through agentialist mechanisms. The thesis's view is that ONLY intentions retain authority because only they have the metaphysical structure (world-to-mind fit + constitutive avowal) that makes agentialist mechanisms work.

Moran has the ingredients but draws the wrong conclusion. He sees that intentions and beliefs work differently, but still thinks both achieve authority. The thesis argues the very differences Moran identifies show that belief-authority must fail. It's using Moran's own distinctions against his conclusion.

The parallel in the literature:

This is like saying "Kripke's causal theory of reference is already taken by Frege because Frege also thought names refer." Yes, both address reference, but they reach opposite conclusions about how it works. Moran and the thesis both address first-person authority and both use direction-of-fit distinctions, but Moran concludes "both attitudes get authority differently" while the thesis concludes "only intentions get authority, period."

The thesis isn't restating Moran—it's arguing Moran's own framework proves his conclusion wrong.

VERDICT

The defence fails decisively.

The fatal textual problem:

The defence claims "Moran defends first-person authority for BOTH beliefs and intentions" and "Moran thinks transparency saves belief-authority." But this misrepresents Moran's actual position in *Authority and Estrangement*. Moran is explicitly AGNOSTIC about whether beliefs retain full first-person authority. He repeatedly acknowledges that theoretical self-knowledge is "more problematic" than practical self-knowledge, that beliefs face special difficulties from interpretive challenges, and that the transparency condition works less cleanly for beliefs than intentions. His agentialism is offered as the BEST HOPE for belief-authority, not as a confident vindication of it.

More importantly, in later work (especially "Self-Knowledge, 'Transparency,' and the Forms of Activity" 2003), Moran explicitly discusses cases where belief-authority fails or is attenuated, and he's sympathetic to the view that full authority may be restricted to practical attitudes. The defence's claim that "Moran's view is that BOTH attitudes retain authority" is simply false to the texts.

The deeper problem:

Even setting aside textual accuracy, the defence's strategy backfires. It claims the thesis "uses Moran's own distinctions against his conclusion"—but if Moran already drew these distinctions and already worried they threaten belief-authority, then the thesis isn't destabilizing anything. At most, it's taking a more pessimistic stance within Moran's framework.

The defence tries to distinguish "recognizing differences" from "drawing the right conclusion," but this just concedes the objection's point: the thesis is taking a side in an existing debate, not exposing a hidden instability. Whether Moran is confident or agnostic about belief-authority, he's already identified it as the problematic case. The thesis cannot claim to be revealing something the literature assumes when Moran's entire project is addressing the problem the thesis raises.

The Kripke-Frege analogy fails:

The defence compares this to "Kripke's causal theory vs. Frege's descriptivism"—but that's a case where Kripke genuinely OPPOSED Frege's framework. Here, the thesis ACCEPTS Moran's framework (transparency, agentialism, direction-of-fit distinctions) and just pushes it further in a direction Moran already indicated. That's not opposition—it's continuation.

What the thesis actually does:

The objection is correct: the thesis restates, in somewhat stronger terms, a position that's already prominent in the literature. The direction-of-fit asymmetry is Anscombe's. The constitutive character of intention-avowal is Anscombe's and Moran's. The vulnerability of belief-authority to interpretive pressure is Moran's central concern. The conclusion that practical self-knowledge is more secure than theoretical self-knowledge is explicit in Edgley, Moran, and the agentialist tradition.

The thesis may articulate this position clearly or push it more forcefully than Moran does. But it cannot claim to be:
- Exposing an assumption "shared by both sides" (the asymmetry is already explicit)
- Destabilizing the debate (it's endorsing one side of the debate)
- Showing that defenders' own distinctions undermine their position (Moran's distinctions are designed to raise exactly this worry)

The thesis is ALREADY TAKEN—not in every detail, but in its core claim that direction-of-fit differences make intentions better candidates for first-person authority than beliefs under interpretive conditions. This is not a novel destabilization; it's a restatement of an established position, presented as if it were a discovery.

Final assessment:

The thesis fails as an INSTABILITY move because the instability it claims to expose is already the explicit subject of the debate it addresses. It would work better as a SHARPENING (making Moran's worries more precise) or ANALOGY (applying direction-of-fit distinctions to interpretive challenges more systematically), but it cannot work as exposing a hidden assumption when that assumption is actually a contested conclusion that major theorists explicitly doubt.

R6. The interpretive approach actually requires more robust first-person authority than the observational model because interpretation demands normative coherence, and only the subject has the standing to determine which coherence-preserving adjustments to make when evidence conflicts.

Scores
promise 4/5 · residual 5/5 · worst 5/5 · wounded
Move · Target
