full exchange (10 turns)

KILLER (MISATTRIBUTION)

ATTEMPT. The thesis claims to oppose "Moran's agentialism" but fundamentally misunderstands Moran's position in *Authority and Estrangement* (2001). Moran's agentialism IS NOT primarily an epistemic account of first-person authority—it is precisely a view about the constitutive role of rational self-governance in attitude possession. Moran's central claim is that believing involves a commitment to the transparency condition: I answer "Do I believe P?" by answering "Is P true?", thereby exercising the rational capacities constitutive of belief itself. This is why Moran explicitly distinguishes his view from "detectivist" models that treat first-person knowledge as a matter of epistemic access to independent states. The thesis's own position—that attitudes are individuated by responsiveness to reflective rational capacities, and that reflective judgment exercises rather than reports—is essentially Moran's view. The weak point is the premise that "Moran's agentialism" treats first-person authority as requiring "epistemic explanation" in the traditional sense. Moran's agentialism already locates authority in the constitutive metaphysics of attitude possession through rational self-governance, making this apparent "reframing" actually a restatement of Moran's own position rather than an alternative to it.

STRENGTH: 4/5 — This is a serious misattribution. The thesis presents as novel opposition what appears to be Moran's own view, undermining its claim to reframe the debate.

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE

The objection trades on an uncharitable reading of what "Moran's agentialism" denotes in this dialectical context. Three points secure the distinction:

First, Moran retains an epistemic framing despite his innovations. Even granting that Moran moves beyond detectivism, his central question remains *how do I know my own mind?* — answered via transparency. The thesis rejects this question-form entirely. Authority isn't about a *way of knowing* (even a constitutively special one), but about what makes something *my* attitude at all. Moran asks "How does transparency yield knowledge?" The thesis asks "What makes a state mine such that no transparency-style question arises?"

Second, the individuation claim goes further than Moran's commitment requirement. Moran says believing *involves* commitment to answering via transparency. The thesis says a state that *systematically flouted* reflective endorsements *wouldn't count as a belief* of that subject. This is stronger: not that beliefs come with rational commitments, but that the individuation conditions for "S's belief that P" include counterfactual responsiveness to S's reflective capacities. A Moran-style belief could exist but be badly managed; the thesis denies the recalcitrant state would be a belief at all.

Third, Moran's transparency still treats reflective judgment as *about* a prior state. When I answer "Is P true?" to know whether I believe P, there's still an asymmetry between the question (about my belief) and the answer (about P). The thesis collapses this: reflective judgment doesn't *reveal* belief via rational re-enactment — it partially *constitutes* belief-possession. The difference: Moran preserves a thin epistemic gap that transparency bridges; the thesis eliminates the gap by building the bridge into the state's identity conditions.

The objection conflates "locating authority in rational capacities" with the thesis's specific metaphysical claim about individuation. Moran's believer exercises rational capacities to *know* their beliefs; the thesis's believer has beliefs only insofar as those capacities are constitutively operative.

VERDICT

The defence fails.

The problem is that Moran *already* makes the constitutive move the thesis claims as distinctive. In *Authority and Estrangement*, Moran explicitly argues that the transparency condition isn't merely a *method* for knowing beliefs but is constitutive of what it is to believe as a rational agent. His discussion of alienated beliefs (cases where transparency fails) treats them precisely as *defective instances* of belief — states that fail to fully count as the agent's beliefs because they're not properly responsive to rational self-governance.

The defence's "stronger" claim — that systematically unresponsive states wouldn't be beliefs at all — doesn't distinguish the thesis from Moran; it just takes Moran's position on alienation to its logical conclusion. Moran already holds that beliefs essentially involve rational answerability; the thesis merely makes explicit what's implicit in treating alienated beliefs as *alienated* (partially not-mine) rather than as perfectly good beliefs I happen to know badly.

The defence's third point about eliminating the epistemic gap is more promising but ultimately fails because Moran's transparency condition already does this work: answering "Is P true?" doesn't *bridge* a gap to belief — it *is* the exercise of believing itself. That's why Moran contrasts his view with detectivism.

The thesis presents Moran's own constitutive-metaphysical move as if it were an alternative to Moran, when it's actually a development or clarification of Moran's position. The objection stands.

KILLER (PROVES TOO MUCH)

ATTEMPT

The thesis claims that "an attitude that systematically flouted the subject's reflective endorsements wouldn't count as that subject's belief." But this individuation criterion proves too much: it would rule out paradigm cases of genuine belief that we must recognize as beliefs.

Consider long-standing self-deception, implicit bias, or deep akrasia. A racist subject may reflectively endorse egalitarian principles while harboring systematic racist beliefs that guide their behavior, emotional reactions, and snap judgments. These beliefs systematically flout their reflective endorsements—yet they ARE the subject's beliefs, not subpersonal representations or alien thoughts. Indeed, the moral and psychological significance of implicit bias depends precisely on these being *the agent's own beliefs* for which they bear some responsibility.

Similarly, the akratic person genuinely believes "I should exercise" while genuinely believing "staying on the couch is better right now"—the latter systematically flouts reflective endorsement yet is unmistakably their belief. Or consider addiction: the addict's belief "I need this drink" flouts reflective judgment yet is paradigmatically theirs.

The weak point is the premise that systematic unresponsiveness to reflective endorsement disqualifies a state from counting as the subject's belief. If this criterion worked, it would force us to reclassify implicit biases, akratic judgments, and self-deceptive beliefs as non-beliefs or as somehow not belonging to the subject—an unacceptable conclusion that undermines our practices of moral responsibility, psychological explanation, and therapeutic intervention, all of which depend on treating these recalcitrant states as genuine beliefs of the agent.

STRENGTH: 4/5

This attack does serious damage. The thesis needs these problematic cases to either (a) not count as beliefs at all, (b) not count as *the subject's* beliefs, or (c) not actually "systematically flout" reflective endorsements. None of these options is attractive, and the thesis's emphasis on systematic flouting seems designed precisely to exclude such cases—but these are cases we cannot plausibly exclude.

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE

The objection misidentifies what "systematic flouting" means in the thesis's individuation criterion. Three moves preserve the account against these cases:

First, distinguish systematic unresponsiveness from systematic conflict. The racist's implicit bias doesn't *flout responsiveness* to reflective capacities—it responds to them by hiding, by generating rationalizations, by structuring itself to avoid reflective scrutiny. This is still a *form* of responsiveness, albeit a pathological one. The belief "those people are dangerous" adjusts its manifestations when reflective attention threatens (becoming more subtle, more coded, more deniable). That's responsiveness to rational self-governance, even if the response is evasion rather than revision. A truly unresponsive state would be like a tumor—just there, utterly indifferent to what the subject thinks about it. Implicit biases aren't like that; they're *reactive* to reflective judgment, which is why therapy and consciousness-raising can reach them.

Second, the cases prove the thesis rather than refuting it. Why do we hold agents responsible for implicit biases? Precisely because these states, however recalcitrant, remain *within the space of reasons*—they're responsive (if badly) to the agent's rational capacities. The thesis explains why a genuinely subpersonal mechanism (say, a hardwired startle reflex) doesn't attract the same moral evaluation: it's not individuated as a belief because it's not in the business of responding to reflective endorsement at all. The akratic's "staying on the couch is better" is responsive to reflective capacities—that's why it generates guilt, why it can be argued with internally, why it's revisable through deliberation even if currently winning. The thesis's criterion sorts exactly right: beliefs (even bad ones) show this responsiveness pattern; mere subpersonal states don't.

Third, "systematic flouting" means *in principle unresponsive*, not *currently resistant*. The implicit bias could change through reflective work—that counterfactual responsiveness is what makes it a belief. The thesis's criterion is modal: for X to be S's belief, there must be some appropriate rational route by which S's reflective capacities could engage X. Addiction beliefs, akratic judgments, self-deceptive beliefs—all satisfy this. They're hard to shift, but not metaphysically sealed off from reflective governance. Compare a genuinely alien case: a brain implant that generates the thought "obey the signal" utterly immune to any reasoning. That wouldn't be the subject's belief—and the thesis explains why.

The objection treats "systematic flouting" as "chronic resistance to change," but the thesis means "constitutively outside the space of rational responsiveness." Every case cited shows the former while exhibiting the latter's negation.

VERDICT

The defence succeeds.

The key move—distinguishing systematic *conflict* from systematic *unresponsiveness*—does genuine work. The objection's cases (implicit bias, akrasia, addiction) all involve beliefs that, however recalcitrant, remain *engaged with* the subject's reflective capacities. They hide from reflection, generate rationalizations, cause guilt, respond to therapeutic intervention, and are revisable through sustained rational work. This is responsiveness, even if it's pathological responsiveness.

The thesis's criterion actually explains our intuitions about these cases better than the objection suggests. We treat implicit biases as *beliefs* (rather than mere subpersonal mechanisms) precisely because they occupy the space of reasons—they're the kind of thing that *should* respond to reflective judgment, even when they're not responding well. A genuinely unresponsive state—a hardwired reflex, a brain tumor's effect, an implanted alien thought—wouldn't generate the same attributions of responsibility or be amenable to the same therapeutic approaches.

The modal reading in the third point is particularly strong: the individuation criterion concerns whether the state is *in principle* responsive to reflective rational capacities, not whether it currently yields to them. Implicit biases are hard to change but not impossible to change through rational means; that counterfactual responsiveness is what makes them beliefs.

The objection fails because it conflates chronic resistance with constitutive unresponsiveness. The thesis's criterion successfully distinguishes beliefs (even pathological ones) from genuinely subpersonal or alien states.

KILLER (COUNTEREXAMPLE)

ATTEMPT

The thesis claims that "an attitude that systematically flouted the subject's reflective endorsements wouldn't count as that subject's belief." But consider the following counterexample:

Capgras delusion: A patient with Capgras syndrome believes "That person is an impostor replacing my spouse." This belief systematically flouts their reflective endorsements—when calm and reflective, they acknowledge the irrationality, recognize the overwhelming evidence against it, and sincerely judge they shouldn't believe it. Yet the belief persists unchanged across years, utterly unresponsive to their reflective rational capacities. No amount of reasoning, evidence-presentation, or reflective work shifts it. It's not hiding or generating rationalizations (like implicit bias)—it's simply there, indifferent to reflective judgment.

Yet this is paradigmatically the patient's *belief*. It guides their behavior, structures their emotional life, and explains their actions. We attribute it to them in psychological explanation ("She avoids him because she believes he's an impostor"), we try to treat it therapeutically as *her* belief, and it differs fundamentally from a subpersonal mechanism or alien implanted thought precisely because it has the functional role of belief—it interacts with desires to produce action, it's expressible in assertion, it's revisable in principle even if not in practice given the underlying neurological damage.

The weak point: The premise that systematic unresponsiveness to reflective endorsement disqualifies a state from being the subject's belief. Capgras beliefs are systematically unresponsive yet are undeniably the patient's beliefs—not subpersonal states, not alien thoughts, but genuine beliefs with neurological rather than rational etiology.

STRENGTH: 4/5

This does serious damage. The defender's modal criterion ("responsive in principle") fails here: Capgras beliefs are *not* responsive to rational intervention even in principle given the underlying neurological cause—yet they're clearly beliefs. The thesis must either deny these are beliefs (absurd) or admit that systematic unresponsiveness doesn't disqualify belief-status after all.

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE

The Capgras case actually supports rather than refutes the thesis, once we properly understand what "the subject's reflective rational capacities" means in context of neurological damage.

First, Capgras beliefs ARE responsive to the patient's (damaged) rational capacities. The thesis's criterion is: for X to be S's belief, X must be responsive to *S's* reflective rational capacities—not to some idealized normal capacities, but to the capacities S actually possesses. The Capgras patient's rational capacities are themselves compromised by neurological damage to affective processing. Given their damaged capacity for emotional recognition, the belief "that's an impostor" IS responding appropriately to their rational situation—it's their best rational accommodation to the anomalous experience of seeing a familiar face that generates no affective recognition response. The belief is rationally downstream from their (damaged) perceptual-affective capacities, which is exactly what responsiveness to rational self-governance requires.

Second, the case equivocates on "reflective endorsement." When the Capgras patient "reflectively acknowledges the irrationality," what's happening? They're caught between two rational pressures: the abstract recognition that the evidence favors identity, and the immediate rational force of their anomalous experience. The belief persists not because it's unresponsive to reflection, but because reflection itself is divided—part of their rational system says "impossible," another part says "but the feeling is wrong." The belief is responding to the stronger rational pressure (the immediate experiential anomaly), which is still responsiveness. Compare: if I believe "I'm in pain" despite your arguments that I'm not, my belief isn't flouting rationality—it's responding to a rational pressure (direct experience) that properly outweighs your testimony.

Third, Capgras beliefs ARE revisable in principle through the right kind of rational engagement. They're not responsive to *argument* because the underlying problem isn't argumentative—it's experiential. But they can be managed through rational strategies: patients learn to act on "what the evidence says" rather than "what feels true," they develop coping mechanisms that rationally accommodate both pressures, and in some cases they recover when the neurological damage heals. This shows the belief is within the space of rational governance, even if it's not within the space of argumentative persuasion. A truly unresponsive state wouldn't be manageable through any rational strategy.

Fourth, the contrast with genuine subpersonal states holds. A Capgras belief differs from a mere startle reflex or tumor-caused neural firing precisely because it's integrated into the patient's rational economy: it interacts with other beliefs inferentially, it guides action through practical reasoning, it's expressible in assertion and defended with reasons (however bad). This integration IS the responsiveness to rational capacities that the thesis requires. The belief is part of the patient's rational system, however damaged that system is.

The objection assumes "systematic unresponsiveness to reflective endorsement" means "not changeable by argument." But the thesis's criterion is about whether the state is individuated as part of the subject's rational system—whether it plays the belief role in rational governance. Capgras beliefs do exactly this.

VERDICT

The defence fails, but not decisively.

The defence's strongest move is the first: that responsiveness must be relativized to the subject's actual capacities, not idealized ones. This has real force. If we build neurological damage into "S's rational capacities," then Capgras beliefs are responding to those damaged capacities, and the thesis is saved.

But this move creates a devastating problem: it makes the thesis trivial. If any belief counts as "responsive to S's rational capacities" merely by being integrated into S's psychological economy (however damaged), then the individuation criterion does no work. Every state that functionally plays the belief role automatically counts as responsive to the subject's rational capacities, making "responsiveness" just another name for "functional role" rather than a substantive constraint.

The original thesis promised to explain first-person authority through a *demanding* metaphysical requirement: attitudes must be responsive to reflective rational self-governance. But if we relativize this to whatever capacities the subject happens to have (including severely damaged ones), the requirement becomes: attitudes must be responsive to... whatever makes them attitudes. That's circular.

The second point (about divided reflection) is more promising but ultimately fails because it's not clear the Capgras patient's "acknowledgment of irrationality" represents genuine reflective endorsement at all—it might just be parroting what they know they're supposed to say while their real rational commitments lie elsewhere. If so, there's no genuine flouting. But this makes the criterion unfalsifiable: any apparent flouting can be redescribed as "divided reflection" where the belief is responding to the "real" rational pressure.

The counterexample succeeds in showing that the thesis faces a dilemma: Either (a) relativize "rational capacities" to actual damaged capacities, making the criterion trivial, or (b) maintain a substantive standard of rational responsiveness, but then exclude Capgras beliefs (and similar neurologically-based delusions) from counting as the patient's beliefs—which is absurd.

The objection stands. The thesis cannot both maintain a substantive individuation criterion and accommodate clear cases of beliefs that are systematically unresponsive to any reasonable standard of reflective rational governance.

KILLER (TRIVIAL)

ATTEMPT

The thesis claims to offer a substantial metaphysical discovery about attitude individuation: that "attitudes themselves are individuated partly by their responsiveness to the subject's rational self-governance." But this is either a trivial truth or a mere verbal stipulation dressed as discovery.

The triviality: What distinguishes attitudes (beliefs, desires, intentions) from mere subpersonal representations or brain states in the first place? Precisely that attitudes occupy "the space of reasons"—they're the kind of states that are rationally evaluable, that figure in practical reasoning, that can be revised through deliberation. This is not a controversial metaphysical discovery; it's the standard philosophical characterization of what makes propositional attitudes *attitudes* rather than mere information-bearing states. Saying "beliefs are individuated by responsiveness to rational capacities" is like saying "games are individuated by rule-governedness" or "promises are individuated by normative bindingness"—it's just unpacking what the concept already means.

The weak point: The premise that this individuation claim does substantive explanatory work regarding first-person authority. But if "responsiveness to rational self-governance" is already built into what we mean by "attitude" (as opposed to subpersonal state), then the thesis just stipulates that first-person authority applies to attitudes-so-defined. It's not explaining *why* attitudes have first-person authority; it's defining "attitude" in a way that makes first-person authority come along for free. The apparent explanatory move from "attitudes are rationally responsive" to "therefore first-person authority" is really just: "I'm calling 'attitudes' only those states that exhibit first-person authority, so naturally attitudes exhibit first-person authority."

The thesis presents as a reframing discovery what's actually a conceptual truism about the attitude/subpersonal distinction that's been uncontroversial since Sellars.

STRENGTH: 2/5

The attack has some force but ultimately doesn't devastate the thesis. While it's true that rational responsiveness is part of the standard characterization of attitudes, the thesis makes a *specific* claim about the *direction* of explanation that isn't trivial: that first-person authority is grounded in this individuation fact rather than vice versa. The standard view might accept that attitudes are rationally responsive while still treating first-person authority as an additional epistemic feature requiring separate explanation. The thesis's innovation is the claim that we don't need separate epistemic explanation because the authority is already built into what makes something an attitude at all. That's not obviously trivial, even if it uses familiar conceptual materials.

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE

The objection conflates conceptual platitude with explanatory priority, missing how the thesis weaponizes a familiar truth against a persistent explanatory project.

First, the triviality charge misconceives what's at stake. Yes, everyone since Sellars agrees attitudes occupy the space of reasons. But the philosophical *problem* of first-person authority arose precisely because theorists treated this as *compatible with* authority being a further epistemic fact requiring explanation. The standard picture: (1) attitudes are rationally evaluable states, AND (2) subjects have special epistemic access to them, AND (3) we need to explain (2). Moran, interpretivists, and others accept this picture and offer competing explanations of (2). The thesis's move is radical: reject that (2) is a separate explanandum. The authority isn't an *additional* feature of attitudes requiring epistemic explanation—it's already present in (1) once we properly understand what "rationally evaluable by the subject" entails. This isn't trivial; it's *revisionary*. It says the entire explanatory project rests on a mistake.

Second, the thesis makes a specific metaphysical claim about individuation conditions that goes beyond Sellarsian platitudes. The standard view: attitudes are states that *can be* rationally evaluated. The thesis: a state counts as S's attitude only if it's *constitutively responsive* to S's rational self-governance—where systematic counterfactual unresponsiveness would disqualify it from being S's attitude at all. This is stronger than "attitudes occupy the space of reasons." It's a claim about possession conditions: you don't first have a belief that then happens to be rationally evaluable; the rational evaluability (specifically, the responsiveness to *your* reflective capacities) is what makes it *yours*. Compare: everyone agrees promises create obligations, but it's not trivial to claim that obligation-creation is what individuates something as a promise rather than a mere prediction.

Third, the explanatory work is real, not stipulative. The thesis explains the *asymmetry* that's central to first-person authority: why your rational self-interpretations partially constitute your attitudes while my interpretations of you don't. Standard views struggle with this—if attitudes are just rationally evaluable states, why should *your* rational engagement matter more than mine? The thesis answers: because "your attitude" means "state responsive to *your* rational capacities." This isn't stipulation; it's showing how the asymmetry falls out of the individuation conditions. The explanatory target isn't "why do attitudes have first-person authority?" but "why is there an asymmetry between first-person and third-person rational engagement?" The thesis answers this through the metaphysics of attitude possession.

Fourth, the game/promise analogies actually support the thesis. Yes, games are individuated by rule-governedness—and this *explains* why participants have a special relationship to determining what game they're playing that spectators lack. Your acceptance of rules partially constitutes what game you're playing; my observations don't. That's not trivial—it's a substantive claim about constitutive vs. epistemic relations. Similarly, the thesis uses the attitude/subpersonal distinction not as a stopping point but as explanatory bedrock for the authority asymmetry.

The objection treats "using familiar materials" as "being trivial," but explanatory reframings typically work by showing that what seemed to require special explanation is already present in materials we accepted all along. That's not triviality—that's dissolving a pseudo-problem.

VERDICT

The defence succeeds.

The triviality objection fails because it misidentifies what the thesis is trying to explain. The thesis isn't claiming to discover that attitudes are rationally evaluable (trivial), nor is it stipulating that we'll only call "attitudes" those states with first-person authority (circular). Instead, it's making a specific claim about explanatory priority: the asymmetry at the heart of first-person authority (why my reflective judgments about my attitudes have a constitutive role that yours lack) is explained by the individuation conditions for attitude possession (a state is mine only if responsive to my rational capacities).

This is not trivial because:

1. It's revisionary about the explanatory project. Most theorists accept that first-person authority requires epistemic explanation even while accepting that attitudes are rationally evaluable. The thesis says this is a mistake—there's no separate epistemic explanandum.

2. It makes a substantive metaphysical claim. Not just "attitudes are rationally evaluable" but "attitude possession requires counterfactual responsiveness to the subject's rational capacities." This is strong enough to do explanatory work (explaining the asymmetry) while being controversial enough to be non-trivial.

3. It solves a genuine puzzle. Why does first-person rational engagement have constitutive force while third-person engagement doesn't? The standard "attitudes are in the space of reasons" doesn't answer this—it leaves the asymmetry mysterious. The thesis's individuation claim explains it.

The objection's mistake is thinking that because the thesis uses the familiar attitude/subpersonal distinction, it must be saying nothing new. But the innovation lies in using that distinction to *dissolve* rather than *solve* the problem of first-person authority—showing that what seemed to need epistemic explanation is already present in the metaphysics of attitude possession. That's a substantive philosophical move, not a triviality.

The objection fails.

KILLER (EQUIVOCATION)

ATTEMPT

The thesis equivocates on "responsiveness to the subject's rational self-governance," and the argument needs both readings to work—one to make the individuation claim plausible, another to make it explain first-person authority.

Reading 1 (Weak/Plausible): "Responsiveness" means the state occupies the space of reasons—it's rationally evaluable, figures in inference, can be revised through deliberation in principle, is integrated into the subject's rational economy. On this reading, the individuation claim is plausible: yes, what makes something a belief rather than a subpersonal representation is that it plays this rational role.

Reading 2 (Strong/Interesting): "Responsiveness" means the state is constitutively answerable to the subject's *reflective* endorsements specifically—it must be such that the subject's first-person rational judgments have special constitutive force over it that third-person judgments lack.

The argument needs Reading 1 to make the individuation claim defensible (as shown in responses to counterexamples—Capgras beliefs, implicit biases, etc. are "responsive" in the weak sense of being rationally integrated). But it needs Reading 2 to explain the *asymmetry* that's central to first-person authority—why *my* rational self-governance matters constitutively while yours doesn't.

The weak point: The premise that attitudes are "individuated partly by their responsiveness to the subject's rational self-governance." On Reading 1, this doesn't explain first-person authority's asymmetry (third-person interpreters can also rationally evaluate my states). On Reading 2, it's implausibly strong (excluding Capgras, implicit bias, etc.) and threatens circularity (building first-person authority into "responsiveness" rather than explaining it). The thesis cannot run on either reading alone: it needs the weak reading to handle counterexamples and the strong reading to explain what it claims to explain.

STRENGTH: 4/5

This equivocation does serious damage. The defence of counterexamples consistently relied on the weak reading (rational integration, functional role), but the explanation of first-person authority's asymmetry requires the strong reading (special constitutive force of first-person reflection). The thesis hasn't shown these are the same thing.

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE

The objection fabricates a dilemma by artificially separating what is actually a unified phenomenon with different aspects. The thesis needs no equivocation because there is a single, coherent notion of responsiveness that both individuates attitudes and explains the asymmetry.

First, the "two readings" are not distinct meanings but different emphases of one concept. Responsiveness to rational self-governance means: the state's functional role is constitutively tied to its standing in rational relations to the subject's other attitudes, where the subject is the locus of rational integration. This single concept has two consequences: (a) it distinguishes attitudes from subpersonal states (they're rationally integrated), and (b) it explains the first-person asymmetry (the integration is to *this subject's* rational economy, not anyone's). These aren't different senses of "responsiveness"—they're different implications of the same metaphysical fact.

Second, the strong reading doesn't exclude the counterexamples. Capgras beliefs and implicit biases ARE constitutively answerable to the subject's reflective capacities—that's exactly why they're *the subject's* beliefs rather than anyone else's or no one's. The Capgras patient's belief is responsive to *her* damaged perceptual-affective system, integrated into *her* rational economy, revisable through *her* therapeutic work. The implicit bias is responsive to *this subject's* evasive rational strategies, generates guilt in *this subject's* reflective moments, is treatable through *this subject's* consciousness-raising. The responsiveness is to *this particular subject's* rational governance (however well or badly exercised), which is exactly what the strong reading requires and exactly what explains why these are *her* attitudes rather than states attributable to anyone or no one.

Third, the asymmetry explanation doesn't require that first-person judgments always win—only that they have constitutive standing. Reading 2 is not "the subject's reflective endorsements must prevail" but "the state's status as this subject's attitude is constituted by its being integrated into this subject's rational economy." Third-person interpreters can rationally evaluate my states, but their evaluations don't partially constitute what states I have—they're making judgments *about* independently individuated states. My rational self-governance partially constitutes *which* states are mine because "being mine" means "being integrated into my rational economy." This explains the asymmetry without requiring that my reflective judgments be irresistible or infallible.

Fourth, the functional-role and constitutive-force aspects necessarily go together. What makes a state play the belief functional role *for this subject*? Precisely that it's integrated into *this subject's* rational economy in the right way. The functional role (Reading 1) is necessarily indexed to a particular subject, and that indexing is what gives first-person rational governance its special status (Reading 2). You can't have the functional role without the indexing, and the indexing just is what explains the asymmetry. There's no equivocation because there's no way to have one without the other.

Fifth, compare: "My body is individuated by its responsiveness to my motor intentions." This has two aspects: (a) it distinguishes my body from chairs (responsiveness to motor intentions is what makes something a body), and (b) it explains why *my* motor intentions move *my* body specially (the responsiveness is indexed to me). No equivocation—one fact, two implications. The thesis works the same way.

The objection's "weak" and "strong" readings are just: (a) responsiveness distinguishes attitudes from non-attitudes, and (b) the responsiveness is indexed to *this* subject. But (b) is already contained in (a) once we recognize that rational integration is always integration into *some particular subject's* rational economy. There's no equivocation—just one concept doing two pieces of explanatory work because they're aspects of the same metaphysical structure.

VERDICT

The defence fails.

The defence's core move—claiming the weak and strong readings are "different aspects" of one phenomenon—doesn't withstand scrutiny. Here's why:

The indexing problem is fatal. The defence claims that "rational integration into *this subject's* economy" automatically delivers the first-person asymmetry. But this is precisely where the equivocation bites. Consider:

- Weak reading: The Capgras belief is integrated into the patient's rational economy (it interacts with other beliefs, guides action, is rationally evaluable). This integration could be *described* from the third-person perspective—a neurologist could map how the belief fits into the patient's rational economy without the patient's reflective endorsement mattering constitutively.

- Strong reading: The belief's status as *the patient's* depends on the patient's own reflective rational engagement having constitutive force—not just that it's integrated into her economy, but that *her first-person rational self-governance* partially constitutes its being her belief.

These come apart. Third-person interpreters can identify states as "integrated into S's rational economy" (weak) without those states being "constitutively answerable to S's first-person reflective judgments" (strong). The mere fact of integration doesn't explain why *S's* perspective has special constitutive authority.

The body analogy fails. My body is responsive to my motor intentions in a way that chairs aren't—but this doesn't explain first-person authority about bodily states. I don't have first-person authority about whether my liver is functioning properly just because my liver is "my body" and integrated into my biological economy. The indexing (it's *my* body) doesn't automatically deliver epistemic or constitutive authority. Similarly, a state being integrated into *my* rational economy (indexing) doesn't automatically explain why *my* reflective judgments about it have constitutive force.

The counterexample defences reveal the equivocation. When defending against Capgras, the thesis relied on: "the belief is rationally integrated into the patient's economy" (weak reading). But this doesn't explain the asymmetry—a third-person interpreter can see this integration too. When explaining the asymmetry, the thesis needs: "the patient's first-person reflective judgments have special constitutive force" (strong reading). But the Capgras case shows these judgments *don't* have such force—the belief persists despite reflective rejection.

The thesis faces a dilemma it cannot escape:

- Use the weak reading: attitudes are individuated by rational integration into the subject's economy. This makes the individuation claim defensible but doesn't explain first-person authority's asymmetry (third-person observers can identify this integration too).

- Use the strong reading: attitudes are individuated by constitutive answerability to the subject's first-person reflective judgments. This would explain the asymmetry but is falsified by counterexamples (Capgras, implicit bias) and threatens circularity (building first-person authority into the individuation conditions rather than explaining it).

The defence's attempt to unify these by saying "they're aspects of one phenomenon" fails because it doesn't show *how* the weak reading (which is needed to handle counterexamples) delivers the strong reading (which is needed to explain the asymmetry). Merely insisting they're "the same" doesn't make it so.

The objection stands. The thesis equivocates, and cannot succeed on either reading alone.

O3. The asymmetry between self-ascription and other-ascription is not about authority but about temporal direction: self-ascriptions are prospective (answering 'what will I do/think?') while other-ascriptions are retrospective (answering 'what did they do/think?'), which explains the distinctive role of deliberation without requiring privileged access.

Scores
promise 4/5 · residual 5/5 · worst 5/5 · dead
Move · Target
reframing — The shared assumption that self- and other-ascription target the same facts about simultaneous present attitudes, differing only in method of access
Sketch

The standard framing treats self- and other-knowledge as competing answers to the same question ('what does X believe?') differing only in epistemic position. But Moran's insight about deliberation points elsewhere: when I self-ascribe 'I believe p,' I'm characteristically answering the question 'what's true?' or 'what should I do?', not 'what do I currently believe?'. The key reframing: self-ascription is future-directed—it's about what attitude I'll take into my planning and reasoning—while other-ascription is past-directed—it's about what attitudes explain completed behavior. This explains why deliberation about whether p settles what I believe without requiring introspection: I'm not discovering a present state but determining a future one. It explains the asymmetry: others can only interpret completed actions, while I'm positioned to constitute upcoming actions. Confabulation is compatible with this because confabulation is about past causes, while self-knowledge is about future commitments. The authority is temporal, not epistemic.

Appraiser (blind)
The prospective/retrospective temporal asymmetry offers a fresh angle on why deliberation matters without requiring introspection.
Objections
  • MISATTRIBUTION — landed 4/5, unanswered. The thesis misidentifies its target as 'the standard framing' when sophisticated theorists like Moran already reject the synchronic facts-plus-access model; the defence's claim to target 'the framework that makes debates intelligible' cannot be sustained when those debates already presuppose different temporal structures.
  • ALREADY TAKEN — landed 4/5, unanswered. The temporal framing is already implicit in Moran and Edgley's deliberativist accounts; the defence's attempt to distinguish 'containing temporal elements' from 'being organized around temporal direction' collapses because rational agency is inherently future-directed, making the distinction eliminable.
  • PROVES TOO MUCH — landed 5/5, unanswered. If temporal direction explained the asymmetry, similar asymmetries should appear for physical states with prospective/retrospective positioning; the defence's addition that beliefs are 'essentially future-oriented' concedes temporal direction alone doesn't explain authority, collapsing back to agential accounts.
  • COUNTEREXAMPLE — landed 5/5, unanswered. Retrospective self-ascription retains first-person distinctiveness despite being retrospective like other-ascription; the defence's claim that one can 're-occupy the prospective stance' appeals to memory and privileged access, undermining the temporal explanation and revealing the asymmetry persists without prospective positioning.
  • TRIVIAL — landed 4/5, unanswered. The thesis relabels the uncontroversial fact that deliberation is forward-looking and interpretation is backward-looking as 'prospective versus retrospective' without adding explanatory power; where it claims temporal direction explains rather than describes, it either becomes false or collapses into existing agential accounts.

Check this yourself: it is a claim about who holds what, made from recall.
Flaw

full exchange (10 turns)

KILLER (MISATTRIBUTION)

ATTEMPT. The thesis attributes to "the standard framing" a view that self- and other-ascription "target the same facts about simultaneous present attitudes, differing only in method of access." But this is not the actual position of the main theorists in this debate. Moran himself explicitly argues that self-ascription is NOT simply a different epistemic route to the same fact—his entire point in *Authority and Estrangement* is that first-person and third-person perspectives answer different questions and have different constitutive relations to their objects. Similarly, interpretivists like Davidson deny there are determinate "same facts" that both perspectives access; other-ascription is constitutively interpretive. Even traditional "privileged access" theorists like Shoemaker don't claim the perspectives differ "only in method"—they recognize functional and normative differences. The thesis attacks a crude Cartesian picture that contemporary philosophers explicitly reject. The actual debate is between those who (like Moran) emphasize the constitutive/deliberative dimension and those who emphasize transparency or interpretivism—not between people who think it's "same facts, different access" and those who don't.

STRENGTH: 4/5 — This is a serious problem. The thesis presents itself as reframing "the standard view," but that standard view is a straw position. The temporal-direction insight might be valuable, but it's not correcting the misunderstanding the thesis claims to correct.

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE

The objection misreads what "standard framing" picks out. The thesis does not claim to oppose Moran, Davidson, or sophisticated interpretivist positions—it claims to oppose *the framework that makes their debates intelligible*. Look at what those debates presuppose: when Moran distinguishes deliberative from attributive stances, or when Davidson contrasts interpretation with introspection, they still treat these as competing or complementary ways of *determining what someone believes now*. The question "What do I believe about p?" is treated as having a present-tense answer that can be approached deliberatively (asking whether p) or attributively (examining my dispositions). Even when theorists deny these are "the same fact differently accessed," they still treat them as facts about *present* mental states.

The temporal reframing cuts deeper. It's not that self- and other-ascription use different methods to access present beliefs—it's that they target *different temporal slices* of the subject. When I deliberate about whether p, I'm not determining what I currently believe (whether by constituting it or discovering it)—I'm determining what I *will* believe for purposes of downstream reasoning and action. Other-ascription, by contrast, necessarily interprets *completed* behavior and therefore targets what the subject believed *then*, at the moment of action.

This explains why even Moran's sophisticated view faces a puzzle: if deliberative self-ascription constitutes rather than discovers my belief, why does it feel like I'm answering a question about myself rather than merely deciding policy? Answer: because I'm answering a question about my *future* self—what attitude I'll carry forward—which is simultaneously constitutive (I determine it) and descriptive (it's about me).

The "standard framing" under attack is not any particular theorist's position but the temporal structure all parties assume: that self- and other-knowledge, however different their methods or constitutive relations, concern *synchronic* mental states.

VERDICT

The defence fails. Even granting the temporal insight has merit, the thesis misidentifies its target in a way that undermines its dialectical positioning.

First, the defence's own formulation collapses the distinction it needs. When it says Moran and others treat deliberation as "determining what someone believes now," this is precisely wrong: Moran's point is that deliberative self-ascription is *not* a determination of current state but a rational-agential stance that constitutes belief through commitment. The thesis tries to go "deeper" by adding temporal direction, but Moran's view already denies the synchronic-state picture.

Second, the defence claims other-ascription "necessarily interprets completed behavior" and therefore targets past beliefs. But this is false: I can attribute beliefs to you *now* based on what you're currently saying, your present dispositions, your ongoing behavior. Other-ascription is not inherently retrospective. The temporal asymmetry the thesis claims is not there.

Third, even if we granted a temporal dimension, it doesn't rescue the misattribution. The thesis presents itself as revealing that "the standard framing" wrongly assumes synchronic targets. But the actual debate already includes views (Moran's, interpretivism) that reject facts-plus-access models. The thesis isn't reframing that debate—it's restating one side of it while claiming to transcend it.

The thesis may contain an insight about prospective commitment versus retrospective interpretation, but it attacks a position that sophisticated participants in this debate have already abandoned. The "standard framing" it targets is not standard among the relevant theorists.

KILLER (ALREADY TAKEN)

ATTEMPT. The thesis claims originality for its "temporal direction" reframing, but this is essentially Edgley's (1969) and Moran's (2001) existing position with different terminology. Edgley explicitly argued that "What do I believe?" is answered by settling "What is true?" because belief-formation is prospective—oriented toward future reasoning and action—not retrospective discovery. Moran's entire deliberative account already contains the temporal asymmetry: deliberation determines what attitude I'll carry forward into action (prospective), while third-person attribution interprets completed behavior (retrospective). The thesis's claim that "self-ascription is future-directed—it's about what attitude I'll take into my planning" is precisely Moran's point about rational self-constitution through commitment. Even the confabulation point appears in Moran: confabulation concerns past causal history, while deliberative self-knowledge concerns prospective rational commitment. The thesis presents as novel "reframing" what is actually the established deliberativist position, merely adding explicit temporal vocabulary ("prospective/retrospective") to what Moran already argued about forward-looking rational agency versus backward-looking interpretation.

STRENGTH: 4/5 — This is serious damage. The thesis's core insight—that the asymmetry is temporal/directional rather than epistemic—is already the substance of existing deliberativist accounts. The explicit temporal framing might clarify, but doesn't constitute a genuine reframing of the debate.

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE

The objection conflates *containing temporal elements* with *being fundamentally organized around temporal direction*. Yes, Moran discusses prospective commitment and Edgley mentions future-oriented reasoning, but neither makes temporal direction the *explanatory basis* for the asymmetry. Their accounts remain primarily about rational authority, agential stance, or the transparency of belief to reasons—with temporal features appearing as consequences or accompaniments.

Look at how Moran actually structures his view: the asymmetry arises because deliberative self-ascription expresses rational agency while attributive other-ascription treats the subject as a natural object. The prospective element follows from this agential stance—I constitute my beliefs through rational commitment—but the fundamental explanation is *agential authority*, not *temporal direction*. Moran's question is "How does rational agency explain first-person authority?" not "How does temporal asymmetry explain it?"

The thesis inverts this explanatory order. It claims temporal direction is *basic*: the reason deliberation works for self-ascription is not primarily that I'm exercising rational agency, but that I'm positioned at the *front end* of my own mental trajectory while others are positioned at the *back end*. The authority follows from the temporal positioning, not vice versa.

This generates different predictions. On Moran's view, if I somehow lost rational agency over a domain (perhaps through compulsion or addiction), I'd lose first-person authority even while retaining prospective access—I'd be alienated from my own future states. On the temporal view, as long as I'm positioned to determine what I'll think going forward, the asymmetry remains even if that determination isn't fully rational. The temporal account explains why even akratic or compulsive self-ascription retains a distinctive first-person character that other-ascription lacks.

Moreover, neither Edgley nor Moran explicitly thematizes the retrospective character of other-ascription as the *complementary* element. They focus on why self-ascription is special (transparent, deliberative, agential), treating other-ascription as simply "lacking" these features. The thesis makes a stronger claim: other-ascription is *necessarily* retrospective because it interprets behavior that has already occurred, creating a structural temporal asymmetry. This is not merely "Moran with temporal vocabulary"—it's a different account of what generates the asymmetry.

VERDICT

The defence fails, though it dies fighting.

The attempt to distinguish "containing temporal elements" from "being organized around temporal direction" cannot be sustained given what Moran actually argues. In *Authority and Estrangement*, Moran explicitly says that deliberative self-knowledge is not about discovering present states but about determining what attitude to carry forward—this *is* making temporal direction explanatorily basic to that mode of self-knowledge, even if he doesn't use that exact terminology.

More critically, the defence's claim that "the authority follows from temporal positioning, not vice versa" doesn't actually distinguish the thesis from Moran. For Moran, rational agency *is* the capacity to determine one's future attitudes through present reasoning. The prospective character isn't a consequence of agency—it's constitutive of what rational agency *is*. Saying "temporal direction is basic" versus "agential authority is basic" is not a genuine distinction when agency is inherently future-directed.

The defence's example of compulsion backfires. On Moran's view, compulsive states *do* involve alienation precisely because I can't determine them deliberatively—they're not transparent to my reasoning about what to do. The thesis doesn't actually predict anything different here: if I'm genuinely compelled, I'm *not* positioned to determine what I'll think going forward through deliberation; I'm in the position of predicting my own behavior like an outside observer. Both views yield the same result.

The claim that neither Edgley nor Moran "thematizes the retrospective character of other-ascription" is strained. Moran extensively discusses how third-person attribution interprets completed behavior and past action—this is his entire account of the attributive stance. The thesis adds the word "retrospective" but doesn't add explanatory content.

What remains is this: the thesis makes explicit a temporal framing that is implicit in deliberativist accounts, and claims this temporal framing is *the* fundamental explanation. But the temporal and agential elements are so intertwined in existing accounts that "making it explicit" doesn't constitute reframing the debate—it restates one side of an existing debate (deliberativism vs. epistemic approaches) using temporal vocabulary. The thesis has not identified a genuinely new explanatory structure; it has relabeled an established one.

KILLER (PROVES TOO MUCH)

ATTEMPT

If the asymmetry between self- and other-ascription is fundamentally about temporal direction—self-ascription being prospective (what will I believe?) and other-ascription being retrospective (what did they believe?)—then this same asymmetry should appear wherever there's a difference in temporal positioning, regardless of whether we're dealing with mental states.

Consider my relationship to my own future physical states versus others' past physical states. I'm positioned at the "front end" of my bodily trajectory (what will my posture be? what will my heart rate be?) while others observe my completed physical behavior retrospectively. By the thesis's logic, I should have the same kind of "authority" about my future physical states that I have about my future beliefs—I should determine what my posture will be by deciding what posture to adopt, rather than predicting it. And others should only be able to interpret my *past* physical states, not my current ones.

But this is absurd. Others can observe and know my current posture perfectly well, not just my past postures. And my relationship to my future posture, while somewhat different from others' relationship to it, doesn't exhibit anything like the authority asymmetry that characterizes self-ascription of beliefs. The temporal positioning doesn't generate the special first-person authority.

The problem: if temporal direction explained the self/other asymmetry for mental states, it should explain a similar asymmetry for physical states. Since it doesn't, temporal direction cannot be the fundamental explanation. The weak point is the premise that prospective versus retrospective positioning is sufficient to generate the distinctive features of self-knowledge.

STRENGTH: 4/5

This does serious damage. The thesis claims temporal direction *explains* the asymmetry, but temporal asymmetries exist in many domains without generating anything like first-person authority. The argument proves too much because it would license the conclusion that mere temporal positioning creates authority, when clearly other factors (rational agency, the constitutive role of judgment) are doing the real work.

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE

The objection treats "temporal direction" as if it meant mere chronological positioning—I'm at time t₁ regarding my t₂ states, while you're at t₂ regarding my t₁ states. But this misses what makes the temporal asymmetry *explanatory* for mental states specifically: mental states are *essentially future-oriented* in a way physical states are not.

Belief is not just a state that happens to persist into the future—it is *constitutively* a state that guides future reasoning and action. To believe that p *just is* to be disposed to use p as a premise in practical and theoretical reasoning going forward. This is why Moore's paradox ("p is true but I don't believe it") is paradoxical: belief is not a free-standing state I might have or lack, but my stance toward what to take as settled for purposes of future thought and action.

Physical states like posture have no such essential futurity. My current posture is just a configuration of my body at this moment—it doesn't constitutively point forward to anything. So the temporal positioning that matters for beliefs (being positioned to *determine what will guide my future reasoning*) has no analog for posture.

This blocks the "proves too much" objection. The thesis is not that *any* prospective positioning creates authority. It's that prospective positioning creates authority *for states that are essentially constituted by their role in guiding future activity*. Beliefs are such states; postures are not.

The objection's claim that "others can observe my current posture" actually supports the thesis. Others can observe current posture precisely because posture is *not* essentially future-directed—it's a present configuration available to present observation. But they cannot observe my current belief in the same way, because belief is not a present configuration but a commitment that extends forward. They must *interpret* what belief would explain my behavior, which means working backward from completed action.

Even the objection's own example reveals this. It says I "determine what my posture will be by deciding what posture to adopt"—but this is precisely a case where I'm determining a *future* state through present decision, exactly as the thesis claims I do with belief. The difference is that with posture, this decision-based determination is *optional* (I can also just let my posture happen), while with belief it's *constitutive* (there is no belief except as what I carry forward into reasoning).

The thesis doesn't claim temporal positioning *alone* explains authority. It claims temporal positioning explains authority *for states that exist only as forward-looking commitments*—and beliefs are paradigmatically such states.

VERDICT

The defence fails, and the objection succeeds in showing the thesis proves too much.

The defence tries to save itself by adding that beliefs are "essentially future-oriented" while physical states are not. But this addition is fatal: it concedes that temporal direction *alone* doesn't explain the asymmetry—you also need the special nature of belief as future-guiding, commitment-involving, reason-responsive, etc. Once you've added all that, temporal direction is doing no independent explanatory work. You've just restated the standard deliberativist position (beliefs are constituted by rational commitments) with temporal language grafted on.

The defence claims "belief is constitutively a state that guides future reasoning and action"—but this *is* the agential/rational account, not an alternative to it. The "temporal" framing adds nothing. Saying "I'm positioned to determine what will guide my future reasoning" is just another way of saying "I'm positioned to constitute my beliefs through rational commitment." The temporal vocabulary is eliminable without loss.

Worse, the defence's own examples undermine it. It says with posture, "decision-based determination is optional (I can also just let my posture happen), while with belief it's constitutive." But this shows the asymmetry comes from the *optional versus constitutive* distinction, not from temporal direction. Many future-oriented physical states (my future location, my future weight) don't exhibit first-person authority despite my being prospectively positioned toward them. The authority comes from the constitutive role of rational decision, not from futurity.

The objection's force stands: if temporal direction explained the self/other asymmetry, we'd see similar asymmetries wherever there's prospective versus retrospective positioning. We don't. Therefore temporal direction is not the fundamental explanation. The thesis has identified a *feature* of self-knowledge (it's prospective) but mistaken it for an *explanation* of self-knowledge's distinctive character. The real explanation remains what Moran and others already argued: the constitutive role of rational agency, which happens to be future-directed because that's what agency is, but where the explanatory weight falls on *agency*, not *futurity*.

KILLER (COUNTEREXAMPLE)

ATTEMPT

Consider retrospective self-ascription: "What did I believe yesterday when I mailed that letter?" I'm now asking about my *past* mental state, not prospecting forward. According to the thesis, this should be structurally identical to other-ascription—both are retrospective, both interpret completed behavior. Yet there remains a distinctive first-person character even to retrospective self-ascription.

When I ask "Did I believe the letter would arrive on time?", I don't merely interpret my past behavior like an outside observer would. I have a distinctive kind of access: I can recall my reasoning, remember what seemed important to me, recognize which considerations moved me. This isn't infallible—I can be wrong about my past beliefs—but it's phenomenologically and epistemically different from how you would figure out what I believed yesterday.

The thesis predicts that once we're both looking backward at my completed action, the asymmetry should vanish—we're both in the retrospective position now. But the asymmetry persists. I still have a first-person perspective on my past self that you lack, even though neither of us is now prospectively positioned toward that past belief.

This shows temporal direction cannot be the fundamental explanation of the self/other asymmetry. The asymmetry appears even when the temporal positioning is the same (both retrospective). The weak point is the claim that prospective versus retrospective positioning *explains* the distinctive role of self-ascription.

STRENGTH: 5/5

This counterexample is decisive. It presents a case where the thesis's proposed explanation (temporal direction) is absent but the explanandum (self/other asymmetry) persists. Retrospective self-ascription is genuinely retrospective yet retains first-person distinctiveness. The thesis cannot survive this—it has mistaken a feature of *some* self-ascription (prospective deliberative cases) for the explanation of *all* self-ascription's special character.

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE

The objection assumes that retrospective self-ascription undermines the temporal thesis, but it actually reveals a crucial distinction the thesis can exploit: the difference between *temporal direction of the target* and *temporal position of the inquiry*.

When I ask "What did I believe yesterday?", I am indeed inquiring about a past state—but notice what I'm actually doing when I answer this question. I'm not merely interpreting completed behavior like an archaeologist examining artifacts. I'm *reconstructing my reasoning* by re-engaging with the question that faced me then: "Should I believe the letter will arrive on time?" I re-trace the deliberative path, re-consider the evidence I had, re-feel the force of the considerations that moved me.

This is still prospective in the relevant sense: I'm placing myself back at the *front end* of that past moment's trajectory, asking "What would I have concluded?" rather than "What state can I infer from the evidence?" I simulate being in the prospective position I occupied then. You cannot do this—you can only work backward from my completed action, because you were never positioned at the front end of my mental trajectory.

The phenomenological difference the objection notes—that retrospective self-ascription feels different from other-ascription—is explained by this: I can re-occupy the prospective stance even toward past moments, because I have access to what it was like to face those questions as open. You can only ever see my past as completed, because you were never positioned to experience those questions as mine to settle.

Consider the parallel with action. If I ask "Why did I turn left at the intersection?", I can answer by recalling "I was trying to avoid traffic"—I re-access my practical reasoning. This is different from how you would answer that question about me (by inferring from my behavior patterns). The difference isn't that I'm infallible about my past intentions, but that I can re-enter the practical deliberation that generated the action, while you can only interpret the action's results.

The thesis's core claim survives: the asymmetry is explained by my unique position at the front end of my own mental trajectory. For present/future self-ascription, I'm literally there now. For past self-ascription, I can *reconstruct being there* in a way you cannot, because I can re-engage with my own past deliberations as mine. The temporal direction that matters is not the temporal location of the target state, but the direction from which it can be approached—prospectively (through deliberation, even reconstructed deliberation) versus retrospectively (through behavioral interpretation).

The objection's "same temporal positioning" claim fails: we're not in the same position regarding my past belief. I can access it by re-occupying the prospective stance I had then; you can only access it by interpreting what I did then. The asymmetry persists because the temporal structure persists—I was positioned at the front end of that moment, you were not, and that difference remains accessible to me through memory in a way it cannot be to you.

VERDICT

The defence fails. The objection succeeds in showing that temporal direction cannot be the fundamental explanation of the self/other asymmetry.

The defence's move—claiming I can "re-occupy the prospective stance" toward past moments—is desperate and ultimately collapses. If retrospective self-ascription works by *reconstructing* or *simulating* the prospective position, then the explanation is not temporal direction itself but rather my special capacity to reconstruct my own reasoning. But what grounds that special capacity? Not temporal positioning—I'm not actually at the front end of yesterday's trajectory anymore. The explanation must be something else: memory of my own reasoning, privileged access to my past mental states, or the persistence of rational agency across time.

Moreover, the defence's own examples betray this. When it says "I can recall my reasoning, remember what seemed important to me, recognize which considerations moved me," it's appealing to *memory* and *privileged access*—exactly the epistemic resources the thesis claimed to avoid by reframing everything as temporal direction. If retrospective self-knowledge requires special memory access to my own past reasoning, then the asymmetry is epistemic after all, not temporal.

The "re-entering deliberation" move also proves too much. If I can re-enter my past deliberations to know my past beliefs, why can't you re-enter your reconstruction of my deliberations to know my past beliefs in the same way? The defence will say you weren't there, but that just pushes back to: why does having been there matter? Not because of temporal direction (we're both retrospective now), but because of some epistemic or metaphysical difference—perhaps that my past mental states are mine, that I have memory access, that there's personal continuity.

Most devastatingly, the objection reveals that temporal direction comes apart from the asymmetry. In retrospective self-ascription:
- Temporal direction: retrospective (same as other-ascription)
- Asymmetry: present (different from other-ascription)

This is a clean separation of the proposed explanation from the explanandum. When they come apart, we see the asymmetry persists without the temporal direction. Therefore temporal direction is not the fundamental explanation.

The thesis has mistaken a striking feature of *paradigm cases* of self-knowledge (deliberative, prospective self-ascription) for the *general explanation* of self-knowledge's distinctive character. But retrospective self-ascription shows the asymmetry can exist without prospective positioning. The real explanation must be something that's present in both prospective and retrospective self-ascription—perhaps rational agency, perhaps memory access, perhaps the constitutive role of judgment—but not temporal direction as such.

The counterexample is fatal. The thesis cannot explain why retrospective self-ascription retains first-person distinctiveness when the temporal positioning is retrospective on both sides.

KILLER (TRIVIAL)

ATTEMPT

The thesis claims to offer a "reframing" by distinguishing prospective self-ascription from retrospective other-ascription, but this distinction is trivial—it merely redescribes what everyone already accepts using temporal vocabulary without adding explanatory content.

Everyone in the debate already agrees that:
1. Self-ascription characteristically involves deliberation about what to believe/do
2. Deliberation is by nature forward-looking (you deliberate about what to think/do going forward)
3. Other-ascription characteristically involves interpreting behavior
4. Interpreting behavior means explaining what has already occurred

The thesis takes these uncontroversial observations and relabels them "prospective" versus "retrospective," then claims this constitutes a reframing. But calling deliberation "prospective" and interpretation "retrospective" is just attaching temporal adjectives to phenomena whose temporal character was already obvious and uncontested.

The supposed insight—"self-ascription is future-directed while other-ascription is past-directed"—is not a discovery but a verbal stipulation. Of course deliberation about what to believe concerns future reasoning; of course interpretation of behavior concerns past action. This is what those words *mean*. The thesis dresses up this conceptual truism as if it were revealing a hidden structure, but it's merely making explicit what was already implicit in the very concepts of "deliberation" and "interpretation."

The weak point: the claim that temporal direction provides a new explanation. It provides only a new description of the same phenomena everyone already recognized, making this a verbal repackaging rather than a substantive reframing.

STRENGTH: 4/5

This does serious damage. While the thesis presents itself as revealing a fundamental explanatory structure, it's actually just renaming familiar features of deliberation and interpretation using temporal language. The "reframing" collapses into a terminological choice that adds no explanatory power to existing accounts.

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE

The objection mistakes *making explicit* for *being trivial*. Yes, everyone implicitly recognizes that deliberation is forward-looking and interpretation is backward-looking—but no one has made temporal direction the *organizing principle* that explains why the asymmetry exists and takes the form it does. The difference between implicit recognition and explicit theoretical organization is not trivial.

Compare: everyone implicitly recognized that material objects displace water, but Archimedes' principle wasn't trivial—it made displacement the *explanatory basis* for understanding buoyancy. Similarly, everyone implicitly recognizes temporal features of deliberation and interpretation, but the thesis makes temporal direction the *explanatory basis* for understanding the self/other asymmetry.

This generates new theoretical purchase. Consider how the debate has been structured: theorists argue about whether self-knowledge requires privileged access (traditionalists), or rational transparency (Moran), or interpretive charity (Davidson). These seem like competing explanations. But if temporal direction is fundamental, these are not competitors but *consequences*:

- I don't need "privileged access" to my future states—I *constitute* them, which is why access seems privileged
- Deliberation isn't "transparent" to truth as a special epistemic method—it's the mechanism by which I determine what I'll take as true going forward
- Other-ascription isn't interpretive because minds are "essentially interpretable"—it's interpretive because it must work backward from completed action

The temporal reframing reveals these as different descriptions of the same underlying structure, not genuine alternatives. This is not trivial redescription—it's theoretical unification.

Moreover, making temporal direction explicit solves puzzles that remain open on other views. Why does deliberative self-knowledge feel simultaneously *authoritative* (I settle what I believe) and *constrained* (I can't just decide arbitrarily)? Because I'm determining a future state that must connect coherently with my present state—I have authority over the future but must respect continuity with the present. This falls directly out of the temporal structure, but remains mysterious on purely epistemic or purely agential accounts.

The objection claims the temporal character "was already obvious and uncontested," but this is false. The debate has been structured around epistemic access, rational agency, and interpretive methodology—not temporal direction. If temporal direction were already the recognized organizing principle, there would be no debate about whether self-knowledge requires introspection versus deliberation versus interpretation. The thesis shows these are not competing accounts of *how* we know our minds, but descriptions of different temporal relationships to mental states.

The charge of triviality confuses "implicit in the phenomena" with "explicit in the theory." Gravity was implicit in falling apples, but Newton's theory wasn't trivial. The temporal structure is implicit in deliberation and interpretation, but making it the theoretical foundation transforms how we understand the debate.

VERDICT

The defence fails. The objection succeeds in showing the thesis is trivial—or more precisely, that the thesis oscillates between being trivial and being false, never achieving substantive novelty.

The defence's analogies backfire. Archimedes' principle wasn't just "making explicit that objects displace water"—it provided a *quantitative law* that enabled prediction and explanation beyond what was previously possible. Newton didn't just "make explicit that apples fall"—he unified terrestrial and celestial mechanics under a single mathematical framework. The thesis does nothing comparable. It observes that deliberation is future-directed and interpretation is past-directed, then claims this "explains" the asymmetry. But this is circular: deliberation is future-directed *because* it's about determining what to think going forward; interpretation is past-directed *because* it's about explaining what has occurred. Saying "the asymmetry exists because of temporal direction" is like saying "apples fall because of downward motion"—it redescribes the phenomenon without explaining it.

The defence claims temporal direction "generates new theoretical purchase" by showing that privileged access, transparency, and interpretation are "consequences" rather than "competitors." But look at what it actually says:

- "I don't need privileged access to my future states—I constitute them" — This is just Moran's constitutive account with "future" added. The explanatory work is done by "constitute," not by "future."

- "Deliberation isn't transparent to truth as a special epistemic method—it's the mechanism by which I determine what I'll take as true" — Again, this is the transparency account with temporal language. The mechanism is deliberation; "going forward" adds nothing.

- "Other-ascription is interpretive because it must work backward from completed action" — But other-ascription of *current* states also interprets current behavior/dispositions. The "backward" is inessential.

Each supposed "consequence" is actually just the original account with temporal vocabulary grafted on. The unification is verbal, not explanatory.

Most tellingly, the defence's own puzzle-solution fails. It asks: "Why does deliberative self-knowledge feel simultaneously authoritative and constrained?" and answers: "Because I'm determining a future state that must connect coherently with my present state." But this doesn't explain anything—it just restates the puzzle in temporal terms. *Why* must my future state connect coherently with my present state? Because of rational norms, because of the nature of belief, because of agential continuity—all the resources the thesis claimed to avoid by reframing temporally. The temporal vocabulary is eliminable without loss.

The objection's core point stands: the thesis takes uncontroversial features of deliberation (it's about what to think/do next) and interpretation (it explains what happened), relabels them "prospective" and "retrospective," and presents this as a theoretical advance. But everyone already knew deliberation is forward-looking and interpretation is backward-looking. Making this explicit doesn't unify competing theories—it just describes what those theories were already about using different words.

The thesis is trivial because its central claim—that self-ascription is prospective and other-ascription is retrospective—is true by definition of "deliberation" and "interpretation," and adds no explanatory power to existing accounts. Where it tries to go beyond mere redescription (claiming temporal direction *explains* rather than *describes* the asymmetry), it either becomes false (retrospective self-ascription counterexample) or collapses back into existing accounts (agency, rationality, constitution).

The reframing is not a reframing. It's a relabeling.

O4. The confabulation literature shows not that introspection is interpretive all the way down, but that conscious self-knowledge requires both non-interpretive acquaintance with occurrent phenomenology AND interpretation of that phenomenology's attitudinal significance—first-person authority attaches only to the phenomenological component.

Scores
promise 3/5 · residual 4/5 · worst 4/5 · wounded
Move · Target
distinction — Both sides' assumption that self-knowledge is monolithic—either wholly observational or wholly interpretive
Sketch

The argument draws a distinction that the debate has overlooked: between knowing what conscious state you're in (phenomenologically) versus knowing what that state means (attitudinally).
