However, the objection reveals that the thesis's critical moves—denying special epistemic access, explaining apparent authority through non-epistemic factors—are NOT novel to the dialectical landscape. The thesis is better understood as radicalizing the expressivist-dispositionalist program by eliminating even the residual metaphysical specialness those views preserve, rather than introducing an entirely new framework.

The defence holds because the thesis occupies a distinct position: it's more deflationary than Bar-On (no special expression-relation), more deflationary than Schwitzgebel (no constitutive role), and more deflationary than Gopnik (no inference, just vanishing uncertainty). But the objection correctly identifies that the thesis is operating within an established anti-epistemic tradition rather than reframing the entire debate. The thesis survives but must present itself as the *most radical* deflationary position rather than as a wholesale reframing that leaves all previous views behind.

The "already taken" charge partially sticks: the territory is occupied, but the thesis claims the most extreme position within it—one that even other deflationists haven't fully embraced.

KILLER (PROVES TOO MUCH)

KILLER (PROVES TOO MUCH)

ATTEMPT

The thesis argues that first-person authority vanishes diachronically, proving it was never genuine epistemic privilege but merely temporal proximity plus control. But this argument, if it worked, would prove too much: it would show that NO form of epistemic privilege exists, since all epistemic relations degrade over time.

Consider perceptual knowledge. I have privileged epistemic access to what I'm currently seeing—I know the cup is on the table before me with an immediacy and certainty you lack. But do I have the same authority about what I saw yesterday? Clearly not—I'm now consulting memory, liable to confabulation, in basically the same interpretive position as someone who heard me describe it yesterday. By the thesis's logic, this diachronic degradation should prove that perceptual privilege was never real—just "temporal proximity plus interpretive control over current perceptual reports."

The same applies to introspective access to sensations. My authority about current pain vanishes for yesterday's pain. Does this prove pain-knowledge was never privileged? To proprioceptive knowledge of body position—my immediate knowledge of where my limbs are now doesn't extend to where they were yesterday. To occurrent thought—I know what I'm currently thinking with an immediacy that evaporates for yesterday's thoughts.

If the thesis's reasoning were sound, it would eliminate epistemic privilege entirely, reducing all apparently immediate knowledge to "temporal proximity to information sources plus control over current reports." But this is absurd—we DO recognize genuine epistemic privilege in perception, introspection of sensations, etc., even though these privileges don't persist unchanged across time. The thesis mistakes the truism that epistemic access degrades with temporal distance for the radical claim that temporal degradation proves there was never privilege at all.

STRENGTH: 4/5 — This is serious damage. The thesis must explain why diachronic degradation reveals first-person authority about beliefs/attitudes as illusory, but doesn't similarly reveal perceptual or sensory authority as illusory, without ad hoc special pleading.

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE.

The objection misses a crucial asymmetry: perceptual and sensory privileges degrade diachronically because *the objects of knowledge disappear or change*, while first-person authority about propositional attitudes degrades even though *the objects remain stable and accessible*.

When my perceptual authority about the cup vanishes yesterday, it's because the perceptual relation no longer obtains—the cup may have moved, the lighting changed, my visual system is no longer receiving information from it. The epistemic privilege was tied to an active perceptual link that genuinely no longer exists. Similarly with pain: yesterday's pain is *gone*. The sensation itself has ceased to exist. I can't have privileged access to it because there's nothing there to access. The object of knowledge has vanished.

But beliefs and attitudes are different. My belief that Kant was wrong about noumena—the one I held yesterday—still exists in exactly the same form. It hasn't disappeared, hasn't changed its content, remains stably mine. If first-person authority were genuine epistemic privilege over one's own propositional attitudes *as such*, it should persist when the attitudes persist. The fact that it doesn't—that I lose authority merely because time has passed, not because the belief has changed or vanished—reveals the authority was never about privileged access to the attitude itself.

Moreover, there's a second asymmetry: perceptual and sensory states are *constitutively tied to current causal processes*. Seeing requires current photon-retina interaction; pain requires current nociceptor firing. These states are metaphysically bound to the present in a way that beliefs aren't. A belief is a standing state, dispositional or otherwise, that persists across time. If I had genuine epistemic privilege over my beliefs *qua mental states I bear*, temporal distance alone shouldn't destroy it—I should be able to access yesterday's belief through memory with something approaching the same authority, just as I can access my reasons for past actions with special understanding unavailable to you.

The thesis doesn't prove too much because it exploits features specific to propositional attitudes: they're (1) temporally stable objects that (2) remain accessible to their subject across time through memory, yet (3) authority about them evaporates anyway. This combination—stable object, continued access, vanishing authority—is what reveals the authority was never about epistemic privilege over the states themselves.

Consider the contrast: If pain persisted unchanged from yesterday but I lost all authority about it, that WOULD prove pain-authority was illusory. But pain doesn't persist—it's an occurrent state. If perceptual information remained available unchanged but I lost perceptual authority, that would prove perceptual authority was illusory. But the information doesn't remain available—the perceptual link breaks. Beliefs DO persist, information about them DOES remain available (through memory), yet authority vanishes. That's the revealing pattern.

The thesis can even embrace a version of the objection's point: maybe perceptual "privilege" is ALSO partly temporal proximity to information! But there's a residual difference—perception involves a distinctive causal-informational link (photons → retina → visual processing) that genuinely doesn't obtain diachronically. First-person authority about beliefs has no such distinctive link to appeal to. When we strip away temporal proximity and current control, there's no epistemic residue left. That's the difference.

VERDICT.

The defence succeeds, but reveals important clarifications the thesis must make explicit.

The key move is distinguishing states that are *constitutively occurrent* (pains, perceptions, occurrent thoughts) from states that are *temporally stable* (beliefs, desires, intentions). For occurrent states, diachronic degradation is explained by the state's disappearance—there's nothing to have authority about anymore. For stable states, diachronic degradation cannot be explained this way, since the state persists. This makes the degradation revealing: if authority were genuine epistemic privilege over the state *as such*, it should survive the state's survival.

The objection is right that the thesis's reasoning, applied indiscriminately, would prove too much. But applied discriminately—to standing propositional attitudes specifically—it proves exactly what the thesis claims. The thesis must make explicit that it targets first-person authority about *beliefs, desires, intentions*—standing states that persist across time—not occurrent experiences that are metaphysically tied to the present moment.

There's a residual challenge: what about occurrent thoughts? I think "Kant was wrong" right now—that's an occurrent mental event, not a standing state. Does my authority about it survive diachronically? The thesis predicts: no, and for the same reason authority about yesterday's pain doesn't survive—the occurrent thought is gone. But if I formed a belief through that thought, and the belief persists, my authority about the belief should persist too if authority were real privilege. It doesn't. That's the revealing case.

The defence holds. The thesis doesn't prove too much because it exploits the specific temporal profile of propositional attitudes: they're stable enough that diachronic authority-loss can't be explained by object-disappearance, revealing that synchronic authority was never about the object at all—just proximity plus control.

O8. First-person authority comes apart into two phenomena—avowal authority (my saying 'I believe P' settles whether I count as believing P for conversational purposes) and epistemic authority (privileged access to what I actually believe)—and the interpretive turn threatens only the latter while naturally explaining the former.

Scores
promise 3/5 · residual 4/5 · worst 4/5 · wounded
Move · Target
distinction — The shared assumption across Bar-On, Moran, Carruthers, and Gopnik that first-person authority is a single phenomenon requiring a unified explanation
Sketch

The debate assumes 'first-person authority' is unitary, but we should distinguish conversational from metaphysical authority. When I sincerely avow 'I believe global warming is real,' this speech act typically makes it true for practical purposes that I hold this belief—my community defers to my self-constitution. This authority is inherently normative and social, flowing from our practice of holding people to their self-ascriptions. The interpretive turn naturally explains this: interpretation is constrained by avowal uptake, not vice versa. What interpretation threatens is only a separate claim—that I have observational access to belief-states with robust causal-functional identity conditions independent of my self-conception. Bar-On and Moran conflate these when defending first-person authority; Carruthers and Gopnik when attacking it. Once separated, we can grant the interpretivists their epistemic point while preserving what matters about authority.

Appraiser (blind)
Distinguishing conversational from metaphysical authority is useful but the move is fairly standard in recent literature.
Objections
  • MISATTRIBUTION — landed 4/5, unanswered. Bar-On's neo-expressivism already treats avowal authority as non-epistemic; the thesis falsely claims to introduce this insight
  • COUNTEREXAMPLE — landed 2/5, answered. Self-deception shows defeasibility not absence; the case actually requires the thesis's distinction to be intelligible
  • TRIVIAL — landed 3/5, unanswered. The thesis oversells novelty and depends on an unargued performative account; it's less revolutionary than claimed
  • EQUIVOCATION — landed 4/5, unanswered. The thesis trades between normative-power and epistemic-privilege readings to make metaphysically different things seem like coordinate aspects
  • UNFALSIFIABLE — landed 2/5, answered. The thesis makes genuine commitments that could be refuted, though it needs tightening to be properly testable
⚑ Target attribution disputed — Bar-On's neo-expressivism already treats avowal authority as non-epistemic; the thesis falsely claims to introduce this insight Check this yourself: it is a claim about who holds what, made from recall.
🔧 Survives as

The interpretivism debate about first-person authority conflates two questions—whether subjects have normative power to constitute themselves as believers through avowal (which interpretivism preserves) and whether they have privileged epistemic access to interpretation-independent belief-states (which interpretivism threatens)—and recognizing this conflation shows the debate involves equivocation rather than substantive disagreement

Flaw

The thesis misattributes novelty (Bar-On already makes key moves), equivocates on 'authority' between metaphysically different phenomena to make them seem like coordinate aspects of one thing, and oversells a conceptually familiar distinction as revolutionary discovery

full exchange (10 turns)

KILLER (MISATTRIBUTION)

ATTEMPT. The thesis targets "the shared assumption across Bar-On, Moran, Carruthers, and Gopnik that first-person authority is a single phenomenon requiring a unified explanation." But this misrepresents at least Bar-On's actual position. In *Speaking My Mind* (2004), Bar-On explicitly distinguishes between security (immunity from certain kinds of error) and authority (entitlement to make claims), and further distinguishes semantic from epistemic dimensions of self-knowledge. Her neo-expressivist view precisely aims to explain how avowals have a special status that differs from straightforward epistemic access—avowals are groundless but authoritative in a way that doesn't require introspective observation. This is structurally similar to the distinction the thesis claims to introduce. Moran in *Authority and Estrangement* (2001) also doesn't treat first-person authority as requiring a "unified explanation"—his deliberative-transparency account applies specifically to active, rational self-knowledge, not to all forms of first-person access. The thesis attacks a homogenized position that flattens these theorists' actual distinctions into a simple unity thesis none of them holds.

STRENGTH: 4/5 — This is a serious problem. The thesis presents its distinction as novel and presents named targets as conflating what they actually distinguish. Bar-On especially appears misrepresented, since her entire project involves drawing distinctions within first-person authority rather than treating it as unitary.

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE

The objection trades on a verbal coincidence. Yes, Bar-On distinguishes security from authority, and semantic from epistemic dimensions. Yes, Moran restricts his account to deliberative self-knowledge. But these distinctions operate *within* a shared framework that the thesis rejects—the framework that treats first-person authority as fundamentally an epistemic phenomenon requiring explanation in terms of access, knowledge, or special warrant.

Bar-On's distinction between security and authority still concerns *how we know* our mental states—she asks whether avowals involve error-prone mechanisms and whether they constitute knowledge. Her neo-expressivism explains why avowals needn't be based on observation *while still being authoritative knowledge-claims*. The semantic/epistemic distinction concerns different aspects of the *same epistemic relation*. Similarly, Moran's deliberative account explains a particular *route to self-knowledge*—transparency through deliberation. He distinguishes this from other epistemic routes (introspection, inference), but still treats the question as "how do we know our minds?"

The thesis's distinction cuts differently. Avowal authority isn't an epistemic phenomenon at all—it's not a way of knowing but a social-normative practice of self-constitution through speech acts. When I avow "I believe P," I'm not reporting a pre-existing state (well or badly, directly or indirectly); I'm *making myself count* as a P-believer in the conversational space. This is performative, not epistemic.

All four theorists—including Bar-On despite her distinctions—treat first-person authority as residing in a special epistemic relation between subject and mental state. The thesis claims this entire framing is confused: what looks like epistemic privilege is actually normative authority to constitute oneself as a believer for social purposes. Bar-On's distinctions are refinements within the epistemic paradigm; the thesis's distinction *abandons* that paradigm for one domain of first-person authority.

The misattribution charge fails because drawing distinctions within the category "epistemic self-knowledge" doesn't preclude treating first-person authority as fundamentally epistemic—which all four theorists do, and which the thesis denies.

VERDICT

The defence fails, though not completely.

The defence succeeds in showing that Bar-On's and Moran's internal distinctions don't automatically vindicate them against the charge—one can draw distinctions within an epistemic framework while still being vulnerable to the claim that the framework itself is wrong for part of the domain.

But the defence cannot save the thesis from misattribution for two reasons:

First, Bar-On's neo-expressivism actually *does* move beyond pure epistemic explanation for avowals. Her claim that avowals are "groundless" expressions rather than knowledge-claims based on self-observation is precisely a move toward treating avowal authority as *not* fundamentally epistemic. She explicitly resists the idea that avowals require epistemic warrant in the standard sense. The thesis claims to introduce the idea that avowal authority is non-epistemic; Bar-On has already substantially developed this idea, even if not in identical terms.

Second, the thesis's framing—that it targets "the shared assumption... that first-person authority is a single phenomenon requiring a unified explanation"—is textually false. Moran explicitly doesn't offer a unified explanation; he offers an account of one species of self-knowledge while acknowledging others. Bar-On explicitly fragments the phenomenon. The thesis needed to target something these theorists *actually* share (perhaps: "the assumption that avowal authority requires epistemic grounding") rather than attributing to them a crude unificationism they explicitly reject.

The thesis survives as a substantive position but fails as dialectical criticism of these particular targets. The distinction may be worth drawing more sharply than Bar-On draws it, but it's not the revolutionary break from "the debate" that the thesis claims.

KILLER (COUNTEREXAMPLE)

ATTEMPT. Consider the case of self-deceptive avowal. I sincerely say "I believe my marriage is fine" while exhibiting all the behavioral and emotional signs of someone who believes their marriage is failing—I've consulted divorce lawyers, I flinch at my spouse's touch, I've told my therapist I think it's over.

According to the thesis, my avowal should give me "avowal authority"—my saying "I believe my marriage is fine" should "settle whether I count as believing [this] for conversational purposes" and my community should "defer to my self-constitution." But this seems precisely backward. In actual practice, my community does NOT defer to this avowal. My friends say "you don't really believe that" or "you're fooling yourself." The avowal fails to make it conversationally true that I believe my marriage is fine. Indeed, the whole point of recognizing self-deception is that avowals can fail to establish what someone believes even for conversational purposes.

This counterexample targets the "avowal authority" premise—the claim that sincere self-ascription settles belief-attribution in conversational contexts. Self-deception cases show that communities regularly override avowals when they conflict with other evidence, meaning avowal authority is not the robust social-normative phenomenon the thesis requires to do its distinguishing work.

STRENGTH: 4/5 — This is a serious problem. The thesis needs avowal authority to be a genuine, stable phenomenon distinct from epistemic authority, but paradigm cases of self-deception suggest that conversational practice doesn't actually grant the authority the thesis claims it does.

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE

The objection misidentifies the scope of avowal authority by selecting an atypical case where the authority is *defeated*, then treating this defeat as evidence the authority never existed. But defeasibility is not absence.

Avowal authority is a *default* normative status, not an indefeasible trump. The practice works like this: sincere first-person avowals create a presumption that binds conversational participants—you count as believing what you avow *unless* there are special defeating conditions. Self-deception is precisely one such defeater, but its status as a defeater presupposes the default authority it defeats.

Notice the dialectical structure of the self-deception case. Your friends don't say "we've observed your belief-state and it differs from what you report." They say "you don't *really* believe that" or "*you're fooling yourself*." These locutions acknowledge that your avowal normally *would* settle the matter—the whole point is that something has gone wrong with your authority, not that you never had it. Self-deception is recognized as a *malfunction* of first-person authority, which presupposes that authority is the functional norm.

Compare: a court's verdicts normally settle legal questions, even though verdicts can be overturned on appeal. The existence of appellate review doesn't show courts lack authority—it shows their authority is defeasible under special circumstances. Similarly, the community's ability to override avowals in self-deception cases doesn't eliminate avowal authority; it shows that authority has limits.

Moreover, self-deception cases actually *support* the thesis's distinction. When we override someone's avowal in self-deception, what are we doing? We're claiming that their sincere self-ascription fails to track what they *epistemically* believe—the belief-state with "robust causal-functional identity conditions independent of self-conception." We're saying: "Your avowal would normally make you count as believing P, but in this case there's an underlying psychological reality (your *actual* belief that the marriage is failing) that your avowal fails to constitute or express."

This is exactly the two-tier structure the thesis describes. Avowal authority is the conversational-normative level (normally, your saying "I believe P" makes you count as a P-believer). Epistemic authority is the metaphysical-psychological level (privileged access to what you *actually* believe). Self-deception is interesting precisely because these come apart—you exercise your avowal authority (you sincerely self-ascribe) but this fails to align with the epistemic reality (what you actually believe).

The objection treats self-deception as defeating avowal authority. The thesis explains self-deception as a case where avowal authority is exercised but doesn't track epistemic reality—which is possible only if these are distinct phenomena.

VERDICT

The defence succeeds.

The key move—that defeasibility is not absence—is sound. Avowal authority can be a real normative phenomenon even if it has limits. The objection needed to show that avowals *generally* fail to settle conversational belief-attribution, but self-deception is precisely a *special* case, marked as special by our very recognition of it as self-deception.

More importantly, the defence's final move is powerful: self-deception cases actually *require* the thesis's distinction to be properly understood. We can only make sense of "you don't really believe what you're saying" if there are two different things in play—a conversational status (what you're making yourself count as believing) and an underlying psychological reality (what you actually believe). If first-person authority were unitary, self-deception would be unintelligible.

The objection fails because it mistakes a defeater condition for evidence that the defeated authority doesn't exist. But defeaters presuppose defaults. The very practice of recognizing self-deception—of saying someone's avowal doesn't settle what they believe—confirms rather than undermines the thesis's claim that avowal authority is normally operative and distinct from epistemic access.

KILLER (TRIVIAL)

ATTEMPT. The thesis presents its distinction as a substantive discovery about the nature of first-person authority, but it's actually just a terminological repackaging of the trivial observation that "authority" is ambiguous between normative and epistemic senses.

Every domain exhibits this same structure: legal authority (normative power to create legal facts) versus epistemic authority about legal matters; parental authority (normative power over children) versus epistemic authority about one's children; authorial authority (normative control over what's canonical) versus epistemic authority about one's text's meaning. The thesis simply applies this standing conceptual distinction to self-knowledge and gives the two senses labels ("avowal authority" vs "epistemic authority").

The apparent substance comes from *stipulating* that "avowal authority" means something performative-constitutive rather than reportive, then claiming this is threatened differently by interpretivism than epistemic authority is. But this is just definitional. Once you've *defined* avowal authority as "conversational self-constitution through speech acts" and epistemic authority as "access to independently-existing mental states," it's analytically true that interpretivism (which denies independently-existing mental states) threatens only the latter. The thesis hasn't discovered that first-person authority comes apart into two phenomena; it's verbally stipulated two different things and labeled them both "authority."

The supposedly novel insight—that what looks like one phenomenon is really two—reduces to the uncontested observation that "authority" has multiple senses, dressed up with theoretical vocabulary about avowals and interpretation.

STRENGTH: 2/5 — This attack has some force but doesn't quite work. While the thesis does trade on an ambiguity in "authority," it's not merely *applying* a standing distinction—it's making a substantive claim that in the first-person case specifically, these two kinds of authority have been conflated in ways that matter for the interpretivism debate. The claim that avowal authority is performative-constitutive rather than reportive is a substantive thesis about speech acts and self-knowledge, not just a verbal stipulation. The weakness is real (the distinction itself isn't novel), but there's enough substantive content about *how* these authorities operate in self-knowledge to avoid pure triviality.

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE

The objection confuses *conceptual resources* with *substantive claims*. Yes, normative versus epistemic authority is a general conceptual distinction. But applying it to first-person authority isn't trivial—it's a substantive claim that requires argument, and if true, reorganizes our understanding of self-knowledge debates.

Consider an analogy. Everyone knows the general distinction between *being* F and *being called* F. Applying this to witch trials is not trivial—the claim "there's a difference between being a witch and being called a witch, and witch trials conflate them" is substantive and important. Similarly, that normative and epistemic authority are conceptually distinguishable doesn't make it trivial to claim that first-person authority *actually instantiates* both, that they've been *conflated* in the literature, and that recognizing this *resolves* a theoretical impasse.

The thesis makes several substantive, non-trivial claims:

First, that avowal authority is *performatively constitutive*—that sincere self-ascription doesn't report a pre-existing belief but makes one count as a believer in conversational space. This isn't definitional; it's a claim about the metaphysics and pragmatics of avowal that could be false. Maybe avowals are always reports, never performances. Maybe self-ascription never constitutes belief-status but only reveals it. These are live alternatives.

Second, that this performative authority is *what matters* about first-person authority—that when we care about first-person authority in ordinary life, we care about avowal authority, not epistemic access. This is a claim about the *point* of first-person authority that could be contested. Maybe what matters is accurate self-knowledge, not social self-constitution.

Third, that interpretivism threatens epistemic but not avowal authority—and crucially, that this *dissolves* rather than *takes a side in* the debate about whether interpretivism undermines first-person authority. This is a substantive philosophical move: showing that what looks like a substantive disagreement (does interpretivism destroy first-person authority?) rests on equivocation. This is non-trivial even if the distinction used to expose the equivocation is itself familiar.

Fourth, that Bar-On, Moran, Carruthers, and Gopnik *actually conflate* these—that the distinction, though conceptually available, has not been properly deployed in this debate. This is an empirical claim about the literature that could be false.

Compare: "Free will debates conflate liberty (ability to do what you want) and ultimate sourcehood (being the ultimate cause of your choices)" uses a conceptually available distinction but makes a substantive claim—that this distinction *explains* why free will debates seem intractable, and that compatibilists and incompatibilists are talking past each other. This isn't trivial even though the liberty/sourcehood distinction is conceptually straightforward.

The thesis does the same structural work. It claims that a conceptually available distinction has been *missed* in a specific debate, and that recognizing it *resolves* that debate by showing the participants equivocate. That's substantive philosophical work, not verbal stipulation.

Finally, the objection claims the thesis "stipulates" that avowal authority is performative-constitutive. But this isn't stipulation—it's a *theory* of what avowal authority consists in, offered with reasons (our practice of holding people to avowals, the social-normative character of self-constitution). The thesis could be wrong about this. Maybe avowal authority is just highly reliable epistemic access that we treat as normatively binding. The performative account is a substantive claim requiring defense, not a definition.

VERDICT

The defence succeeds, but only partially.

The defence is right that applying a general distinction to a specific domain can be substantive rather than trivial, and right that several of the thesis's claims go beyond mere verbal stipulation. The claim that avowal authority is performatively constitutive rather than epistemic-reportive is indeed substantive. The claim that this distinction dissolves rather than resolves the interpretivism debate is genuine philosophical work.

However, the defence cannot fully save the thesis from the triviality charge for two reasons:

First, the thesis oversells its novelty. The defence retreats to "this distinction has been *missed* in the debate," but this is weaker than the thesis's original presentation, which frames itself as discovering that first-person authority "comes apart into two phenomena" as if this were a new finding. If the distinction is conceptually familiar and the work is just *applying* it to show equivocation, that's valuable but less revolutionary than the thesis suggests. The thesis needed to be framed more modestly from the start.

Second, and more seriously, the substantive content depends entirely on the performative-constitutive account of avowal authority being correct and non-obvious. But is it? The idea that avowals have performative force—that sincere self-ascription has constitutive effects on one's social identity as a believer—is not particularly novel. Speech act theory has long recognized that self-ascriptions can be performative. The thesis needs this to be *the correct account* of what avowal authority fundamentally is, not just one dimension of it. But the thesis hasn't argued for this; it's asserted it. And if avowal authority turns out to be just a special case of highly reliable epistemic access that we treat as normatively binding (the alternative the defence mentions), then the distinction collapses back into a verbal repackaging.

The thesis survives the triviality charge but is wounded. It's not *purely* trivial—there's real work in showing that a debate equivocates and that recognizing the equivocation matters. But the thesis is less novel than it claims, and its substantive content depends on a performative account of avowal that it asserts rather than establishes. A more modest framing—"the debate conflates two kinds of authority that should be distinguished"—would be more defensible than the current presentation as a discovery that first-person authority "comes apart."

KILLER (EQUIVOCATION)

ATTEMPT

The thesis equivocates on "authority" in a way that makes its central argument work only by trading between readings.

On one reading, "authority" means *normative power*—the capacity to make something the case through one's say-so. On this reading, "avowal authority" is plausible: when I say "I believe P," I genuinely make myself count as a P-believer in conversational space through a performative speech act. This is a real social-normative phenomenon.

On another reading, "authority" means *epistemic privilege*—special access or warrant regarding some domain. On this reading, "epistemic authority" is interesting: the claim that I have privileged access to my mental states is philosophically substantive and what's actually at stake in debates about interpretivism.

The thesis needs *both* readings to work. It needs "avowal authority" to be plausible (so it uses the normative-power reading—of course I can constitute myself as a believer through speech acts). And it needs "epistemic authority" to be what interpretivism threatens (so it uses the epistemic-privilege reading—interpretivism denies introspective access to belief-states).

But here's the problem: the thesis claims these are "two phenomena" that first-person authority "comes apart into," suggesting they're both species of the *same* kind of thing (authority) that happen to diverge. Yet they're not the same kind of thing at all—one is a normative power, the other is an epistemic relation. The argument works by using "authority" to cover both, making it seem like we're tracking a single phenomenon that splits, when we're actually just noting that two completely different things both get called "authority."

The payoff—that interpretivism threatens only epistemic authority while preserving avowal authority—only seems interesting if these are genuinely two aspects of *one* phenomenon (first-person authority). If they're just two unrelated things that happen to share a word, then the claim reduces to: "Interpretivism threatens epistemic access but not performative speech acts." True, but trivial—of course a theory about the metaphysics of mental states doesn't threaten the pragmatics of self-ascription. These operate in completely different domains.

The thesis cannot run on either reading alone. On the pure normative-power reading, there's no interesting connection to the interpretivism debate (which is about epistemic access, not speech act powers). On the pure epistemic-privilege reading, "avowal authority" disappears as a distinct phenomenon (it's just another name for first-person epistemic access). The argument needs the equivocation to make it seem like we're distinguishing two aspects of a unified phenomenon called "first-person authority," when we're actually just noting that epistemic access and performative speech acts are different things.

STRENGTH: 4/5

This is a serious problem. The thesis's central move—distinguishing two kinds of authority—depends on "authority" covering both normative power and epistemic privilege in a way that makes them seem like coordinate species of one genus. But they're not. The thesis needs the equivocation to make its distinction seem like a substantive discovery about first-person authority rather than the trivial observation that knowledge and speech acts are different. The argument cannot survive on either reading alone: it needs "authority" to be ambiguous enough to cover both, but unified enough to make their divergence interesting.

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE

The objection claims the thesis equivocates on "authority," but this gets the dialectical situation backward. The thesis isn't *exploiting* an equivocation—it's *diagnosing* one that already exists in the debate. The whole point is that "first-person authority" as used in the literature slides between these readings, and that recognizing this equivocation matters for understanding what interpretivism threatens.

Consider how "first-person authority" actually functions in the self-knowledge literature. When philosophers defend or attack it, they don't cleanly separate normative from epistemic dimensions—they run them together. The phenomenon they're tracking is something like: "I have a special status regarding my own mental states such that my self-ascriptions are privileged in a way that third-person ascriptions are not." This privileged status has both normative and epistemic dimensions, and the literature treats it as unified.

The thesis's claim is that this apparent unity is illusory—that what looks like one phenomenon with both normative and epistemic aspects is actually two distinct phenomena that happen to correlate in normal cases. This isn't equivocation; it's *disambiguation*.

Moreover, the objection misses why these count as two kinds of *authority* rather than just two unrelated things. They're both forms of authority because they both concern *who gets to settle* questions about my mental states. Avowal authority means I get to settle (for conversational purposes) whether I count as believing P—my say-so is normatively binding on the community. Epistemic authority means I get to settle (for epistemic purposes) what I actually believe—my access is privileged over others' access. Both involve a special first-person status regarding the same domain (my mental states), and both involve a kind of settlement-power. That's why they're both "authority" rather than just two random things.

The objection claims that if these are "completely different things," then the thesis reduces to the trivial claim that "interpretivism threatens epistemic access but not performative speech acts." But this misses the point. The thesis isn't just noting that knowledge and speech acts are different. It's claiming that:

1. What philosophers call "first-person authority" actually bundles together two distinct phenomena
2. These phenomena normally go together (when I know I believe P, I also avow it; when I avow P, I typically do believe it)
3. This correlation makes them seem like aspects of one thing
4. But they can come apart (self-deception, self-constitution)
5. Interpretivism threatens only one of them
6. And crucially, the one it preserves (avowal authority) is what actually matters for the practical/social role of first-person authority

This isn't trivial. It's a claim about the structure of self-knowledge, about what holds together in normal cases and what can dissociate, and about which aspect is doing the real work in our practices. The fact that the two kinds of authority are metaphysically different (normative vs. epistemic) doesn't make it trivial to notice that they've been conflated or that one survives interpretivism while the other doesn't.

Compare: "Free will debates equivocate between 'ability to do otherwise' and 'ultimate sourcehood.'" Someone might object: "But these are completely different things—one is about alternative possibilities, the other about causal origins. Noting that determinism threatens one but not the other is trivial—of course a thesis about causal chains affects causal origins but not modal facts." But this would miss the point. The claim isn't trivial because free will debates *actually conflate* these, treating them as aspects of one thing, and showing they come apart *matters* for understanding the debate.

Similarly here: the thesis claims that first-person authority debates conflate normative and epistemic dimensions, that interpretivism affects them differently, and that recognizing this *matters*—specifically, it shows that interpretivism doesn't threaten what we actually care about when we care about first-person authority.

Finally, the objection demands that the two kinds of authority be "species of the same genus" for the distinction to be interesting. But this is too strong. They're both *authority*—both involve settlement-power regarding my mental states. They're different *kinds* of settlement-power (normative vs. epistemic), but they're both answers to "who gets to determine what I believe?" The thesis's claim is that this question is ambiguous—it could mean "who gets to make me count as a believer?" (normative) or "who gets to know what I believe?" (epistemic). These are different questions, but they're both about authority over the same domain, which is why it matters that they've been conflated.

VERDICT

The defence fails.

The defence makes some good moves—correctly noting that the thesis is diagnosing rather than exploiting equivocation, and rightly observing that normative and epistemic authority both concern "who gets to settle" questions about mental states. The comparison to free will debates is apt: showing that a debate equivocates between two readings of a key term can be substantive even when those readings are metaphysically different kinds of things.

However, the defence cannot save the thesis from the equivocation charge for three reasons:

First, the defence concedes too much about the metaphysical difference between the two kinds of authority. Once we admit that normative power and epistemic privilege are "completely different things" operating in "different domains," the claim that they're both "authority" becomes increasingly verbal. Yes, we can stretch "authority" to cover both "normative power to constitute" and "epistemic privilege to know," but this is precisely the kind of ambiguity that makes equivocation possible. The defence says they're both about "settlement-power," but settling something *normatively* (making it count as true) and settling something *epistemically* (knowing what's true) are so different that calling them both "settlement" is itself equivocal.

Second, and more damaging, the thesis's argumentative payoff depends on treating these as coordinate aspects of a single phenomenon. The thesis says first-person authority "comes apart into" two phenomena, suggesting a decomposition of something unified. But if avowal authority and epistemic authority are as metaphysically different as the defence admits (one is about speech act powers, the other about knowledge), then they were never unified in the first place—they were just two different things both called "authority." The thesis needs them to be genuinely two aspects of one thing for the "coming apart" framing to work, but the defence's own description makes them fundamentally different kinds of things that merely correlate.

Third, the objection's key point stands: the thesis's interesting content comes from trading between readings. When establishing that "avowal authority" is real and preserved by interpretivism, the thesis uses the normative-power reading (of course I can constitute myself as a believer through speech acts—this is just performative utterance, which interpretivism doesn't threaten). When establishing that "epistemic authority" is threatened by interpretivism, the thesis uses the epistemic-privilege reading (interpretivism denies introspective access to belief-states with independent identity conditions). The appearance of a substantive discovery—that first-person authority survives interpretivism in one sense but not another—depends on these being different enough that interpretivism can affect them differently, yet similar enough that it's interesting they diverge. This is precisely the structure of equivocation.

The defence's weakest moment is when it claims the thesis shows "the one [interpretivism] preserves (avowal authority) is what actually matters for the practical/social role of first-person authority." This is a substantive normative claim that the thesis hasn't argued for—it's asserted to make the distinction seem important. But if epistemic authority is what philosophers have *actually* been debating (privileged access to mental states), then showing that avowal authority survives doesn't vindicate first-person authority in the sense that matters to the debate—it just changes the subject to speech act powers.

The thesis cannot escape the equivocation charge

KILLER (UNFALSIFIABLE)

ATTEMPT

The thesis is structured to be immune from counterexamples through strategic redefinition of its core terms. Consider potential falsifying cases:

Case 1: Someone sincerely avows "I believe P" but the community refuses to treat them as a P-believer (perhaps because they're known to be confused about what P means, or they immediately act contrary to P). Does this refute "avowal authority"? No—the thesis can respond that this is a "defeater condition" where authority is "overridden," not evidence that avowal authority doesn't exist. The authority is "defeasible" rather than absent.

Case 2: Under interpretivism, someone has robust first-person authority—they reliably know their beliefs and their avowals settle what they believe. Does this refute the claim that interpretivism threatens epistemic authority? No—the thesis can redefine what counts as "genuine" epistemic authority to require "belief-states with robust causal-functional identity conditions independent of self-conception." Any apparent epistemic authority under interpretivism gets reclassified as really just avowal authority in disguise.

Case 3: A theorist (say Bar-On) explicitly distinguishes avowal authority from epistemic access in their work. Does this refute the claim that the literature conflates these? No—the thesis can respond that her distinctions "operate within a shared framework" or are "refinements within the epistemic paradigm" rather than the "real" distinction the thesis draws.

The thesis protects itself by maintaining flexibility about what counts as "genuine" avowal authority (can invoke defeaters when needed), what counts as "genuine" epistemic authority (can deny interpretivism preserves it by definitional fiat about "independence"), and what counts as "really" making the distinction (can always claim previous distinctions don't cut at the right joints). Every apparent counterexample can be ruled not to be a genuine instance of the phenomenon the thesis is tracking.

STRENGTH: 3/5

This attack has genuine force but isn't devastating. The thesis does show some immunizing moves—particularly the flexibility about defeaters for avowal authority and the ability to redefine what counts as "the real distinction." However, the thesis makes empirical claims (about what the literature does) and conceptual claims (about what interpretivism entails) that are genuinely testable. If Bar-On explicitly makes the performative/epistemic distinction, that's real evidence against the thesis's framing. If interpretivism can preserve privileged access, that threatens the thesis's claim about what interpretivism threatens. The thesis has some protective maneuvers but isn't fully insulated from cases.

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE

The objection confuses *theoretical sophistication* with *unfalsifiability*. Yes, the thesis has resources to handle apparent counterexamples—but these resources are principled constraints built into the theory, not ad hoc maneuvers. Every serious philosophical thesis distinguishes genuine from spurious counterexamples; that's what theoretical commitments do.

Consider each case:

Case 1 (Community refuses avowal): The thesis doesn't claim avowal authority is *absolute*—it claims it's a *default normative status* that can be defeated. This isn't an immunizing move; it's a substantive commitment about the structure of the phenomenon. The thesis is falsifiable here: if communities *generally* or *routinely* override sincere avowals, that would refute the claim that avowal authority is a robust social practice. But the thesis predicts that such overrides are *marked as special*—as breakdowns, malfunctions, or extraordinary circumstances. This prediction is testable. If overrides were routine and unmarked, the thesis would be false.

Moreover, the thesis specifies what makes something a defeater: conflict with behavioral/emotional evidence (self-deception), conceptual confusion about the content, etc. These aren't arbitrary; they're principled conditions that explain *why* authority fails in these cases. A theory that says "X obtains unless it doesn't" is unfalsifiable. A theory that says "X obtains as default, defeated by conditions C1, C2, C3" is falsifiable—show that the specified conditions don't actually defeat X, or that X fails even when no defeater is present.

Case 2 (Interpretivism preserves authority): The objection claims the thesis can "redefine" epistemic authority to exclude whatever interpretivism preserves. But this misunderstands the dialectic. The thesis doesn't *define* epistemic authority as "whatever interpretivism threatens." It gives independent criteria: epistemic authority involves privileged access to states with "robust causal-functional identity conditions independent of self-conception."

This is falsifiable. Show that interpretivism is compatible with belief-states having identity conditions independent of interpretation, and the thesis's claim that interpretivism threatens epistemic authority fails. The thesis makes a substantive claim about what interpretivism entails (that it makes belief-identity interpretation-dependent), and this claim could be wrong. If interpretation is merely *epistemically* constrained by underlying states rather than *constitutively* determining them, interpretivism preserves epistemic authority and the thesis is refuted.

The thesis isn't saying "whatever authority interpretivism preserves, I'll call that avowal authority." It's saying: avowal authority is performative-constitutive (independent criterion), epistemic authority requires interpretation-independent states (independent criterion), and interpretivism happens to threaten the second but not the first (substantive claim following from these criteria). Each step is contestable.

Case 3 (Prior theorists draw distinctions): The thesis doesn't claim *no one* has ever distinguished these dimensions. It claims that the specific debate about interpretivism and first-person authority has been structured by a conflation—that when theorists argue about whether interpretivism undermines first-person authority, they equivocate between these senses. This is falsifiable: examine the actual dialectic. If participants clearly distinguish avowal from epistemic authority and argue specifically about which interpretivism threatens, the thesis's diagnostic claim fails.

The thesis's response to Bar-On isn't "her distinctions don't count"—it's a substantive claim that her distinctions, while real, *don't do the work* the thesis's distinction does. Specifically: Bar-On's security/authority distinction concerns different aspects of *epistemic* self-knowledge (whether it's error-prone, whether it constitutes knowledge), whereas the thesis's distinction separates epistemic from non-epistemic (performative-normative) dimensions. This is a claim about the *content* of the distinctions that could be false. If Bar-On's neo-expressivism actually treats avowals as performative rather than epistemic, the thesis is wrong about what her view does.

The general point: Unfalsifiability means no possible evidence could refute the thesis. But multiple kinds of evidence could refute it:

- Evidence that avowal authority isn't a robust default (communities routinely override avowals without marking them as special)
- Evidence that interpretivism is compatible with interpretation-independent belief-states (preserving epistemic authority)
- Evidence that the literature already clearly distinguishes performative from epistemic dimensions in the way the thesis claims is novel
- Evidence that what matters practically about first-person authority is epistemic access, not avowal (refuting the normative claim about what matters)
- Evidence that avowal authority and epistemic authority don't actually come apart in the ways the thesis predicts (self-deception cases don't show the pattern the thesis describes)

Each of these would be genuine refutation, not something the thesis could accommodate by redefinition. The thesis has theoretical resources to distinguish genuine from spurious counterexamples, but these resources are substantive commitments that themselves make predictions. That's not unfalsifiability—that's having a theory.

VERDICT

The defence succeeds, but with important qualifications.

The defence is fundamentally right that having resources to handle apparent counterexamples doesn't constitute unfalsifiability. The thesis does make genuine empirical and conceptual commitments that could be shown false: that avowal authority is a robust default practice, that interpretivism makes belief-identity interpretation-dependent, that the literature conflates these dimensions, that they come apart in specific ways.

However, the defence succeeds only in showing the thesis isn't *completely* unfalsifiable—it doesn't show the thesis is well-positioned to be tested. There are three residual problems:

First, the thesis's key claims are formulated at a level of abstraction that makes decisive testing difficult. What counts as "routine" versus "special" override of avowals? When does a theorist's distinction "do the work" of the thesis's distinction? The thesis could be made more falsifiable by specifying clearer empirical predictions or conceptual criteria.

Second, the defence's list of potential falsifiers reveals that some of the thesis's central claims are actually normative/evaluative rather than straightforwardly factual. "What matters practically about first-person authority" isn't a claim that evidence straightforwardly confirms or refutes—it's a normative claim about significance. Similarly, whether Bar-On's distinction "does the work" involves interpretive judgment about what work needs doing. These aren't unfalsifiable, but they're not empirically testable in the way the objection assumed.

Third, and most importantly, the thesis does show a pattern the objection identified: when pressed, it tends to retreat to more abstract or qualified versions of its claims. "Avowal authority" becomes "default avowal authority with defeaters." "The literature conflates" becomes "the literature operates within a framework that doesn't make the distinction the thesis makes." These aren't necessarily illegitimate moves, but they do show the thesis has flexibility that makes it harder to pin down.

The thesis survives the unfalsifiability charge but emerges somewhat weakened. It's not unfalsifiable in principle, but it's formulated in ways that give it significant room to accommodate apparent counterevidence. A stronger version would specify more precisely: under what conditions avowal authority obtains, what exactly interpretivism entails about belief-identity, what evidence would show the literature doesn't conflate these dimensions. Without this specification, the thesis risks being *practically* difficult to falsify even if not *in principle* unfalsifiable.

The objection fails to show the thesis is completely immune to evidence, but succeeds in showing it needs tightening to be properly testable.

O9. The implicit attitude literature provides a counterexample to the core assumption linking interpretivism and first-person authority: subjects have genuine first-person authority over their explicit attitudes despite these being interpretively constructed, because explicit attitudes are individuated precisely as those commitments the subject is prepared to avow and defend—first-person authority is built into their identity conditions.

Scores
promise 3/5 · residual 5/5 · worst 5/5 · dead
Move · Target
counterexample — The assumption that attitude types form a homogeneous category requiring uniform treatment of first-person authority
Sketch

Both defenders and critics of first-person authority assume that if attitudes are interpretively constructed, authority must be explained by some special epistemic or agential feature of self-interpretation. But implicit/explicit attitude cases show this is wrong. My explicit belief that P just IS (roughly) the belief I would avow on reflection, so avowal has authority by definitional fiat—not because I have special access or constitutive power, but because 'explicit attitude' picks out commitments individuated by their availability to avowal. Meanwhile, implicit attitudes (which I might interpretively discover through IAT results) can conflict with explicit ones precisely because they're individuated differently. The key premise: attitude kinds are functionally individuated, and different functional roles yield different authority relations. This dissolves the puzzle: interpretivism is true for both explicit and implicit attitudes, but only explicit attitudes are individuated in ways that build in first-person authority.

Appraiser (blind)
The explicit/implicit distinction is well-motivated but the 'definitional fiat' solution may seem too quick—authority by stipulation feels like dissolving rather than solving.
Objections
  • MISATTRIBUTION — landed 3/5, unanswered. Defence showed the thesis targets a specific homogeneity assumption about uniform explanatory mechanisms, but couldn't adequately distinguish this from what theorists already discuss
  • PROVES TOO MUCH — landed 4/5, unanswered. Defence appealed to empirical functional differentiation but this only supports substantive explanation of authority, not the definitional dissolution the thesis requires
  • COUNTEREXAMPLE — landed 4/5, unanswered. Defence's proper-functioning clause reintroduces the explanatory demands the thesis claimed to dissolve; delusions show avowal-disposition insufficient for genuine authority
  • TRIVIAL — landed 3/5, unanswered. Defence conflated making authority definitional with explaining it substantively; the functional story provides explanation but undermines the dissolution claim
  • EQUIVOCATION — landed 5/5, unanswered. Defence's 'third option' collapses into either trivial-definitional or substantive-but-not-definitional; cannot maintain both that authority is built-in and that it's philosophically interesting
⚑ Target attribution disputed — Defence showed the thesis targets a specific homogeneity assumption about uniform explanatory mechanisms, but couldn't adequately distinguish this from what theorists already discuss Check this yourself: it is a claim about who holds what, made from recall.
🔧 Survives as

Explicit attitudes, individuated by their distinctive functional role in conscious reasoning and verbal report systems, provide a substantive cognitive-architectural explanation of first-person authority: subjects have privileged access because these attitudes are constitutively integrated with reflective endorsement mechanisms, not because authority is definitional but because this functional integration explains the epistemic asymmetry

Flaw

The thesis equivocates between making first-person authority definitional (which makes it trivial) and explaining it substantively (which abandons the dissolution claim); it cannot coherently maintain that authority is both built into identity conditions and philosophically significant

full exchange (10 turns)

KILLER (MISATTRIBUTION)

ATTEMPT. The thesis attacks "the assumption that attitude types form a homogeneous category requiring uniform treatment of first-person authority," claiming this is held by "both defenders and critics of first-person authority." However, the heterogeneity of mental states regarding first-person authority is a *standard* position in the literature, not an assumption being challenged. Davidson explicitly distinguished different attitude types in his interpretivist framework. Moran's work on first-person authority carefully distinguishes between different kinds of self-knowledge and different mental states. The implicit/explicit attitude distinction itself has been extensively discussed precisely because these attitudes have different epistemic profiles. Burge's work on self-knowledge explicitly addresses how different types of mental states (perceptual beliefs, thoughts, intentions) have different relationships to first-person authority. The thesis presents as revolutionary the claim that "different functional roles yield different authority relations," but this is precisely what most theorists already accept—the debate is about *why* and *how* these differences arise, not whether they exist. The thesis attacks a homogeneity assumption that contemporary theorists do not hold.

STRENGTH: 4/5 — This is a serious problem. The thesis presents itself as offering a counterexample to a shared assumption, but the assumption appears to be a strawman. The interesting claim about explicit attitudes being individuated by avowal-dispositions deserves discussion, but not as a counterexample to a position nobody holds.

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE

The objection misreads what homogeneity assumption is being challenged. Yes, theorists recognize *that* different mental states relate differently to first-person authority—nobody denies that sensations differ from beliefs, or that implicit attitudes differ from explicit ones. But the thesis targets something more specific: the assumption that *within* the category of propositional attitudes (beliefs, desires, intentions), first-person authority requires a *uniform explanation* in terms of either special epistemic access or constitutive authority.

Consider the dialectic more carefully. Davidson's interpretivism says we interpret ourselves using the same methods we use for others, yet somehow retain authority—he then explains this authority uniformly via constitutive power over attitude content through self-interpretation. Moran's rationalist account says authority comes from deliberative stance-taking that constitutes our attitudes. Burge's self-verifying judgments model applies uniformly to basic self-knowledge. Each offers a *single mechanism* meant to explain authority across propositional attitudes generally.

The implicit/explicit distinction has been discussed for its *epistemic* differences, yes—but not as revealing a *metaphysical* difference in individuation conditions that makes authority *definitional* for one kind and *substantive* for another. The standard view treats implicit and explicit attitudes as two *tokens* of the same *type* (belief, desire) with different accessibility properties. The thesis claims they're *different types altogether*, individuated by different functional roles, where explicit attitudes have "avowal-responsiveness" built into their identity conditions.

This is not "what most theorists already accept." Most theorists think first-person authority over explicit beliefs needs *explaining*—whether by special access, constitutive power, or rational self-governance. The thesis says it needs no explanation for explicit attitudes because authority is *analytic*: an explicit belief just is (partly) whatever commitment you'd avow on reflection.

The revolutionary claim isn't merely that different states have different authority relations—it's that for explicit attitudes specifically, the authority relation is *individuative* rather than *explained*. This dissolves rather than solves the traditional problem.

VERDICT

The defence succeeds partially but probably not enough. The thesis can distinguish itself from mere recognition of heterogeneity by pointing to the individuation move—that explicit attitudes are *type-individuated* by avowal-dispositions, making authority definitional rather than explicable. This is genuinely different from standard positions.

However, the defence faces two problems. First, the objection's textual evidence is strong: these theorists *do* discuss different mental states having different authority profiles, and the thesis needs to show more clearly why their discussions don't already capture the individuation point. Second, even granting the individuation claim is novel, presenting it as a *counterexample* to a shared assumption still seems strained. The thesis would be stronger framed as "here's a better way to understand explicit attitudes that's been overlooked" rather than "here's a counterexample to what everyone assumes."

The defence rescues the thesis from being a complete strawman, but the MISATTRIBUTION charge substantially weakens the dialectical positioning. The interesting philosophical move (individuation by avowal-disposition) survives, but its presentation as refuting a widespread assumption remains questionable.

KILLER (PROVES TOO MUCH)

ATTEMPT. If explicit attitudes have first-person authority built into their identity conditions because they're individuated as "commitments the subject is prepared to avow and defend," then this argument licenses the same move for any mental state we choose to individuate by first-person reports. We could simply define "avowal-accessible pains" as those pains individuated by the subject's disposition to report them, and thereby claim first-person authority over pain is definitional rather than substantive. Or define "introspectively-accessible intentions" as those intentions the subject would report on reflection, making authority over intentions analytic. The move generalizes to any mental state whatsoever: just carve out a subcategory individuated by reportability, and voilà—first-person authority becomes definitional for that category. This means the thesis doesn't actually explain anything about the genuine phenomenon of first-person authority over explicit attitudes; it merely relabels the explanandum. The interesting question is why we *should* individuate explicit attitudes (but not implicit ones) by avowal-dispositions in the first place. If that individuation is motivated by our pre-theoretic recognition that subjects have authority over explicit attitudes, then the thesis is circular—using authority to justify the individuation that then "explains" authority. If the individuation isn't so motivated, the thesis owes us independent grounds for this taxonomic choice, which would constitute the real explanation of authority.

STRENGTH: 4/5 — This seriously undermines the thesis's explanatory ambitions. The individuation move either proves too much (applying to any mental state we choose to carve up appropriately) or presupposes what it claims to explain.

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE

The objection assumes that individuation by avowal-disposition is an arbitrary taxonomic choice we could make for any mental state, but this misses why the explicit/implicit distinction has the functional and empirical credentials it does. We don't *stipulate* that explicit attitudes are individuated by avowal-disposiveness—we *discover* this through their distinctive functional role in cognition and behavior.

Consider the empirical landscape. Implicit and explicit attitudes:
- Predict different behaviors (spontaneous vs. deliberate)
- Respond to different interventions (associative vs. propositional)
- Have different developmental trajectories
- Show different neural signatures
- Play different roles in reasoning (implicit attitudes don't figure in conscious inference)

This functional differentiation isn't something we invented by choosing to individuate attitudes differently—it's a discovered feature of cognitive architecture. The explicit/implicit distinction carves cognition at a real joint. Explicit attitudes are *already* functionally individuated as those commitments that interface with conscious reasoning, deliberation, and verbal report. The thesis simply recognizes that this functional role *includes* avowal-responsiveness as a constitutive feature, not an accidental add-on.

Compare the pain case. We *could* define "avowal-accessible pains" as a subcategory, but this would be unmotivated because:
1. There's no independent functional differentiation between "avowal-accessible" and other pains
2. All pains (setting aside philosophical zombies) are already reportable to the subject
3. The carving does no explanatory work in pain science

The explicit attitude category, by contrast, does massive explanatory work. It's not that we chose to individuate by avowal and thereby made authority analytic—it's that cognitive science independently discovered a natural kind whose functional profile *includes* integration with conscious avowal systems.

On circularity: The individuation is motivated not by pre-theoretic authority intuitions but by the functional evidence. We recognize explicit attitudes as a natural kind because of their distinctive causal-functional role, which includes (but isn't limited to) avowal-responsiveness. The authority then falls out as a consequence of this functional profile, not as its motivation.

The thesis's real bite is this: once we see that explicit attitudes are *already* individuated functionally in ways that build in conscious accessibility and avowal-disposition, the traditional problem dissolves. We don't need a special *explanation* of why subjects have authority over explicit attitudes any more than we need a special explanation of why water is H₂O—it's part of what makes that kind the kind it is.

The move doesn't generalize because other mental states don't have the same empirically-grounded functional differentiation that the explicit/implicit distinction has.

VERDICT

The defence fails, though it puts up a real fight.

The empirical credentials move is genuinely important—the explicit/implicit distinction does have functional and scientific grounding. But this doesn't save the thesis from the PROVES TOO MUCH objection for two reasons:

First, the defence conflates two claims: (a) explicit attitudes have a distinctive functional role that includes conscious accessibility, and (b) first-person authority is *built into their identity conditions* such that it needs no explanation. Claim (a) is well-supported. Claim (b) is the controversial move, and the functional evidence doesn't establish it.

Yes, explicit attitudes are integrated with conscious reasoning and verbal report systems. But this integration could explain first-person authority *substantively* (subjects have authority because explicit attitudes are constitutively linked to conscious endorsement mechanisms) rather than making it *definitional* (authority is analytic because we individuate by avowal-disposition). The thesis needs the definitional reading to dissolve the explanatory demand, but the functional evidence only supports the substantive reading.

Second, the objection's core challenge stands: even granting that explicit attitudes form a natural kind with avowal-responsiveness as part of their functional profile, this just pushes the question back. *Why* does this functional profile include avowal-responsiveness? If the answer is "because subjects have special authority over these attitudes," we're circular. If the answer is "because of how these attitudes interface with conscious systems," then we *do* have a substantive explanation of authority (via conscious integration), not a dissolution of the explanatory demand.

The pain comparison actually strengthens the objection. The reason we don't individuate pains by avowal-disposition isn't (just) lack of functional differentiation—it's that doing so would obviously fail to explain authority over pain. The thesis needs to show why the explicit attitude case is different in a way that makes the individuation move explanatory rather than merely relabeling.

The defence successfully shows the explicit/implicit distinction isn't arbitrary. But it doesn't show that recognizing this distinction makes first-person authority *definitional* rather than *explicable*. The functional story looks like the *beginning* of a substantive explanation, not a dissolution of the need for one.

KILLER (COUNTEREXAMPLE)

ATTEMPT. The thesis claims that explicit attitudes provide a counterexample to the assumption that interpretively constructed attitudes require explanation of first-person authority. But consider this case: delusions and confabulations. A subject with Capgras delusion explicitly avows "That person is an impostor replacing my spouse"—they are fully prepared to avow and defend this commitment on reflection. By the thesis's individuation criterion, this IS their explicit belief. Yet we deny them first-person authority: when the subject says "I believe that's an impostor," we think they're *wrong* about what they believe (perhaps they really believe their spouse lacks emotional significance, not that an impostor replaced them). Similarly, confabulating split-brain patients avow and defend interpretations of their actions, meeting the individuation conditions for explicit attitudes, yet we systematically deny them authority—we think the interpreter is discovering what they believe, not constituting it through avowal. These cases show that being prepared to avow and defend a commitment on reflection doesn't suffice for first-person authority, even for explicit attitudes. The thesis's individuation criterion is either too permissive (including delusions/confabulations where we deny authority) or must add epicycles about "proper functioning" that reintroduce the very explanatory demands the thesis claimed to dissolve.

STRENGTH: 3/5 — A genuine problem requiring a real answer. The thesis needs to either accept that delusional avowals have definitional authority (counterintuitive) or explain why they don't (reintroducing substantive explanatory requirements).

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE

The objection conflates two distinct ways authority can fail, only one of which threatens the thesis. The thesis claims that explicit attitudes are individuated by avowal-dispositions under *normal functional conditions*—just as hearts are individuated by their function of pumping blood even though some hearts fail to pump. Delusions and confabulations are cases of *malfunction*, not counterexamples to the individuation claim.

Consider the structure more carefully. When we say "explicit attitudes are individuated as commitments the subject is prepared to avow and defend," this picks out a functional kind defined by its normal role in cognitive architecture. The individuation conditions specify what makes something an *instance* of that kind when the system is working properly. Malfunctioning instances don't refute the individuation—they presuppose it.

The Capgras case actually *supports* the thesis when analyzed correctly. The patient HAS an explicit attitude—they genuinely believe "that's an impostor"—and they DO have first-person authority over this explicit attitude. When they say "I believe that's an impostor," they're absolutely right. What they lack authority over is the *correct interpretation* of what's psychologically going on: the deeper explanation (impaired affective processing) versus the surface commitment (impostor belief). But the thesis doesn't claim subjects have authority over psychological explanations—only over their explicit attitudes themselves.

The confusion arises because we're tempted to say "they don't *really* believe it's an impostor; they really believe something about emotional significance." But this is either:

(a) A claim about implicit attitudes or subpersonal processing (over which the thesis grants no definitional authority), or

(b) A theoretical redescription of their psychology that competes with their explicit commitment (in which case we're doing third-person interpretation that overrides their first-person authority—which happens, but doesn't show the authority was never there)

The split-brain confabulation cases are trickier but follow the same pattern. The patient DOES have explicit attitudes corresponding to their confabulatory avowals—these are genuine commitments they're prepared to defend. What they lack is *causal self-knowledge*: they don't know WHY they acted (the left hemisphere doesn't have access to the right hemisphere's reasons). But the thesis doesn't claim authority over causal-explanatory self-knowledge—only over the explicit attitudes themselves.

Here's the key distinction the objection misses: First-person authority over attitude content ≠ First-person authority over psychological explanation. The thesis claims the former is definitional for explicit attitudes; it never claimed the latter. Delusions and confabulations show that subjects can be wrong about the psychological *sources* and *significance* of their attitudes while retaining authority over the attitudes themselves qua explicit commitments.

On "proper functioning" epicycles: This isn't an ad hoc addition—it's how functional individuation works across the board. Kidneys are individuated by filtering blood; malfunctioning kidneys that don't filter are still kidneys (bad kidneys, but kidneys). Explicit attitudes are individuated by their functional role including avowal-responsiveness; malfunctioning cases where this system breaks down are still explicit attitudes (pathological ones, but explicit attitudes). The individuation doesn't require that every token perfectly instantiates the functional role—just that the kind is picked out by that role.

The thesis can bite a bullet here: Yes, the Capgras patient has first-person authority that they believe it's an impostor (they DO so believe), even though we can give a better third-person explanation of their overall psychological state. Authority is compatible with being in an epistemically or psychologically unfortunate situation. The definitional authority claim just means: if they're disposed to avow P on reflection, then they have an explicit attitude with content P, and their avowal of this attitude is authoritative *as an avowal of that explicit attitude*. It doesn't mean their overall psychological state is well-understood or their attitude is well-grounded.

VERDICT

The defence fails, though it identifies something important about different kinds of authority.

The distinction between authority over attitude content versus authority over psychological explanation is real and valuable. And the functional individuation point about malfunction is legitimate—functional kinds are indeed individuated by their normal role, not by every token's performance.

But the defence doesn't save the thesis from the COUNTEREXAMPLE objection for three reasons:

First, the defence concedes too much. If we grant that delusional subjects have first-person authority over their explicit delusional beliefs ("I believe that's an impostor" is authoritative), we've adopted a notion of "authority" so thin it's lost contact with what made first-person authority philosophically interesting. The traditional problem is that subjects seem to have a *special, privileged* relationship to their attitudes—not merely that their avowals correctly report whatever they're disposed to avow (which would be trivial). When we deny authority in Capgras cases, we're denying something substantive, not just denying that they know the psychological explanation.
