When I say 'I intend to finish this paper,' I'm not reporting an inner state but predicting which interpretation of my behavior I'll endorse when challenged. This is still first-person authority, but it's the authority of being best-positioned to predict your own future interpretive commitments, not the authority of observing present states. The asymmetry between self and other-ascription is just the asymmetry between predicting your own pattern-recognizing behavior and predicting someone else's.

Interesting distinction between standing dispositions and occurrent attitudes, but the predictive authority move feels like relabeling rather than solving the core puzzle.

If I know my attitudes only by interpreting my behavior and context, then I occupy the same interpretive position toward myself as an ideal observer would. The interpretivist might respond that I interpret selectively, attending to some evidence and ignoring other evidence. But selective attention doesn't explain how I could endorse incompatible interpretations—it only explains having an incomplete interpretation. To get genuine self-deception (not mere ignorance), the interpretivist needs me to be a bad interpreter of complete evidence. Yet if interpretation is constitutive of having attitudes, there's no fact about what I 'really' believe beyond what my interpretation says. This shows interpretivism collapses the phenomenon of self-deception into either ignorance or akrasia, neither of which is metaphysically puzzling in the same way.

Competent challenge showing interpretivism's tension with self-deception, but the literature already contains extensive discussion of whether self-deception requires belief pairs or just motivated irrationality.

This is unique to self-interpretation because the interpreter and interpreted share computational resources. Thus first-person interpretation cannot achieve the stability condition required for pure interpretation—the target keeps moving. This explains why self-ascription feels and functions differently: it's not just interpretation but interpretation-plus-interference, forcing a more deliberative, reason-responsive mode that Moran identified but mischaracterized as non-interpretive.

If you claim I don't really believe p, you must appeal to what I believe about my evidence, my reasons, my other beliefs—but these are themselves first-person ascriptions with the same status. This creates not an epistemic regress but a pragmatic one: first-person authority is the default because the alternative generates infinite dialectical cost. This explains both why authority survives interpretation (interpretation must start somewhere, and the interpreter's own states are the only dialectically permissible foundation) and why it's defeasible (pragmatic foundations can be overridden when dialectical costs are worth paying, as in confabulation cases).

The key premise: for instrumental rationality to get off the ground, I must presume my beliefs are mostly true and my desires coherent enough to guide action. This isn't optional bias but constitutive of agency. When interpreting others, such systematic charity would be epistemically irresponsible, but when interpreting myself, it's rationally mandatory. This creates a reliability asymmetry: my self-interpretations track truth better not because I have better evidence but because what makes them true (rational coherence) is something I'm constitutively committed to maintaining. The confabulation data shows this breaks down in non-agential contexts (explaining attitudes formed by manipulation or implicit bias), which is exactly what the theory predicts.

Both Bar-On and Moran defend first-person authority in general. But the key premise is that 'first-person authority' picks out at least three distinct phenomena with incompatible grounds. For pain, authority comes from expression (Bar-On is right here). For beliefs formed through deliberation, authority comes from rational self-constitution (Moran is right here). For implicit attitudes and many standing beliefs, interpretivism is correct and there's no special authority. The instability: any unified theory must either deny authority where we clearly have it (pain) or claim it where we clearly don't (implicit bias). The empirical literature doesn't undermine 'the' observational model—it shows that model never applied across the board. Historical accident that we use one grammatical form ('I believe/want/feel') obscures that these are functionally distinct speech acts requiring different vindicatory stories. The philosophical error is treating self-knowledge as a natural kind.

Fragmenting authority across state-types is plausible but feels more like a concession that there's no unified phenomenon than a positive contribution to understanding any particular case.

The argument distinguishes two kinds of authority: epistemic authority (being right about what you believe) and deliberative authority (having final say over what you will believe given reasons). Interpretivists correctly challenge epistemic authority but wrongly assume this exhausts first-person authority. The asymmetry between self and other isn't that I know better what I believe, but that my rational commitments—what I'll endorse upon reflection, what I'll revise given counterevidence—are answerable only to me in a way yours aren't. When you attribute a belief to me, you predict what I'll defend; when I self-ascribe, I stake a commitment about what I'll defend. This explains why 'I believe P' is defeasible by evidence yet has a normative force that third-person attributions lack: it's a performance of rational agency, not a report on a mental state. The interpretive turn is correct about the epistemology but misidentifies what first-person authority is authority over.

Appraiser (blind)
Distinguishing epistemic from deliberative authority is useful but closely parallels existing work on commitment versus report; incremental rather than transformative.

U34. The confabulation literature shows not that we lack introspective access but that we systematically misidentify cognitive attitudes (beliefs, desires) as perceptual experiences, and first-person authority actually applies only to phenomenal states that we've wrongly extended to propositional attitudes.

Move · Target
reframing — The shared assumption across the debate that beliefs, desires, and intentions form a unified category of 'attitudes' with a uniform epistemic profile
Sketch

Nisbett and Wilson's subjects don't confabulate about their experiences—they accurately report feeling drawn to the rightmost stockings. They confabulate about the cognitive explanation of this draw. The reframing: we have genuine first-person authority over phenomenal what-it's-like-ness (including affective phenomenology like 'feeling certain' or 'feeling motivated'), but the modern concept of 'belief' and 'intention' as propositional attitudes is a philosophical invention that wrongly extends introspective authority from phenomenal to cognitive-functional states. Interpretivist challenges work against propositional attitudes; expressivist defenses work for phenomenal states. The appearance of a unified debate about 'self-knowledge' disguises that defenders and critics are actually talking past each other about different state-types. This explains why both sides marshal strong evidence: introspection works for qualia, interpretation works for cognition, and we've mistakenly assumed these belong to a single epistemic domain.

Appraiser (blind)
The phenomenal/cognitive split is suggestive but the historical claim about wrongly extending introspective authority needs more support; feels somewhat stipulative.

U35. Holding that we learn our beliefs through interpretation commits you to massive first-order belief error, because interpretation requires attributing beliefs that rationalize behavior, while confabulation studies show our behaviors regularly fail to be rationalized by our actual (interpretationally-derived) beliefs.

promise 3/5 · residual –/5 · worst –/5 · unattacked
Move · Target
instability — Carruthers and Gopnik's interpretivist accounts that both rely on rationality constraints and cite confabulation evidence
Sketch

Interpretivism (Carruthers/Gopnik) requires a rationality constraint: we attribute beliefs that make sense of behavior. But the confabulation literature they invoke shows systematic gaps between behavior and the beliefs we'd attribute under rational interpretation. When subjects choose right-positioned stockings, rational interpretation attributes the belief 'position matters,' but they sincerely deny this. The interpretivist faces a dilemma: either (1) the rationality constraint is loose enough that it permits attributing beliefs that don't rationalize the behavior (but then interpretation loses its explanatory power), or (2) we accept that most people hold deeply irrational combinations of beliefs—they simultaneously believe position matters (to rationalize behavior) and believe it doesn't (per their sincere avowals). The second horn means interpretivism, combined with the empirical evidence it cites, entails widespread irrationality far beyond what's plausible. The position is unstable: the evidence interpretivists use to attack introspection undermines the rationality assumptions interpretation requires.

Appraiser (blind)
The dilemma for interpretivism (loose rationality constraint vs. massive irrationality) is sharp, but interpretivists have responses about degrees of rationality this needs to engage.

U36. The motivated reasoning literature shows that first-person authority increases rather than decreases under interpretation: when we construct rather than detect our attitudes, we gain control over what we're committed to, making avowals more rather than less authoritative.

Move · Target

Sketch

Standard assumption across the debate: if interpretation/construction replaces detection, authority diminishes because we lose epistemic access. But motivated reasoning studies (confirmation bias, self-serving attribution) show the opposite dynamic. When subjects construct explanations for their choices, they produce attitudes they'll defend more tenaciously than 'detected' states would warrant—the constructed belief becomes more authoritative, not less, because the agent has invested interpretive labor. This is a counterexample to the shared premise that authority requires accurate detection. The mechanism: construction creates psychological ownership and integration that passive detection lacks. When I interpret my stocking-choice as preference-based, this interpretation becomes constitutive of my preference going forward. I'm not wrong about my preference; I'm creating it through interpretation. First-person authority thus intensifies under interpretivism because avowals are performative constructions that bring attitudes into existence, while third-person attributions remain merely predictive. This inverts the dialectic: interpretation grounds rather than threatens authority.

Appraiser (blind)
The motivated reasoning twist (construction increases authority) is counterintuitive and interesting but needs clearer argument for why constructed attitudes are more rather than differently authoritative.

The empirical evidence for confabulation primarily concerns dispositional states and implicit attitudes—what we'd believe if prompted, what disposes our behavior over time. But we do have a kind of direct access to occurrent attitudes: what we're currently entertaining, committing to, or holding in attention. The key premise is that 'belief' equivocates between dispositional states (which are theoretical posits interpreters attribute) and occurrent commitments (which are phenomenologically available). First-person authority exists but has been mis-located: it's authority about what I'm now treating-as-true, not about my dispositional psychology. This explains why Schwitzgebel's cases cluster around dispositional states while Moran's phenomenology concerns active reasoning.

Appraiser (blind)
The occurrent/dispositional distinction is recognized in the literature; applying it to first-person authority is competent but the move has been explored.

First-person authority survives interpretation because self-interpretation operates under a constitutive norm that other-interpretation doesn't: interpreting myself as believing P makes me prima facie rationally committed to P's truth, creating an asymmetric defeat structure for self-attributions.

Move · Target

Sketch

When I interpret you as believing P, I face the question 'does your belief reflect reality?' but remain neutral. When I interpret myself as believing P, I face 'does my belief reflect reality?' and cannot remain neutral—to sincerely self-attribute belief in P is already to treat P as a candidate truth. The key premise is that belief self-attribution is subject to a transparency condition: I can't coherently judge both 'I believe P' and 'but is P true?' as independent questions. This creates an asymmetric rational structure: challenges to my self-interpretation become challenges to P itself, giving self-interpretation a self-stabilizing character that other-interpretation lacks. This explains first-person authority as dialectical rather than epistemic privilege.

Appraiser (blind)
The transparency/defeat-structure point connects to existing Moran-style arguments; it's a competent development but not a fundamental reframing.

Moran's agentialism says I know my belief by asking what to believe, but this faces the 'whose question?' problem: identifying which considerations count as my reasons (vs. alien urges, social pressure, etc.) requires prior self-interpretation of my commitments. Conversely, Carruthers-style interpretivism can explain how I form beliefs about my attitudes but not how these become self-knowledge rather than fallible hypotheses—that requires treating some self-attributions as rationally binding (the agentialist move). The key premise is that both views try to be reductive but each needs the other's resources at the ground floor. The stable position is that self-knowledge requires both interpretive identification and agentialist ratification in a non-reducible circle.

Appraiser (blind)
Mutual dependence arguments are familiar in philosophy; showing both positions need each other is useful but unlikely to redirect the debate significantly.

There's an ambiguity in 'first-person authority.' In one sense, it means the social-practical authority to have one's self-ascriptions taken at face value without challenge (what survives even with interpretation). In another sense, it means epistemic privilege about one's actual psychological states (what the empirical literature undermines). Bar-On and Moran defend the first by appealing to intuitions about the second. But these come apart: we grant social authority to self-ascriptions precisely because challenging them is socially costly, not because they're especially reliable. The interpretive turn shows that the epistemic version is illusory; what defenders of 'first-person authority' are actually tracking is a social norm of uptake. The debate dissolves because participants are defending/attacking different things under the same label.

Appraiser (blind)
Disambiguating epistemic from social authority is useful clarificatory work, though the social-norm explanation may be too deflationary to satisfy either side.

Moran's agentialist view grounds authority in reasoning about what to believe rather than detecting existing beliefs. But this requires knowing what reasons you're actually responsive to, which is itself a psychological fact subject to confabulation and interpretation. Similarly, Bar-On's expressivist view requires knowing which mental state you're expressing, but the empirical literature shows we're often wrong about what's driving our expressive behaviour (implicit attitudes, etc.). Both views try to avoid the interpretive problem by shifting the locus of authority, but the shifted locus is itself attitudinal content requiring interpretation. The regress can only be stopped by either (a) granting non-interpretive access to some attitudes (abandoning the interpretive turn), or (b) accepting that there's no first-person authority at any level (contradicting their own view).

Appraiser (blind)
The regress worry is a legitimate pressure on agentialist/expressivist views, competently developed but not a novel form of objection.

Both views assume a binary: either you know attitudes through rational deliberation (Moran) or through interpretation of evidence (Carruthers). But consider dispositional beliefs you've never entertained: your belief that penguins don't speak French, formed the instant you read this. You didn't deliberate into this belief (agentialism fails) and you have no behavioral evidence to interpret (interpretivism fails). Instead, you know it predictively: you know your cognitive architecture well enough to predict what belief would be triggered by the question. This reveals both views rely on attitudes that are occurrent enough to generate deliberative experience or behavioral traces. The vast majority of our attitudes are neither, and our knowledge of them requires a third model: architectural self-knowledge. Once we recognize this, both agentialism and interpretivism emerge as special cases applicable only to occurrent, activated attitudes.

Appraiser (blind)
The predictive-knowledge category for dispositional beliefs is an interesting addition to the taxonomy, though whether it's truly distinct from interpretation is contestable.

The debate treats confabulation as evidence against first-person authority. Reframe: confabulation reveals that self-ascription is constitutively authoritative precisely because it's the mechanism that ends interpretive indeterminacy. Behavioral/contextual evidence systematically underdetermines attitude attribution (as Quine saw). For others, we resolve this through charity and ongoing interpretation. For ourselves, sincere self-ascription functions as an interpretive fiat that makes one reading correct by force of commitment. This is why Nisbett & Wilson's subjects aren't just wrong but authoritatively wrong—their confabulations actually constitute what their attitudes now are, even if those attitudes don't explain past behavior. The asymmetry isn't epistemic but metaphysical: self-ascription doesn't report an independent fact but makes attitudes determinate in cases where evidence alone couldn't. This explains both why we defer to self-ascription and why it's often empirically mistaken about causal history.

Appraiser (blind)
Treating confabulation as constitutive rather than epistemic failure is interesting but the payoff seems limited to reinterpreting existing data.

Many philosophers respond to confabulation data by restricting first-person authority to a privileged subset of cases while allowing that other self-ascriptions are interpretive. But this requires drawing a principled line between introspective and interpretive self-knowledge. The argument shows that any candidate principle for drawing this line faces empirical counterexamples: proposed markers like immediacy, confidence, conscious access, or rationality all come apart from accuracy in the empirical literature. The key premise is that first-person authority requires not just sometimes being right through non-interpretive means, but being able to identify which cases these are—and no reliable marker exists. Therefore, preserving any first-person authority while accepting interpretivism commits one to a distinction one cannot sustain.

Appraiser (blind)
The empirical instability of the introspection/interpretation boundary is a real problem but has been noted.

Move · Target

The debate assumes that if self-knowledge is interpretive, it cannot involve privileged access, and if it involves privileged access, it cannot be interpretive. But this misunderstands what makes access 'privileged.' What's distinctive about self-interpretation is not that it bypasses interpretation but that the interpreter and the interpreted are identical—creating a feedback loop where interpretation can directly modify what's being interpreted. When I interpret myself as believing P, this interpretation can constitute or crystallize the belief itself in ways impossible for external interpretation. The key premise is that privileged access consists in this constitutive, self-shaping character of self-interpretation, not in passive observation. This explains both the empirical data (self-interpretation is genuinely interpretive, hence fallible) and first-person authority (self-interpretation has constitutive power other-interpretation lacks).

Appraiser (blind)
Dissolving the access-vs-interpretation dichotomy is valuable, but the identity-feedback mechanism needs more development to show it's not just restating constitutive views.

The argument draws a principled distinction within attitudinal states based on direction of fit. Beliefs aim at truth and thus require getting something independent right—which is why belief self-ascription under interpretation cannot be authoritative (confabulation shows we get it wrong). But intentions aim at making the world match them, and crucially, self-ascription of an intention can itself be part of forming that intention. When I interpret myself as intending to φ, this interpretation can constitute the intention in a way that interpretation of belief cannot constitute belief. The key premise is that world-to-mind direction of fit makes an attitude apt for interpretive constitution, while mind-to-world direction of fit does not. This explains the scattered data: we have more authority about intentions and desires than beliefs (Schwitzgebel's findings), and it vindicates Moran's focus on the deliberative case while explaining the failure of his account for beliefs.

Direction of fit explaining the belief/intention asymmetry is covered in thesis 0; this adds little.

Carruthers and Gopnik argue we know our beliefs through interpretation of behaviour and context. But interpretation itself requires that the interpreter have premises and draw inferences. If I interpret my own behaviour to conclude I believe P, I must rely on background beliefs (e.g., 'People who do X typically believe P') and inferential moves. These background beliefs and inferential steps cannot themselves be known through interpretation on pain of regress—I'd need to interpret my behaviour to know I'm drawing this inference, requiring further background beliefs, ad infinitum. So interpretivism presupposes non-interpretive access to at least some attitudinal states (one's active inferential dispositions) even while denying such access exists. The position is therefore unstable: it must grant the introspectionist enough to make interpretation possible.

Appraiser (blind)
A competent internal critique of interpretivism, but the regress argument has been explored in foundationalist epistemology generally.

The debate wrongly assumes first-person authority is about accurate psychological reporting. This avowal is authoritative not because I have special access to psychological facts but because it constitutively creates a normative fact about what I'm rationally committed to. The confabulation literature shows we're poor at reporting psychological causes, but this is compatible with being authoritative about rational commitments. On this view, the asymmetry between self and other-ascription is normative rather than epistemic: your saying 'You believe P' doesn't commit me to P's inferential role, but my saying it does.

Authority over commitments rather than psychological states is competent but familiar territory.

Many philosophers accept both: (a) implicit attitudes revealed by IAT and behaviour are genuine beliefs/attitudes, even when they conflict with explicit avowals, and (b) there remains some first-person authority for explicit beliefs. But this combination is unstable. If we grant (a), we're saying third-person interpretive evidence (reaction times, behaviour) can override first-person avowal about what one believes—the IAT reveals racist beliefs I sincerely deny having. This implicitly endorses the principle that behavioural/contextual evidence trumps avowal for belief-attribution. But this same principle, applied to explicit beliefs, yields interpretivism: your avowal that you believe P is just more evidence to weigh against your other behaviour and context, with no special authority. You can't consistently say interpretation is authoritative enough to trump avowal in the implicit case but not authoritative in the explicit case—they're the same type of interpretive judgment.

The instability argument is competent but the tension between implicit and explicit attitudes is already widely discussed.

Move · Target
distinction — Both sides' framing of the issue as about epistemic warrant or justification rather than pragmatic constraint
Sketch

The debate treats first-person authority as a purely epistemic asymmetry. But distinguish epistemic from practical asymmetries. When I interpret you, my interpretation can float free of your reality indefinitely—if I'm wrong about your beliefs, only you pay the practical cost. When I interpret myself, I must act on that interpretation, creating immediate feedback: false self-interpretations generate practical incoherence (I think I believe p but act as if not-p). This performative constraint doesn't give me better evidence, but it forces rapid correction through the practical costs of misinterpretation. The 'authority' is really just this: self-interpretations tend toward accuracy not because of superior access but because the interpreter and the interpreted are identical agents, making sustained error pragmatically unsustainable. This explains why authority exists without requiring privileged access.

Appraiser (blind)
The practical-constraint angle is interesting but the claim that this explains authority without privileged access needs more work to be convincing.

The debate conflates two asymmetries: present-tense self-ascription versus other-ascription, and present-tense versus past-tense self-ascription. Draw a distinction: authority holds only for currently-avowed attitudes, not remembered ones. When I say 'I believe p' right now, the interpretation and the attitude co-occur in a way that makes the interpretation partially constitutive—my current construal of my evidence and dispositions just is (part of) my current belief state, because beliefs are functional states defined by how one currently takes things to be. But when I attribute a past belief to myself or any belief to another, there's a genuine gap between interpretation and reality. The key premise: attitudes are temporally local and constitutively involve present self-construal. This explains why Schwitzgebel's cases of error mostly involve past attitudes or standing dispositions, while preserving Moran-style authority for occurrent self-ascription.

The temporal distinction is useful and the self-fulfilling aspect is interesting, but needs sharper development to be more than a clarification.

Interpretivist accounts claim we know our minds by interpreting behavioural and contextual evidence just as we interpret others. But there's an asymmetry the view cannot avoid: I control what I say, what reasons I rehearse internally, what memories I attend to—I'm not just interpreting pre-given evidence but generating the evidence I'll interpret. Crucially, this generative control is itself guided by self-understanding: I rehearse the reasons I take myself to have. The key premise: any interpretive procedure must take *some* self-understanding as input to determine which evidence to generate/attend to, creating vicious circularity. The view collapses into either: (a) accepting uninterpreted self-knowledge of what evidence to generate, or (b) denying we have any control over our evidence-generation, which makes self-interpretation radically passive in a way utterly unlike other-interpretation.

Appraiser (blind)
The authorial-control asymmetry is a real problem for interpretivism, though the argument needs tightening to avoid circularity charges.

Interpretivists claim the asymmetry between self and other interpretation is merely epistemic (more/different evidence). But consider: if I interpret myself as believing that p, I must be able to act on p without the incoherence of 'I believe p but not-p.' If I interpret you as believing p, I face no such constraint—I can hold you believe p while acting on not-p. The key premise: self-interpretation is subject to a constitutive rational pressure—the Moorean constraint that I cannot coherently hold 'I believe p but not-p'—that functions as a correctness condition. This constraint doesn't require uninterpreted access; it's a structural feature of first-person interpretation that makes it self-limiting in a way other-interpretation is not. This explains authority without privileged access: my interpretation must answer to what I can coherently act on, yours need not. Counterexample to interpretivist symmetry thesis: interpretation constrained by practical coherence requirements has different epistemic properties than interpretation constrained only by evidential fit.

Moorean constraints as explaining authority is a solid point, but similar ground has been covered in work on Moore's paradox.

Move · Target
reframing — The shared assumption across the debate that attitudes are determinate states we either do or don't accurately detect
Sketch

Both sides treat interpretation as fundamentally a matter of hypothesis-formation about pre-existing states. But confabulation studies show something stranger: subjects aren't just wrong about pre-existing reasons; they're constructing reasons that become operative going forward. The 'interpretation' isn't a reading of antecedent states but a creative act that brings determinate attitudes into being. On this view, Nisbett and Wilson's subjects aren't failing at introspection—they're succeeding at a different task: crystallizing vague dispositions into articulate attitudes through narrative self-constitution. This explains both the empirical findings (why reports seem confabulatory) and first-person authority (why the subject's word still matters): the authority comes not from accurate detection but from constitutive creation. The asymmetry between self and other-ascription remains because only I can author my attitudes into determinacy; you can only observe the attitudes I've already constituted. The key premise is that many mental states exist in indeterminate form until narratively articulated.

Appraiser (blind)
Narrative construction as generative rather than inferential is interesting but close to existing authorship views.

U58. The expressivist strategy for preserving first-person authority while accepting interpretation actually commits expressivists to denying that self-ascriptions are genuinely knowledge-claims, which collapses their position into a form of non-cognitivism about self-knowledge that cannot capture what's epistemically distinctive about introspection.

Scores
promise 3/5 · residual –/5 · worst –/5 · unattacked
Move · Target
instability — Bar-On's neo-expressivist attempt to preserve first-person authority through a hybrid expressivist-assertoric account
Sketch

Bar-On and other neo-expressivists try to have it both ways: self-ascriptions involve interpretation (to accommodate empirical findings) but aren't based on evidence in the way other-ascriptions are (to preserve asymmetry). They achieve this by treating avowals as simultaneously expressive and assertoric. But this is unstable. If avowals express attitudes rather than report them, they cannot be assessed for epistemic warrant in the usual way—they're more like symptoms than claims. If they can be assessed for warrant, they must be based on something, which returns us to the evidential interpretation model. The expressivist tries to split the difference by saying avowals have 'default authority' without epistemic support, but this just labels the problem rather than solving it. Either default authority is a kind of epistemic entitlement (in which case we need an account of what grounds it, returning us to the impasse) or it's not epistemic at all (in which case avowals aren't knowledge-claims). The key premise is that epistemic authority requires epistemic grounding, which expressivism denies.

Appraiser (blind)
A competent critique of expressivism's instability, though the dilemma may have escape routes that aren't fully closed off here.

U59. First-person authority persists in the interpretive framework not because of any special epistemic access or agential privilege, but because self-ascriptions function as speech acts that change the normative score in a way that creates practical entitlements: avowing a belief commits me to defending it, which gives my avowal practical authority even when it lacks epistemic privilege.

Scores
promise 3/5 · residual –/5 · worst –/5 · unattacked
Move · Target
reframing — The shared assumption that first-person authority must be an epistemic phenomenon requiring special access or warrant
Sketch

The debate assumes first-person authority must be epistemic—either I have better evidence about myself, or I have a special agential relationship to my attitudes. But first-person authority might be primarily a normative-pragmatic phenomenon. When I say 'I believe that p,' I'm not just reporting but undertaking a commitment to defend p, offer reasons for it, and act consistently with it. This speech act changes what I'm entitled and required to do going forward. You cannot undertake these commitments on my behalf; only I can bind myself in this way. This explains the asymmetry: your claim 'S believes that p' doesn't commit S to anything, but S's claim 'I believe that p' does commit S. The authority is practical-normative (my word binds me in ways yours doesn't) not epistemic (my word is more likely true). This dissolves the tension: interpretation can be symmetric epistemically while authority remains asymmetric pragmatically. The key premise is that avowals are commitment-undertaking speech acts, not primarily knowledge-claims.

Appraiser (blind)
Pragmatic-normative authority is a useful distinction from epistemic authority, but needs more development to fully dissolve the tension claimed.

U60. The empirical literature on confabulation undermines not introspection but transparency: what subjects lack is knowledge of the causal history of their attitudes, not knowledge of the attitudes themselves, and this counterexample shows that both agentialists and interpretivists wrongly assume that knowing your attitude requires knowing how you came to have it.

Move · Target

Sketch

Nisbett and Wilson's subjects are wrong about why they chose the stockings but arguably not wrong that they preferred the rightmost ones when asked. The confabulation is about etiology (the causal story), not about the attitude itself (the preference). Both interpretivists and their opponents treat these cases as undermining direct knowledge of attitudes, but they actually only undermine transparency—the idea that introspecting an attitude reveals its genesis or grounds. This distinction rescues a limited form of direct introspective knowledge: I can know what I believe without knowing why I believe it, just as I can know I'm in pain without knowing what's causing the pain. The interpretive work is needed for self-understanding (grasping my reasons), not for self-knowledge (grasping my attitudes). This counterexample to the shared reading of the empirical literature suggests a middle position: basic attitude-awareness can be direct and authoritative, while deeper self-understanding requires interpretation. The key premise is that the confabulation studies demonstrate ignorance of causal etiology, not ignorance of current states.

Appraiser (blind)
Distinguishing attitude-knowledge from etiological knowledge is useful but the move is fairly standard.

U61. First-person authority for attitudes is grounded not in privileged access to those attitudes themselves, but in constitutive authority over what would count as getting them wrong—we are authoritative about our beliefs because we partially determine the correctness conditions for belief-ascriptions to ourselves.

Move · Target

Sketch

The debate assumes first-person authority must be explained by epistemic privilege (either observational or interpretive). But this conflates two kinds of authority: epistemic authority (being a reliable source of information) and constitutive authority (partly determining what the facts are). When I sincerely avow a belief, I don't merely report a pre-existing fact—I constrain what counts as a correct interpretation of my mental state. The interpretive turn is right that we don't have observational access, but wrong to conclude we therefore know ourselves only evidentially. Instead, our avowals function like definitions or stipulations within bounds: they make it the case that certain interpretations are correct, rather than tracking independently correct interpretations. This explains the asymmetry: others must interpret evidence to determine my attitudes, but I partly constitute what my attitudes are through the very act of self-ascription.

Appraiser (blind)
Authority over correctness conditions is an interesting formulation but closely related to constitutive authority views.

U62. The confabulation literature shows not that we lack introspective access but that we systematically misidentify which attitudes we are introspecting—we have genuine access to our occurrent reactive dispositions but confabulate when attributing them to stable beliefs or reasons.

Move · Target
distinction — Both sides' treatment of 'attitudes' as a unified category and the interpretivists' claim that confabulation undermines introspection wholesale
Sketch

Nisbett-Wilson cases are standardly read as showing introspection is unreliable or non-existent. But closer analysis reveals a pattern: subjects accurately report their current inclinations, attractions, and reactive dispositions (they really do prefer the rightmost stockings right now), but err in explaining these as flowing from stable beliefs or principled reasons. The mistake isn't in the immediate introspective access but in the theoretical overlay—the attribution of occurrent states to standing attitudes. This distinction reclassifies the debate: the observational model is correct about occurrent states, the interpretive model is correct about standing attitudes, and the asymmetry exists at the occurrent level only. First-person authority for beliefs-as-dispositions must be explained interpretively, but genuine introspective access to token mental events remains intact.

Appraiser (blind)
Useful distinction between occurrent and standing attitudes, but the hybrid solution feels like splitting rather than resolving the core tension.

U63. First-person authority is an unstable position that interpretivists are right to abandon: the appearance of asymmetry between self and other is an artifact of differential pragmatic constraints on assertion, not a metaphysical or epistemic difference requiring explanation.

Scores
promise 3/5 · residual –/5 · worst –/5 · unattacked
Move · Target
instability — Moran's and Bar-On's projects of preserving first-person authority after the interpretive turn
Sketch

Moran and Bar-On treat the self-other asymmetry as a datum to be explained, but this assumes the asymmetry reflects something deep rather than superficial conversational facts. When I self-ascribe a belief, I'm subject to different Gricean constraints than when attributing beliefs to others: sincerity is presumed, I'm expected to speak from a deliberative rather than theoretical stance, and challenges to my self-ascription count as accusations of insincerity or irrationality rather than mere error. These pragmatic differences fully explain why self-ascriptions have a different dialectical role. The 'authority' is just an entrenched conversational practice of treating self-ascriptions differently. Any view that tries to ground this asymmetry in genuine epistemic or constitutive differences is therefore explaining a pragmatic phenomenon with metaphysical machinery—it's unstable because the explanandum doesn't require the heavyweight explanans.

Appraiser (blind)
Pragmatic deflation is competent but this style of argument has been made in various forms; unlikely to persuade those seeking deeper explanation.

U64. Accepting that implicit attitudes are genuinely ours commits us to denying first-person authority for attitudes generally, because if I can be wrong about implicit attitudes without this threatening their status as mine, the link between ownership and authority is severed.

promise 3/5 · residual –/5 · worst –/5 · unattacked
Move · Target
commitment — Those who try to preserve first-person authority while accepting implicit attitudes as genuine attitudes (including moderate interpretivists)
Sketch

Defenders of first-person authority typically grant that implicit attitudes are genuine attitudes while acknowledging we lack first-person authority over them. But this concession is devastating. If implicit biases are genuine attitudes I can be systematically wrong about, then the traditional package—that attitudes are constitutively mine in a way that grounds privileged access—breaks apart. The authority-theorist must either: (a) deny implicit attitudes are real attitudes (implausibly restrictive), (b) accept a two-tier system where some attitudes carry authority and others don't (unmotivated and ad hoc), or (c) accept that ownership doesn't ground authority (abandoning the traditional view). The implicit attitudes literature thus forces a dilemma: either drastically restrict what counts as an attitude, or abandon the claim that being the subject of an attitude gives you authority over it.

Appraiser (blind)
Implicit attitudes severing ownership from authority is a real tension but widely recognized.

U65. The interpretive model fails on its own terms because interpretation requires attributing interpretive beliefs to the subject, but if those second-order interpretive beliefs are themselves only known through interpretation, we face a regress that either bottoms out in non-interpretive access or makes self-knowledge impossible.

Move · Target
counterexample — Carruthers's and Gopnik's claim that self-knowledge is comprehensively interpretive, paralleling other-knowledge
Sketch

Carruthers and Gopnik argue we know our attitudes by interpreting our behavior and context, much as we interpret others. But this process requires the self-interpreter to believe things about the evidence, draw inferences, and form interpretive judgments. How does the subject know they hold these interpretive beliefs? If the answer is 'by further interpretation,' we face a regress. If at some level there's direct access to occurrent interpretive thoughts, then the interpretive model has conceded the existence of non-interpretive self-knowledge, and the question becomes why this doesn't extend to first-order attitudes. The interpretive model thus contains a counterexample to its own universality: the very cognitive processes of self-interpretation must be known non-interpretively, or the account generates infinite regress. This shows the model can't be the complete story about self-knowledge.

Appraiser (blind)
The regress objection to interpretivism is solid but has been raised before.

U66. First-person authority degrades continuously as we move from occurrent phenomenal states through standing propositional attitudes to implicit attitudes, revealing that 'first-person authority' names three distinct epistemic relations that current theories mistakenly unify.

Move · Target

The debate treats first-person authority as a unified phenomenon requiring a unified explanation, but the empirical evidence shows differential patterns of confabulation and self-interpretation across state-types. For occurrent phenomenal states (pain, visual experience), we have genuine observational access with minimal interpretation. For standing beliefs we consciously endorse, we have constitutive authority (Moran-style) grounded in rational agency. For implicit attitudes, we genuinely lack authority and employ third-personal interpretation. The key premise: the Schwitzgebel-style cases that motivate interpretivism concern only the third category, while agentialist accounts only explain the second, but both camps illegitimately extend their models to all self-knowledge. This explains why both research programs keep finding confirming evidence—they're studying different phenomena.

Appraiser (blind)
Taxonomizing different kinds of authority is useful but risks being seen as conceding rather than resolving the theoretical dispute.

U67. First-person authority for propositional attitudes consists not in privileged epistemic access but in constitutive uptake rights: others must treat your self-ascriptions as partly constitutive of what attitudes you have, even when behavioral evidence conflicts.

promise 3/5 · residual –/5 · worst –/5 · unattacked
Move · Target
reframing — The shared framing by all parties that first-person authority is primarily an epistemological puzzle about differential access to facts about one's mind
Sketch

The debate assumes first-person authority is an epistemic asymmetry requiring epistemic explanation (better evidence, special access, or transparency). But this cannot explain why rational interlocutors often defer to self-ascriptions even when behavioral evidence strongly suggests confabulation. The key move: first-person authority is fundamentally a social-normative phenomenon grounded in our practices of holding each other responsible as rational agents. When you sincerely avow 'I believe P,' rational interlocutors must give your avowal some constitutive weight—not because you have better evidence about your beliefs, but because treating you as a rational agent requires letting your rational endorsements partly determine what attitudes you have. This explains both why authority persists despite interpretive processes (it was never about epistemic access) and why authority fails for implicit attitudes (we don't hold people rationally responsible for them).

Appraiser (blind)
Social-normative grounding is interesting but similar constitutive/normative moves have been explored; needs sharper differentiation from thesis 0.

U68. Agentialist accounts of first-person authority are committed to denying that we have beliefs about matters where we lack rational control, which collapses them into an implausible form of doxastic voluntarism.

Scores
promise 3/5 · residual –/5 · worst –/5 · unattacked
Move · Target
commitment — Moran's agentialist account and similar views that ground first-person authority in rational self-determination
Sketch

Moran's transparency condition says I know what I believe about P by considering P itself, which grounds first-person authority in my rational agency. But this only works for questions within my rational control—I can settle what I believe about ethics by deliberating about ethics. However, I also have beliefs about matters beyond rational control (empirical beliefs about my past, perceptual beliefs, beliefs formed by cognitive biases). For these, Moran cannot invoke transparency and rational agency. The key premise: if agentialist authority requires rational control, then agentialists must either deny these are genuine beliefs (absurd) or admit they lack first-person authority (conceding too much to interpretivism). The attempted escape—claiming rational control over all beliefs via control over evidential standards—commits them to saying we can believe-at-will by adjusting our standards, which is doxastic voluntarism.

Appraiser (blind)
Valid internal critique of Moran but the voluntarism objection has been raised before; competent but not groundbreaking.

U69. First-person authority for intentions survives interpretivism because intentions, unlike beliefs, are essentially self-fulfilling: sincere avowals of intention create obligations that make the avowal retrospectively correct regardless of prior psychological facts.

Move · Target

The debate treats beliefs and intentions symmetrically—if we confabulate about beliefs, we should confabulate about intentions; if we have authority about intentions, we should have it about beliefs. But intentions have a unique logical feature: avowing 'I intend to X' creates a rational commitment to X-ing that didn't necessarily exist before. Even if my avowal of intention initially misrepresents my prior psychological state (I'm confabulating), the avowal creates a normative fact—I am now committed to X-ing—that makes my avowal correct going forward. The key premise: intentions are not purely psychological facts discoverable by observation or interpretation, but are partly constituted by rational commitments that avowals can create. This explains the asymmetry in the confabulation literature: we systematically confabulate about beliefs (which are discovery-apt) but have genuine authority about intentions (which are commitment-apt), without requiring either mysterious inner access or rejecting the interpretive insights.

Appraiser (blind)
The self-fulfilling nature of intention avowals is recognized; framing it as retrospective correctness adds little new.

U70. The confabulation literature shows not that we lack introspective access, but that we have access to motivating reasons while lacking access to the psychological mechanisms that selected those reasons—and first-person authority attaches only to the former.

promise 3/5 · residual –/5 · worst –/5 · unattacked
Move · Target
distinction — Schwitzgebel's reading of the confabulation literature as undermining introspective reliability generally, and Carruthers' use of this literature to motivate pure interpretivism
Sketch

Nisbett and Wilson's studies are typically read as showing we lack access to 'why we act/believe as we do.' But this conflates two questions: access to the considerations that rationalize our attitudes (premises we're disposed to offer in reasoning) versus access to the causal-psychological processes that explain why those considerations moved us. When subjects confabulate about why they chose the rightmost stockings, they may accurately report that 'this one seemed better quality' (the consideration they found compelling) while being wrong about why texture-cues dominated over position-cues in their processing architecture. First-person authority, properly understood, is authority about one's rational position—what considerations one takes to count in favor—not about psychological mechanism. The interpretive turn mistakenly assumes we need mechanism-access to ground authority, but agency and responsibility require only that we're authoritative about our rational commitments.

Appraiser (blind)
Access to motivating reasons versus mechanisms is a useful distinction but not groundbreaking.

U71. The self-interpretation position is unstable because if we know our attitudes only through interpretation, we cannot know we are interpreting rather than introspecting—but distinguishing interpretation from introspection requires independent access to our attitudes.

Move · Target
instability — The pure interpretivist positions of Carruthers and Gopnik
Sketch

Carruthers and Gopnik argue we know our minds through the same interpretive mechanisms we use for others. But this position requires that we can identify when we're engaged in interpretation—otherwise the claim that 'we interpret ourselves' is empty. To know I'm interpreting my behavior to attribute belief B (rather than, say, directly introspecting B), I need to recognize my epistemic position as that of an interpreter working from behavioral evidence. But recognizing my epistemic position is itself a piece of self-knowledge. If all self-knowledge is interpretive, then my knowledge that I'm interpreting must itself be interpretive—but interpretation of what? Not of behavior (which is public), but of my cognitive stance. This requires either (a) a regress of interpretations, (b) non-interpretive access to at least some mental states (my interpretive stance), or (c) giving up the claim that we can know we're interpreting. Pure interpretivism thus either undermines itself or covertly relies on non-interpretive self-knowledge.

Appraiser (blind)
The meta-level regress about knowing one's epistemic position is clever but feels more like a puzzle than a substantive reframing.

The debate treats first-person authority and confabulation as in tension: if we confabulate explanations of our attitudes, how can we be authoritative about them? But this assumes authority and etiological narrative must stand or fall together. Reframe: when I say 'I believe climate change is real,' I'm undertaking a commitment, staking out a normative position I'll defend and reason from. First-person authority is authority about these undertaken commitments. When I confabulate a story about why I formed this belief (maybe I cite scientific evidence when really it was social conformity), that's a separate narrative-constructive act about causal history. The Nisbett and Wilson studies show we're bad at causal-historical narrative, not bad at knowing what commitments we're currently standing behind. The asymmetry between first and third person persists for commitment-authority (you can't tell me what I'm committed to) even while disappearing for etiological narrative (we're both equally positioned to theorize about causes). Current views wrongly bundle these together because they assume self-knowledge must be primarily explanatory rather than primarily normative.

Separating commitment-authority from etiological narrative is clear but the distinction is recognized.

The key premise is that attitude-individuation is radically underdetermined at the time of occurrence—the same neural/behavioural substrate could realize different attitudes depending on subsequent interpretive choices. First-person authority is then the authority to decide which of many admissible precisifications of my own mental history becomes canonical. This explains the asymmetry: others can interpret my past, but only I can make an interpretation stick as the one that fixes what I meant all along. The interpretive turn is thus compatible with authority, but the authority concerns settling indeterminacy backward rather than detecting determinate facts forward.

Retrospective semantic authority is intriguing but the radical indeterminacy premise will be controversial; more speculative than actionable.

Moran's agentialism observes that answering 'Do I believe P?' by answering 'Is P true?' generates authority. But this is usually taken to show self-knowledge is constitutive or non-interpretive. The alternative: endorsement-based self-ascription achieves authority by making the historical question idle. Whether I believed P before answering doesn't matter because endorsing P commits me to believing it now and acting accordingly henceforth. The key premise is that first-person authority doesn't require getting past facts right—it requires that certain past facts become pragmatically irrelevant to ongoing interaction. When I say 'I believe P' through endorsement, challengers cannot gain traction by insisting I didn't really believe it moments ago, because my current commitment supersedes that history. This is compatible with full interpretivism about the past: I might be utterly wrong about whether I believed P yesterday, but that error doesn't undermine my authority because the speech act itself renders the historical question moot for practical purposes.

Making historical facts pragmatically inert is interesting but feels more like explaining away authority than genuinely preserving it.

The implicit attitude literature (implicit bias, etc.) shows others can have systematic epistemic access to our attitudes through instruments (IAT, response-time measures) that we ourselves cannot use from the first-person perspective. If these implicit states are genuinely attitudes, then first-person authority fails: others have better access to what I believe/desire than I do. Those who defend first-person authority while accepting implicit attitudes must either deny that implicit biases are real attitudes (they're mere associations or dispositions), or claim they don't threaten authority because they're not the right kind of attitude (not 'personal-level' or not 'endorsed'). But both moves are costly: the first seems empirically forced by the predictive power of implicit measures; the second fragments our attitude concept so severely that 'first-person authority over attitudes' becomes trivial—authority only over an arbitrarily narrow subset. The stable positions are thus either reject implicit states as attitudes, or abandon first-person authority.

The implicit attitudes challenge is important but this formulation largely repeats thesis 3's dilemma with less development.

Both defenders and critics of first-person authority treat it as an epistemic phenomenon — a matter of reliability, access, or knowledge. But first-person authority is better understood as a social-pragmatic status: the speaker's word about their attitudes has a distinctive role in fixing what attitude we should attribute to them in coordinating action and holding them accountable. The key premise is that even when empirically undermined (I confabulate, I'm self-deceived), there remains a pragmatic asymmetry: if you contradict my sincere self-ascription of belief, you owe justification; if I contradict yours, I merely owe evidence. This explains why first-person authority seems simultaneously robust (we can't just override someone's self-ascription) and fragile (they might be completely wrong). The authority isn't epistemic warrant but something like pragmatic standing.

The debate assumes that if we use the same interpretive mechanisms for self and other, there can be no authority asymmetry. But this ignores a temporal structure: when I now interpret my past behavior to attribute a belief, my current self-attribution becomes a fixed point that must be explained by the interpretation (unless I'm revising). When you interpret my past behavior, your attribution doesn't constrain the interpretation — it's just the output. The key premise is that self-interpretation is retrospective-prospective: I'm both interpreting past evidence and committing to future coherence, creating a rational pressure to make my self-attribution the explanandum rather than merely the explanans. This explains why my word about what I believe carries special weight even after we accept I discovered it through interpretation: I'm not just reporting an interpretation but establishing a going-forward commitment that gives me reason to defend this interpretation over alternatives.

Appraiser (blind)
The temporal/explanatory-direction asymmetry is subtle and potentially important, but the mechanism by which current self-attribution constrains interpretation needs more development to be compelling.

U81. Accepting that we know our attitudes through interpretation commits us to accepting that many disputes about whether someone 'really believes' something are substantively indeterminate, which neither agentialists nor interpretivists acknowledge but which undermines both programs.

Scores
promise 3/5 · residual –/5 · worst –/5 · unattacked
Move · Target
commitment — Both agentialists like Moran and interpretivists like Carruthers who assume attitude-attributions are determinately truth-apt
Sketch

If attitude-attribution involves interpretation of behavioral and contextual evidence, then in cases where evidence underdetermines interpretation, there may be no fact about what someone believes. The key premise is that interpretation-dependence plus evidential underdetermination entails metaphysical indeterminacy, not merely epistemic uncertainty. Both interpretivists and their critics assume that even if we discover our beliefs through interpretation, there remains a determinate fact about what we believe that the interpretation aims to capture. But this is incoherent: if attitudes are whatever best interprets the evidence, and evidence underdetermines interpretation (as confabulation studies suggest), then many first-person attributions are substantively indeterminate. This means Moran's question 'what do I believe about p?' often has no answer, and Bar-On's expressivist self-ascriptions often express nothing determinate. The authority debate presupposes determinacy that the interpretive turn cannot sustain.

Appraiser (blind)
Metaphysical indeterminacy from underdetermination is a real consequence but has been noted.

U82. First-person authority about our attitudes derives not from privileged epistemic access but from constitutive authority: in sincerely avowing a belief, we typically make it the case that we have that belief, whereas confabulation occurs precisely when this constitutive mechanism misfires.

Scores
promise 3/5 · residual –/5 · worst –/5 · unattacked
Move · Target
distinction — The shared assumption between interpretivists like Carruthers and agentialists like Moran that first-person authority must concern knowledge of antecedently existing states
Sketch

The debate assumes first-person authority must be epistemic authority—a superior way of knowing what's already there. But we should distinguish epistemic from constitutive authority. When I sincerely say 'I intend to vote Green,' I'm not always reporting a pre-existing intention; I'm often crystallizing one, making it determinate through the very act of avowal. This explains both authority and confabulation: authority holds when avowal successfully constitutes the attitude; confabulation occurs when the constitutive mechanism fails (perhaps due to social pressure or self-deception) and we mistake interpretation for constitution. The key premise is that many attitudes lack determinate existence prior to avowal—they're dispositionally inchoate. This preserves the asymmetry (others can't constitute my attitudes through their interpretations of me) while accepting the interpretive turn (I do interpret my dispositions, but interpretation here serves constitution, not discovery).

Appraiser (blind)
Constitutive authority is a known move in the literature; this version's contribution is distinguishing successful constitution from misfiring, but the distinction needs more precision.

U83. The confabulation literature provides a counterexample to the shared premise that interpretation aims at truth: confabulators are better described as generating narratives that serve affective regulation and social coordination rather than tracking facts, and once we see attitude-attribution as serving these non-alethic functions, the puzzle about authority dissolves.

Move · Target
reframing — The shared assumption across the debate that self-knowledge is a species of knowledge properly so-called, aimed at truth about attitude-facts
Sketch

Both sides assume that when we self-attribute attitudes, we're trying to get things right—the debate is only about how. But the confabulation data suggests something else: subjects produce self-attributions that serve emotional coherence, self-image maintenance, and social accountability rather than accuracy. Nisbett and Wilson's subjects aren't failing at a truth-tracking task; they're succeeding at a different task—providing socially acceptable explanations. First-person authority then isn't epistemic but pragmatic: others defer to my self-attributions not because I'm likely right but because treating me as the authority serves social coordination (fixing responsibility, enabling communication). This reframes the debate: the question isn't 'how do we know our attitudes despite interpretation' but 'why do self-attributions play a distinctive social role despite their unreliability?' The answer is that attitude-ascription is fundamentally a social-normative practice, not a fact-stating one.

Appraiser (blind)
Non-alethic functions of self-attribution is interesting but the pragmatic turn is familiar.

U84. Holding that implicit attitudes are genuine attitudes commits you to rejecting first-person authority entirely, because implicit attitudes demonstrate that the states doing the causal-functional work of attitudes are systematically inaccessible to interpretation—revealing that what we take to be self-knowledge of attitudes is actually just self-knowledge of our interpretive dispositions, not of the attitudes themselves.

Move · Target
commitment — Philosophers like Schwitzgebel who take implicit attitudes seriously while wanting to preserve some first-person authority for at least explicit attitudes
Sketch

Philosophers discussing implicit bias typically grant that implicit attitudes are real attitudes (they guide behavior, resist counter-evidence, etc.) while trying to preserve first-person authority for explicit attitudes. But this is unstable. If implicit attitudes are genuine attitudes, then the functional states actually driving much of our behavior are precisely the ones we cannot access through either introspection or interpretation. What we do access through reflection—our explicit, avowable attitudes—are then best understood not as the attitudes themselves but as second-order interpretive stances toward our behavior. This means first-person authority, if it exists at all, is only authority about our interpretations, not about our attitudes. The commitment runs: if you accept implicit attitudes as attitudes, you must accept that attitude-individuation privileges causal-functional role over accessibility; but if causal-functional role matters most, then the inaccessible states are the real attitudes; therefore what we have first-person authority about (if anything) cannot be our attitudes.

The implicit-attitude challenge is serious but the argument assumes a contested premise about what counts as 'the real attitude'—dual-process theorists have responses available.

The debate falsely assumes 'belief' picks out a unified kind with respect to self-knowledge. When I judge 'I believe climate change is real' by interpreting my past assertions and behaviors, I interpretively attribute a standing state and lack authority. But when I answer 'Do you believe climate change is real?' by considering the question's merits now, I form or re-form the belief in giving the answer—this is non-interpretive settlement, not discovery. Authority attaches to formation, not possession. The key premise: what expressivists treat as 'transparent' self-knowledge (looking outward to the question, not inward to the state) just IS the formation of occurrent commitment, which happens to update standing state. This explains why I have authority when engaging with 'Do I believe P?' deliberatively but not when asked 'Did you believe P yesterday?'—same state-type, different epistemic relation.

The occurrent/standing distinction is important and underexplored in this debate, but the claim that authority exists only for formation may be too restrictive to match intuitions.

U86. First-person authority for avowals survives the interpretive turn but only as a pragmatic phenomenon: avowals like 'I believe P' are self-verifying speech acts that create the very authority they claim, meaning authority is explained not by special epistemic access or agential settlement but by the conventional force of first-person performatives.

Move · Target

When I say 'I believe climate change is real,' I don't describe a pre-existing state (which would require discovery/interpretation) or settle my attitude through deliberation—I commit myself publicly, and this commitment constitutes my having the belief going forward. The avowal is self-verifying in the pragmatic sense: by asserting it sincerely in appropriate conditions, I make it true. This explains authority without requiring either privileged access or agential settlement. Even if I arrived at this avowal through fallible interpretation (reading off my behaviors, confabulating reasons), the act of avowing creates authority for the state going forward. The key premise: beliefs are at least partially constituted by commitments to defend/maintain/act on certain propositions, and avowals are the paradigmatic way of undertaking such commitments. The interpretive turn is right about how we arrive at self-attributions; expressivists are right that authority attaches to avowals; but both miss that the authority is performatively generated, not epistemically grounded.

Performative self-verification has been explored in the expressivist literature; this restates more than advances.

Everyone assumes confabulation threatens first-person authority by showing our self-reports are wrong. But there's a distinction between the attitudes we actually have and the attitudes we interpretively construct in self-reflection. First-person authority might attach to the latter: I really am authoritative about what I conclude I believe upon reflection, even when that differs from what I actually believe pre-reflection. The confabulation cases show these come apart, but they don't show I lack authority about the interpreted attitude. This explains why Schwitzgebel's cases feel like discovering something surprising about oneself—there's genuine discovery about actual attitudes alongside genuine authority about interpreted ones. The interpretive process creates new attitudes we're authoritative about.

Interesting distinction between actual and interpreted attitudes, but the move to preserve authority by splitting the target has been explored in response to confabulation.

U88. Moran's agentialist account collapses into interpretivism once we recognize that deliberation itself is an interpretive process—determining what to believe requires interpreting one's own reasons as having a particular weight.

Move · Target

Moran contrasts deliberation (asking 'Is P true?') with observation, claiming this explains first-person authority without interpretation. But deliberation about whether P requires assessing whether one's reasons support P, which requires interpreting those reasons—determining what weight they have, how they bear on P, whether one genuinely holds them. This interpretation draws on the same evidence pool interpretivists identify: one's sense of what matters, one's other commitments, one's dispositions. The agentialist tries to ground authority in rational agency rather than interpretation, but rational agency just is a form of self-interpretation. The apparent contrast between the deliberative and interpretive stances dissolves: deliberation is interpretation of reasons rather than observation of mental states.

Appraiser (blind)
Competent criticism showing deliberation involves interpretation, but the collapse of Moran into interpretivism has been noted; incremental rather than transformative.

Interpretivists claim we know our beliefs by interpreting behavioral and contextual evidence. But the occurrent/dispositional distinction—whether I'm currently entertaining P versus merely disposed to affirm it—makes no systematic difference to the evidence available for interpretation. I display the same behavioral dispositions whether a belief is occurrent or merely standing; context doesn't reliably distinguish them. If interpretation is our only access, we cannot maintain that some beliefs are occurrent while others are merely dispositional—that distinction requires the kind of inner awareness interpretivists reject. Yet eliminativism about this distinction is deeply counterintuitive (surely there's a difference between currently thinking about P and merely being disposed to affirm it). Interpretivists face a forced choice: accept the counterintuitive eliminativism or grant some non-interpretive access.

Interpretivism threatening the occurrent/dispositional distinction is a real problem but the issue is known.

Nisbett and Wilson subjects confabulate about what caused their choice (an occurrent process), not about what they chose or intend going forward (a standing state). The literature conflates two things we might have authority about: the causal history of our mental states versus the normative commitments those states involve. First-person authority was always about the latter—I'm authoritative about what I believe, not about why I came to believe it. This distinction reclassifies the debate: interpretivists are right that we self-interpret causal processes, but this doesn't threaten authority over the rational commitments we undertake. The confabulation data actually presupposes subjects have authority about their choices/preferences (that's what they correctly report) while lacking it about psychological mechanisms.

Useful distinction between causal and normative authority, but the move to save first-person authority by restricting its domain is fairly well-trodden.

Interpretivists cite implicit attitudes as evidence we need interpretation to access our real attitudes. But implicit attitudes are posited precisely because they dissociate from what subjects sincerely avow. If we're interpretivists all the way down, we have no principled basis for treating IAT results as revealing 'real attitudes' that subjects are wrong about—they're just more behavioral data requiring interpretation. The interpretivist move requires treating some self-reports as authoritative (to create the contrast with implicit measures) while denying authority in general. Either sincere avowals have default authority—in which case implicit attitudes aren't attitudes at all but mere dispositions—or nothing has authority and implicit 'attitudes' are just patterns we choose to interpret as such. The key premise is that the implicit/explicit distinction requires asymmetric epistemic treatment that interpretivism cannot sustain.

The tension between interpretivism and implicit attitudes is real but extensively discussed.

U92. The agentialist and neo-expressivist accounts are unstable because they require that deliberative reasons-responsiveness grounds authority, but being reasons-responsive requires accurate beliefs about what reasons one has, which returns us to the observational model they reject.

Move · Target
instability — Moran's agentialism and Bar-On's neo-expressivism
Sketch

Moran grounds authority in the transparency method: I answer 'Do I believe P?' by answering 'Is P true?', taking a deliberative stance. Bar-On grounds it in expressive speech acts. Both require that the subject be appropriately responsive to reasons or can expressively manifest genuine attitudes. But this responsiveness requires that I can accurately tell what reasons I actually take to support what, or which attitudes I'm genuinely expressing. If I'm systematically wrong about my reasons (motivated reasoning) or express attitudes I don't have (confabulation), the agentialist move fails. To know I'm being appropriately reasons-responsive rather than rationalizing, I need the very observational access to my psychology that these views were meant to replace. The views collapse back into requiring inner perception of reasons-structures or genuine attitudes.

Appraiser (blind)
Valid internal criticism that agentialism requires what it rejects, but this circularity objection has been raised; competent but not groundbreaking.

distinction — Interpretivists like Carruthers who assimilate self and other interpretation, and traditional observationalists who locate authority in synchronic access

When I interpret myself as believing P based on my behavior, I can retroactively make this interpretation correct by committing now to P and treating my past actions as expressions of this commitment. Third-person interpreters cannot do this—they must take my psychology as whatever explains my behavior, not whatever I now decide it should be taken as. This creates an asymmetry: self-interpretation can be self-fulfilling across time in a way other-interpretation cannot. The power isn't epistemic access but diachronic rational control: I have authority because I can bring my past self into coherence with my current interpretation by undertaking commitments now. The key premise is that attitudes are individuated partly by diachronic rational relations that subjects can author but observers can only discover.

Appraiser (blind)
Diachronic authority to revise past self-interpretation is interesting but the temporal element has been explored.

The debate falsely assumes that either we observe determinate mental states (traditional view) or we interpret evidence that settles facts about us independently of our interpretation (Carruthers/Gopnik). But mental states are often genuinely indeterminate until we take a stance. When I wonder 'Do I really want to go to the party?', the behavioral and phenomenological evidence may radically underdetermine the answer. First-person authority isn't epistemic privilege about pre-existing facts, but practical authority to make certain interpretations true by adopting them. This explains the asymmetry: others can interpret my evidence, but only I can settle it by committing to an interpretation. The key premise is that for many attitudes, there's no fact of the matter independent of self-interpretation—we have interpretive sovereignty over indeterminate cases.

Interpretive sovereignty over indeterminate attitudes is a known position; the formulation is clear but not novel.

Interpretivists like Carruthers assume that if self-knowledge is interpretive, then the asymmetry between first and third person collapses—we're just another interpreter of our own evidence. This creates asymmetric rational pressure: certain self-interpretations become impermissible because they would make me incoherent as an agent, while no such constraint binds third-person interpretation. Rational constraints on self-interpretation creating asymmetry is interesting but the agential coherence requirement angle has been developed in the Moran-adjacent literature.

Even radical interpretivists typically grant direct access to phenomenal consciousness—what it's like to see red isn't something we infer. But recent cognitive science shows that attitudes come with characteristic cognitive phenomenology: feelings of fluency, coherence, rightness, attraction-to-propositions. These aren't mere accompaniments but partial constitutents of what makes something a belief rather than a supposition, or an intention rather than a fantasy. If you grant direct access to visual phenomenology, you're committed to granting it to cognitive phenomenology. And since these cognitive feelings partly constitute attitudes, we have non-interpretive access to attitudinal components. The interpretive work comes in integrating these feelings into full attitude ascriptions, not in accessing the feelings themselves. The key premise is that cognitive phenomenology is no less phenomenal than sensory phenomenology.

Cognitive phenomenology argument is competent and the parity reasoning is valid, but this strategy is already deployed in debates about introspection of thought.
