When I interpret myself, getting it wrong creates practical incoherence in my life (I pursue goals that don't reflect my values, make commitments I can't sustain), generating pressure to revise interpretation until reflective equilibrium is reached. To believe that P is to be disposed to treat P as true across an open-ended range of counterfactual circumstances, including those you've never encountered and cannot anticipate. The key premise is that beliefs and intentions are individuated by normative commitments that transcend their causal basis, making them constitutively underdetermined by any evidence. What philosophers have identified as first-person authority is actually first-person practical impact. This looks like special epistemic access but is actually special practical significance triggering different evidential standards. The debate assumes first-person authority concerns epistemic access to already-constituted attitudes. But we can distinguish two temporal relations to our own attitudes: archaeological (discovering what we already think) and constructive (settling what we think through the very act of self-ascription). Confabulation studies actually show archaeological self-knowledge failing, but they presuppose subjects have determinate prior attitudes to get wrong. When I sincerely avow 'I intend to quit smoking,' I'm not reporting a pre-existing intention but crystallizing an inchoate one — making it the case that I intend this by committing to it. The authority here is performative, not observational or interpretive. This explains the asymmetry: others can observe my smoking behavior, but they cannot constitute my intention by their ascriptions the way my avowal does. The interpretive theorists are right that we often discover our attitudes through interpretation, but wrong to think all first-person authority works this way.

Appraiser (blind)
The archaeological/constructive distinction is clear but the performative account has been explored in the literature already.

U105. Interpretive self-knowledge and first-person authority come apart because interpretation yields knowledge of attitudes-as-dispositions while authority concerns attitudes-as-commitments, and these are genuinely different states despite sharing the same ordinary language terms.

Move · Target
distinction — Both sides who assume the empirical literature on confabulation/implicit attitudes and the philosophical literature on first-person authority are studying the same phenomenon under the label 'belief' or 'attitude.'
Sketch

When Schwitzgebel shows we're ignorant of our beliefs through interpretation-demanding cases, and when Moran defends first-person authority, they're talking past each other because they're using 'belief' for different things. Interpretation reveals my dispositional profile — what I'm disposed to say, infer, feel in various circumstances. But first-person authority concerns my normative commitments — what I'm willing to stand behind as my view. These can diverge: I might be disposed to reason as though p, yet refuse to commit to p when directly asked. The authority asymmetry holds for commitments (you can't make me have committed to p by your say-so), but not for dispositions (you might know my dispositions better than I do). The confabulation literature threatens only dispositional self-knowledge. The mistake is thinking 'belief' in philosophical debate picks out a single kind of state rather than equivocating between these two.

Appraiser (blind)
Diagnosing equivocation between dispositions and commitments is helpful but doesn't clearly advance beyond existing distinction-drawing moves.

U106. First-person authority survives the interpretive turn because interpretation requires treating the target as rational, but self-interpretation uniquely allows direct intervention on the rationality constraint itself — I can make myself more interpretable by revising toward coherence.

Move · Target
reframing — The shared epistemic framing of the debate, where first-person authority is understood as a form of privileged knowledge rather than privileged control.
Sketch

All interpretation, whether of self or other, requires a rationality assumption (Davidson's principle of charity, Dennett's intentional stance). Others interpret my attitudes by assuming coherence and working backward from behavior; I interpret myself the same way. But here's the asymmetry: when you discover I'm less coherent than expected, you adjust your interpretation. When I discover I'm less coherent than expected, I can adjust my attitudes instead. If I notice my dispositions conflict with what I thought I believed, I don't just reinterpret — I can revise my commitments to restore coherence. This isn't because I have observational access to my attitudes, but because I have agentive control over them. First-person authority isn't about better epistemic access but about constitutive control: my self-ascriptions tend to be correct not because I see my attitudes better, but because I can make my attitudes conform to my ascriptions. The debate has been framed as epistemic (who knows better?) when it's really about agency (who can intervene?).

Appraiser (blind)
The intervention/observation contrast is valuable but the agentive control story has been developed by Moran and others.

U107. Accepting the interpretive view commits you to denying that there are facts about your own fine-grained attitude contents, which means first-person authority trivially survives because there's nothing substantive to be authoritative about.

Move · Target
commitment — Interpretive theorists (Carruthers, Gopnik) who assume their view is compatible with attitude realism — that there are determinate facts about what we believe that interpretation is supposed to uncover.
Sketch

The interpretive view holds that attitudes are constituted by patterns in behavior and context, accessible through interpretation. But interpretation, as Quine showed, is radically underdetermined — the same behavioral pattern can be rationalized by indefinitely many attitude attributions. For others, we just pick the simplest interpretation and move on. But the interpretive theorist must say this about self-interpretation too: there's no fact about whether I believe that Hesperus is bright versus believing that Phosphorus is bright, beyond which interpretation best systematizes my dispositions. This means attitude contents are interpretation-relative, not objective features of my mental life. But then the authority question becomes trivial: I'm authoritative about my attitudes in the same deflated sense that I'm authoritative about the meter stick in Paris — it's whatever I say it is, but only because there's no substantial fact to get right or wrong. The interpretive view thus commits you to a kind of attitude anti-realism that makes first-person authority uninteresting rather than false. Interpretive theorists want to naturalize self-knowledge while keeping attitudes robustly real; they can't have both.

Appraiser (blind)
The anti-realist consequence is interesting but whether interpretivists are actually committed to it is contestable.

U108. Accepting the interpretive account commits one to denying that subjects can have immediate knowledge of attitude content individuation, which collapses the view into an unstable position: if content is partly determined by environmental and social factors that require interpretation to discern, then subjects cannot know what they believe without potentially lengthy empirical investigation of their context.

commitment — Gopnik and Carruthers's interpretivist accounts, which aim to preserve some asymmetry and immediacy while adopting the interpretive framework

Interpretivists like Carruthers argue we know our attitudes through the same interpretive mechanisms we use for others, relying on behavioral and contextual evidence. But attitude content is widely held to be partly individuated by environmental factors (Twin Earth externalism) and social-linguistic practices. If self-knowledge is interpretive, then knowing what I believe requires interpreting not just my behavior but my extended context—causal relations to water vs. XYZ, social role, community linguistic practices. This makes self-knowledge a potentially open-ended empirical project, destroying the phenomenology of immediacy that even interpretivists typically grant. The key premise is that interpretation requires identifying all the relevant content-individuating factors, and if those extend beyond the skin, immediate self-knowledge becomes impossible on interpretivist grounds. Interpretivists thus face a dilemma: either restrict content to narrow/internalist content (abandoning externalism) or accept that we typically don't know what we believe.

Appraiser (blind)
The externalism problem for interpretivism is real but interpretivists have responses about immediate vs. complete knowledge available.

U109. Moran's agentialist account is unstable: it collapses into either transparent-access epistemic agency (which the empirical literature refutes) or non-epistemic stipulation (which abandons first-person authority as knowledge).

instability — Moran's agentialist account and its attempt to ground first-person authority in rational agency rather than epistemic access

Moran claims I know my belief that P by answering whether P, exercising rational agency rather than observation. But parse this carefully: either (1) the deliberative procedure reliably tracks what I actually believe, functioning as an epistemic method, or (2) it constitutes/determines what I believe going forward, functioning prescriptively. If (1), we need an explanation of why deliberation is more reliable than behavioral observation for accessing pre-existing attitudes—but the confabulation literature suggests it isn't. We get the reliability of transparent access without its mechanism. If (2), I'm not discovering but deciding, which means I don't have authority about what I believed but only about what I'll believe—this is prospective commitment, not retrospective knowledge. The dilemma's key premise is that knowledge requires a success term (getting it right about something independent of the knowing) while agency requires independence from what's known. Moran needs both simultaneously but can sustain neither horn. First-person authority requires that my self-ascription answers to something, but Moran's agency dissolves the answering-to relation.

Appraiser (blind)
The dilemma for Moran is clearly stated but agentialists have resources for resisting both horns that aren't engaged here.

All parties assume first-person authority is a general feature of self-knowledge of attitudes. But consider: you ask me whether I believe climate change is anthropogenic. I'm not currently thinking about this, so it's a standing belief. I access it exactly as the interpretivist predicts—by consulting what I've said before, imagining what I'd say now, considering my other commitments. There's no special authority here; I could be wrong in exactly the ways you could be wrong about my beliefs. The asymmetry only exists for attitudes I'm occurrently entertaining right now—and even then, only for those I'm entertaining deliberately rather than passively experiencing. For these narrow cases, Moran-style transparency might work: I know I'm wondering whether P by wondering whether P. But this is a tiny subset. The key premise is that standing attitudes are causally-functionally constituted dispositions that we access through the same kinds of evidence regardless of whose attitudes they are. The debate has been theorizing a marginal case while treating it as paradigmatic, which explains why every theory seems to capture something while missing something else.

Appraiser (blind)
The scope-restriction challenge is important but whether standing attitudes really lack asymmetry is empirically and conceptually contestable.

The argument turns on distinguishing epistemic from constitutive authority. This explains both the interpretive/constructive element (there's no determinate fact to discover) AND first-person authority (my avowal has special weight because it's performatively constitutive, not because I have better evidence). The key premise: many attitudinal states are metaphysically indeterminate prior to avowal, existing only as clusters of partially inconsistent dispositions. This differs from both discovery models (which assume determinacy) and pure interpretation models (which treat self-ascription as merely evidentially based).

Constitutive authority crystallizing indeterminate states is already a standard move in this literature.

The debate assumes there are determinate facts about our attitudinal states that we might know well (vindicating first-person authority) or poorly (vindicating the interpretive turn). The question 'do I have first-person authority?' then misfires: I have neither privileged epistemic access nor parity with third-person interpreters, because there's nothing fully determinate to have access to until interpretation occurs. The asymmetry between first and third person is real but not epistemic—it's that my interpretation plays a constitutive role that yours doesn't.

The interpretive theorists assume interpretation is purely epistemic—a matter of discovering what's already there. But self-interpretation is simultaneously constitutive and epistemic. This is why I have authority: not because I have better evidence (I don't), but because my interpretive act has world-to-mind direction of fit while yours has mind-to-world. The key premise is that beliefs are determinables that require the subject's interpretive uptake to become fully determinate, making self-interpretation completion rather than detection.

The constitutive self-interpretation idea has been developed by others; this version doesn't add enough novelty to the existing literature.

Moran says avowal expresses rational commitment; Bar-On says it expresses one's state directly without inference. The key premise is that expression requires successful reference to the expressed state, which reintroduces the original epistemic burden. These views trade an epistemic problem for a semantic one that has the same structure.

The argument begins by noting that first-person authority manifests primarily in conversational contexts where challenging someone's self-ascription ('You don't really believe that') carries special social costs. This explains why the authority is defeasible (we do sometimes override it), context-sensitive (stronger for avowal than for hedged self-interpretation), and extends even to cases where the interpretive account suggests the person is clearly confabulating. The asymmetry isn't that first-person and third-person use different methods, but that we have pragmatic reasons to play different social games with them.

This argument shows that Carruthers and Gopnik, in emphasizing that we use interpretation for both self and other, overlook that interpretation can yield asymmetric reliability when the evidence base is asymmetric. The key premise is that interpretation is an evidence-sensitive process, and the first-person interpreter has exclusive access to certain categories of evidence (the stream of conscious rehearsal during decision-making, the felt resistance when trying to form certain intentions, the full memory of reasoning history). Just as you can interpret a text better when you have access to draft versions and author's notes, you can interpret your own attitudes better when you have access to the cognitive workspace. This generates first-person authority not as a different kind of knowledge but as an evidential advantage within the same interpretive framework—explaining why it's defeasible (interpretation can still go wrong) but real (the asymmetry in evidence is genuine).

The evidential-advantage-within-interpretation move is natural and has been made; it doesn't sufficiently challenge the interpretive framework's commitments.

Moran argues that we know our beliefs through deliberation—by asking not 'What do I believe about P?' but 'Is P true?'—and this deliberative stance grounds first-person authority. But the argument shows this collapses: when I deliberate about whether P, I must interpret what my evidence supports, assess which considerations are relevant, determine what my experiences mean. This interpretive work is identical in structure to what I do when figuring out what you should believe given your evidence. The key premise is that there's no deliberation without interpretation of reasons, and interpretation of reasons is symmetric between first and third person. The deliberative stance doesn't bypass interpretation; it is a species of interpretation—specifically, interpretation aimed at what to think rather than what one does think. So agentialism cannot ground an authority asymmetry because it reduces to an interpretive process that applies equally to self and other.

The collapse argument against Moran has been pressed before; this version is clear but doesn't add new dialectical pressure.

Interpretivists claim we know our minds through interpretation of evidence. But interpretation is underdetermination-managing: we select among multiple hypotheses consistent with data. This requires some data that isn't itself an interpretation. For self-interpretation, what could this be? Not raw behavior, because individuating behavior already requires mental concepts (is that motion a wave or a flinch?). Not neural states, because we lack introspective access to those. The interpretivist might say 'phenomenology'—but if we have authoritative access to phenomenology, we have the privileged access that interpretivism denies. Alternatively, if phenomenology is itself interpreted, we face regress. The interpretivist faces a dilemma: either posit some self-presented mental reality (reinstating a non-interpretive ground), or deny any uninterpreted given (making interpretation unconstrained, unable to explain why we converge on stable self-ascriptions). The position collapses either back toward observationalism or forward toward an unworkable holism.

Appraiser (blind)
The regress/fixed-point argument against interpretivism is a standard move in debates about interpretation and holism; competent but familiar.

Nisbett and Wilson show subjects confabulate reasons, but interpretivists overlook a pattern: our confabulations don't match what third-person interpreters conclude from the same behavioral evidence. The systematic divergence suggests we access our attitudes through a mechanism unavailable to observers—not infallible introspection, but something like partial access to sub-personal processing that generates confabulations different from purely behavioral interpretation. The key premise: if interpretation from behavioral evidence were symmetric, error patterns would be symmetric; they're not; therefore access is asymmetric.

Nisbett and Wilson show subjects misreport the causes of their choices (e.g., choosing right-side items while citing quality). But this is a counterexample to first-person authority only if we assume authority extends to causal-explanatory reasons. If instead authority concerns normative reasons—the considerations that figure in our rational deliberation—the studies are perfectly compatible with authority. When subjects say 'I chose this for its quality,' they correctly report what they took to be their reason, even if they're wrong about what caused their choice. The key premise is that a properly Moorean account of first-person authority concerns the space of reasons, not the space of causes, and confabulation studies systematically fail to distinguish these.

First-person authority appears to be an epistemic asymmetry requiring special explanation. This explains why authority is defeasible (we override it when stakes are high enough) and why it doesn't extend to all self-attributions (not to unconscious states where the social norm doesn't apply). Standard interpretations of Nisbett and Wilson take subjects to be wholly confabulating—making up attitudes they don't have. But reanalyze the classic experiments: when subjects choose stockings from a display and cite quality rather than position, they aren't confabulating a preference (they genuinely preferred that stocking) but confabulating a reason-explanation for the preference. The mistake is metarepresentational: they have introspective access to what moved them (an attraction to rightward items) but misrepresent this motivation as a rational justification (quality assessment). This dissolves the apparent conflict: introspection delivers attitudes reliably, but our self-understanding of which attitude-type we're accessing is theory-laden and corruptible. The debate falsely assumes that if introspection fails for reason-explanation, it fails entirely. The key premise is that accessing an attitude and correctly categorizing what kind of attitude it is are separable achievements.

Another variant of distinguishing attitude-types to save introspection from confabulation data; the metarepresentational twist is minor.

Many philosophers accept both that implicit biases are genuine attitudes (beliefs or preferences) and that we need special interpretation to identify them—they're not introspectively available. But if attitudes can be fully genuine while requiring interpretation for identification, what makes explicit 'introspectively available' attitudes non-interpreted? The natural answer is that explicit attitudes are constituted by introspective seemings. But this recreates the pre-interpretive access model that the implicit attitudes literature was supposed to undermine. Alternatively, explicit attitudes are also interpreted, just more easily—but then the distinction between first-person and third-person attribution collapses entirely, as both are equally interpretive. The dialectic forces a choice: either implicit 'attitudes' aren't really attitudes (they're mere dispositions we interpret as if they were attitudes), or explicit attitudes have no special first-person status. You cannot consistently maintain both that implicit attitudes are real attitudes and that explicit attitudes enjoy first-person authority. The key premise is that attitude-hood cannot come in epistemically different varieties without collapsing into a distinction between real attitudes and interpreted-as-if attitudes.

The tension between implicit and explicit attitudes under interpretivism has been extensively discussed.

Both accounts try to ground self-knowledge in something other than state-identification (deliberation or expression), but that grounding relation itself presupposes successful attitude identification. They don't eliminate the need for interpretive or introspective identification; they just postpone addressing it. The accounts thus collapse back into either observationalism (we must somehow identify attitudes pre-deliberatively) or interpretivism (we identify them through the same evidence everyone else uses).

Interpreters of others can attribute irrationality, inconsistency, or unintelligibility when evidence runs out. But Davidson's principle of charity shows that self-interpretation cannot coherently proceed this way: treating oneself as fundamentally irrational or unintelligible defeats the conditions for having a perspective from which to interpret at all. This means first-person interpretation operates under a constitutive rational constraint: we must interpret ourselves as making sense. This constraint doesn't give us infallible access, but it does make self-interpretation systematically more constrained than other-interpretation, because we cannot invoke 'they're just being irrational' as an interpretive resource. Therefore, accepting the interpretive view commits you to accepting an asymmetry that grounds a deflationary version of first-person authority.

The implicit attitudes literature is usually treated as a problem for all accounts of first-person authority. But it actually vindicates a restricted version of Moran's agentialism while showing why that view must accept sharp limits. Moran grounds first-person authority in our stance as rational agents who settle what to believe by reasoning about the world. But implicit attitudes are precisely those attitudes that are insulated from this rational-agential process—they don't respond to my deliberating about reasons. The key move: accepting Moran's account commits you to denying first-person authority for implicit attitudes, since they lie outside the rational-agential domain. This isn't a bug but reveals the underlying structure: we have authority where we have rational control, and confabulation occurs exactly where we attempt to assert authority beyond that domain. This explains both why we're authoritative about explicit beliefs and why we confabulate about implicit ones—it's the same mechanism.

Nisbett-Wilson cases involve subjects correctly detecting genuine mental states (the preference, the attraction) but misattributing their etiology—they mistake an enabling causal condition (the music, the position) for a reason-giving attitude. The key premise is that attitudes are constituted by inferential role, not mere causal efficacy: the music enabled the preference but wasn't what the preference was about. When subjects confabulate, they accurately introspect the preference itself (showing introspection works) but err in reconstructing its rational-causal history (a different cognitive task). This distinction reclassifies the debate: confabulation threatens our grasp of attitude genealogy, not attitude presence. We can preserve both observational introspection for current attitudes and the interpretive story for understanding their sources. First-person authority holds for 'what I believe/intend' but not for 'why I believe/intend it.'

But interpretation is itself an intentional activity requiring attitudes: the intention to interpret, beliefs about which interpretive principles to apply, preferences among competing interpretations. If these interpretive-enabling attitudes are also known only through interpretation, we face regress. The interpretivist must grant that at least some attitudes (those constituting the interpretive activity itself) are known non-interpretively—through direct awareness, stipulation, or constitution. But once we admit any attitudes are knowable non-interpretively, the principled motivation for interpretivism elsewhere collapses: if direct access works for interpretive intentions, why not for other attitudes? The position thus collapses into either regress or a hybrid view where interpretation rests on a foundation of non-interpreted self-knowledge, undermining the interpretive turn's claim to comprehensiveness.

Appraiser (blind)
Another regress argument against interpretivism; similar to thesis 4 and 8, covering familiar anti-interpretivist ground.

U152. First-person authority is preserved not because self-interpretation is privileged but because self-ascription itself constitutes a distinctive kind of evidence that other-ascription cannot access—not evidence about a prior state, but evidence that partly brings the state into determinate existence.

Move · Target
reframing — The shared assumption across both transparency theorists (Moran) and interpretivists (Carruthers, Gopnik) that attitudes have determinate contents prior to our epistemic access to them
Sketch

The debate assumes attitudes have determinate content prior to and independent of self-ascription, making self-ascription either observation (undermined by confabulation data) or interpretation (losing authority). But many attitudes—especially higher-order ones like intentions and normative beliefs—are metaphysically indeterminate until articulated. Self-ascription doesn't report or interpret a fully formed state; it crystallizes it. This explains asymmetry without requiring privileged access: when you self-ascribe believing P, you're not merely reporting but also settling what you believe, creating evidence unavailable to third parties. The key premise is that mental states can be metaphysically vague in content until self-interpretation resolves them, similar to how quantum states are indeterminate until measured, but without requiring consciousness to play a constitutive role for all attitudes.

Appraiser (blind)
Self-ascription crystallizing indeterminate states is well-covered territory.

U153. Holding that self-interpretation and other-interpretation use the same evidence commits you to denying that avowals can be insincere, which interpretivist theorists implicitly reject when they distinguish lying from confabulation.

Move · Target
commitment — Strong interpretivism (Carruthers, Gopnik) that denies any epistemic asymmetry between first and third-person attribution
Sketch

Interpretivists like Carruthers and Gopnik claim we know our minds through the same interpretive process we use for others, applied to our own behavior and circumstances. But this entails that avowal ('I believe P') has the same relationship to belief-states as third-person attribution does. When interpreting others, we can recognize insincere reports—they're lying, not merely wrong. But if I have no special access to my beliefs beyond behavioral interpretation, then my saying 'I believe P' is just more behavior to be interpreted. I cannot then coherently distinguish between lying about my belief (which requires knowing what I believe independently of my avowal) and confabulating about it (being wrong). Yet interpretivists clearly maintain this distinction—they treat confabulation as epistemic failure, not deception. This reveals they're implicitly committed to some form of privileged access after all.

Appraiser (blind)
The lying/confabulation distinction is interesting but interpretivists have responses available (lying requires meta-interpretive capacity); the internal tension is overstated.

U154. The asymmetry between self-ascription and other-ascription exists but has the wrong explanation: it derives not from epistemic privilege but from pragmatic immunity—social norms make challenging first-person avowals conversationally costlier than challenging third-person attributions, creating apparent authority that is actually just conventional deference.

Scores
promise 2/5 · residual –/5 · worst –/5 · unattacked
Move · Target
reframing — The shared assumption that first-person authority requires an epistemic explanation rather than a merely pragmatic one
Sketch

Both sides treat first-person authority as an epistemic phenomenon requiring epistemic explanation (either privileged access or rational agency). But the asymmetry might be purely pragmatic. In normal discourse, contradicting someone's self-ascription ('No, you don't really believe that') carries higher social costs than contradicting other-ascription ('No, she doesn't really believe that'). This isn't because speakers have better evidence about themselves, but because self-ascriptions have a performative element: challenging them questions the speaker's sincerity or rationality, not just accuracy. We treat avowals as authoritative by default because the pragmatic costs of rejection are high, not because they're epistemically secure. The confabulation literature then shows this conventional authority is unjustified—we defer to avowals more than accuracy warrants. The key premise is that conversational norms can create apparent epistemic asymmetries.

Appraiser (blind)
Pragmatic explanations of authority have been explored; while the conversational-cost angle is specific, it doesn't sufficiently explain why these norms exist or why they're so robust.

The interpretive theorists' own position is unstable: if we really self-attribute through interpretation of behavioral evidence, then the confabulation literature shows we should have no more confidence in our self-attributions than in attributions to others, yet interpretive theorists themselves exhibit first-person authority in their theorizing.

Move · Target

Carruthers and Gopnik argue we know our minds through interpretation just as we know others' minds, relying on confabulation studies to undermine privileged access. But the key premise is that if this were true, the rational response would be systematic self-doubt — treating one's own self-attributions as no more credible than attributions from observers who have the same behavioral evidence. Yet interpretive theorists don't actually adopt this stance; when they assert 'I believe interpretation explains self-knowledge' they don't qualify it with 'but an observer might be equally warranted in attributing to me the belief that it doesn't.' Their practice reveals a commitment to first-person authority even while their theory denies it. Either they must adopt radical self-doubt (making their own theorizing self-undermining) or admit that interpretation-based self-knowledge has some feature that preserves asymmetry.

Appraiser (blind)
The performative contradiction charge is familiar from debates about self-refutation; interpretivists can respond that theoretical self-ascription has different standards than ordinary cases.

U156. The asymmetry between self- and other-attribution survives the interpretive turn because self-interpretation has exclusive access to experienced reasons while other-interpretation must infer them, and attitudes are individuated partly by the reasons that rationalize them from the first-person perspective.

Move · Target
commitment — Carruthers and Gopnik's claim that the interpretive model undermines first-person authority by making self- and other-knowledge merely quantitatively different (more evidence vs. less)
Sketch

Interpretivists like Carruthers are committed to the claim that if we know our attitudes through interpretation of evidence, then any asymmetry must derive from different evidence sets available to self vs. other. But they overlook that one crucial type of evidence—experienced reasons (the considerations that feel like reasons to me in deliberation)—is available only first-personally, not through any amount of behavioral observation. Moreover, attitude individuation is partly constituted by rational relations to reasons, not just by functional role. When I interpret my donation as expressing belief that charity X is effective, I'm not just reading off behavior; I'm identifying which reasons I experienced as motivating. Others can hypothesize about my reasons but cannot experience them. This grounds an ineliminable asymmetry: self-attribution individuates attitudes more finely because it has access to experienced rational relations that behavior underdetermines.

Appraiser (blind)
The experienced-reasons asymmetry has been discussed; while the attitude-individuation angle adds something, interpretivists have responses about functional role being sufficient for individuation.

U157. First-person authority is unstable: it necessarily collapses into either discredited Cartesian infallibility or mere difference in evidence-gathering efficiency, because any middle position requires simultaneously claiming both that self-interpretation is epistemically special and that it can systematically err—a combination that cannot be coherently maintained.

Move · Target
instability — The moderate positions of Moran, Bar-On, and anyone trying to preserve first-person authority while accepting interpretivism
Sketch

Moran, Bar-On, and moderate interpretivists all seek a middle ground: rejecting Cartesian infallibility while preserving something distinctively authoritative about self-knowledge. But this position is unstable. If self-knowledge can err (as confabulation shows), then whatever makes it authoritative must be something other than reliability or accuracy. The usual candidates—immediacy, non-inferentiality, special evidence access—all reintroduce the epistemic privilege that interpretivism denies. If instead authority means something non-epistemic (like Moran's deliberative stance), then it's unclear why we should call systematically unreliable self-attributions 'knowledge' at all, or why others should defer to them. The moderate position requires 'authority without reliability,' but authority in any recognizable epistemic sense just is a matter of being reliably right. Any account that grants the empirical findings about confabulation while insisting on preserved authority must either redefine authority into insignificance or smuggle back Cartesian assumptions.

Appraiser (blind)
The instability argument is forceful but the dilemma is too stark—moderate positions can distinguish types of authority or accept limited, non-Cartesian epistemic privilege.

U158. Confabulation studies demonstrate not that self-interpretation is pervasive but that first-person authority is question-relative: we have authority about whether we φ but not about why we φ, undermining the assumption that self-knowledge is an all-or-nothing epistemic relation to a mental state.

Move · Target
reframing — Both interpretivists who use confabulation data to argue against first-person authority globally, and expressivists who must explain away the confabulation data
Sketch

Nisbett & Wilson's subjects accurately reported choosing the rightmost stockings but confabulated explanations for why. This pattern recurs: accurate introspective reports of attitudes, poor reports of their etiology. The debate misreads this as showing attitudes themselves are interpretationally accessed. Instead, the data show we have non-interpretive access to THAT we prefer X, intend Y, believe Z (the attitude itself), but must interpret WHY (the attitude's causal history). First-person authority holds for the former, not the latter. The key premise: an attitude is individuated by its content and force (believing-that-P), not by its causal history; confabulation studies probe causal self-knowledge, not attitudinal self-knowledge. Moran is right that we have authority, interpretivists are right that we confabulate—they're just talking past each other about different questions.

Appraiser (blind)
The what/why distinction is valuable but arguably already recognized in careful work; presenting it as resolving the debate overstates its novelty and force.

U159. Accepting first-person authority while embracing interpretive access commits you to an implausible asymmetry: you must hold that self-interpretation is simultaneously more error-prone than other-interpretation (per confabulation studies) yet yields stronger epistemic authority, which is coherent only if authority and reliability come apart more radically than anyone in the debate accepts.

Move · Target
commitment — Interpretivist positions (Gopnik, Carruthers) that attempt to preserve some form of first-person authority while maintaining the interpretive symmetry thesis
Sketch

Interpretivists like Gopnik claim symmetry: we know ourselves like we know others, via interpretation. But they want to preserve some first-person authority. Meanwhile, confabulation studies show we're systematically worse at self-interpretation than the debate assumes (we explain our choices post-hoc, confabulate reasons, etc.). Others observing our behavior plus context often predict our attitudes better than we do. So if self-knowledge is interpretive, and self-interpretation is less reliable than other-interpretation, yet we grant first-person authority, we're committed to authority being independent of reliability. The key premise: no participant in the debate actually accepts this independence—even Bar-On's neo-expressivism grounds authority in a special epistemic access. Interpretivists who want to keep authority must either abandon the interpretive symmetry thesis or embrace that I can have authority about my beliefs despite you knowing them better than I do.

Appraiser (blind)
The reliability-authority gap is real but the argument that no one accepts this separation is empirically false—some pragmatist positions explicitly embrace it.

U160. The agentialist view that self-knowledge involves rational settlement rather than discovery collapses into the interpretivist position it opposes, because rational settlement is itself a process of interpreting which commitments best cohere with one's existing attitudes and values—Moran's deliberative transparency is just interpretation with a first-person practical spin.

Move · Target
instability — Moran's agentialist account and those who treat the deliberative/transparency approach as a genuine alternative to interpretivism
Sketch

Moran argues that answering 'Do I believe P?' by considering whether P (not by introspecting) preserves first-person authority through rational agency: I settle what to believe, not discover what I believe. But this settlement process requires me to survey my existing commitments, values, and evidence to determine whether I should believe P—this IS interpretation, just interpretation aimed at coherence rather than causal explanation. When I deliberate whether P, I'm interpreting which doxastic stance best fits my overall evaluative and cognitive economy. The key premise: any process that takes existing mental states as input and yields a verdict about one's current attitudes via coherence-assessment is interpretive in the relevant sense, even if it's also agentive. The difference between Moran and Carruthers isn't discovery vs. settlement but backward-looking vs. forward-looking interpretation. Agentialism thus doesn't escape the interpretive turn—it just redescribes it in agential vocabulary.

Appraiser (blind)
The claim that agentialism collapses into interpretivism underestimates the difference between forward-looking normative settlement and backward-looking causal interpretation—agentialists have responses.

U161. First-person authority for beliefs derives not from privileged epistemic access but from the fact that avowing a belief constitutively alters its rational standing in ways that observing it cannot.

Move · Target
reframing — The shared assumption between interpretivists and anti-interpretivists that authority must be explained by epistemic superiority or retained despite epistemic parity

The debate assumes first-person authority must be grounded in either superior evidence (perception models) or retained despite equal evidence (expressivist/agentialist models). But this misses how self-ascription itself changes what rational relations the belief has. When I say 'I believe P,' I undertake a rational commitment to P and to defending it that I don't undertake when merely observing behavioral evidence. This commitment-transformation explains why self-ascriptions have distinctive rational force without requiring either privileged access or mysterious expressivist mechanisms. The authority isn't about knowing better—it's about doing something different that generates new rational requirements.

Appraiser (blind)
Avowal altering rational standing is standard expressivist/agentialist territory.

U162. Interpretivist accounts can explain first-person authority once we recognize that agents have preferential interpretive access to their own standing intentions, which serve as evidence unavailable to external interpreters.

Sketch

The interpretive turn assumes all evidence available to self-interpretation is in principle available to others (behavior, context, etc.). But standing intentions—the dispositional states that structure our ongoing projects—are both (a) genuinely attitudinal states requiring interpretation rather than observation, and (b) evidentially available to the agent in a way they aren't to others, because the agent knows what she's trying to do across time in a way that no momentary behavioral slice reveals. These aren't occurrent thoughts (which would return us to inner perception) but standing commitments that the agent interprets her occurrent states against. This preserves the interpretive insight while explaining asymmetry: we interpret ourselves using evidence others lack.

Appraiser (blind)
Standing intentions as special evidence is a familiar move; the claim that they're interpretive yet privileged doesn't clearly escape existing objections to hybrid views.

The debate assumes a discovery model: either I discover my attitudes through inner perception or through self-interpretation. But self-interpretation is performative for second-order attitudes. When I interpret myself as believing P, this interpretation—if sincere—constitutes a second-order endorsement of P that itself counts as a belief-like state with distinctive rational commitments. The asymmetry between self and other isn't epistemic but constitutive: your interpretation of me can't make me committed to anything, but my interpretation of myself creates new rational obligations. This preserves authority (I determine what I'm committed to defending) while accepting that first-order attitudes may be interpretively accessed. The key premise is that sincere self-ascription is a speech act that creates normative, not just descriptive, facts.

Self-interpretation constituting second-order commitment is familiar ground.

distinction — Both empirically-minded interpretivists and critics of introspection who treat confabulation studies as undermining all first-person authority
Sketch

Nisbett and Wilson's studies show people are poor at identifying causal influences on their behavior, but interpretivists wrongly infer that we therefore lack privileged access to our attitudes themselves. The distinction collapses two questions: (1) What is my attitude? versus (2) What caused my attitude or behavior? We have first-person authority only about (1). When subjects confabulate about why they preferred certain stockings, they may still know non-interpretively that they preferred those stockings. The error lies in causal self-explanation, not attitude self-ascription. This explains the data pattern: we err when reconstructing causal histories but can still authoritatively report our current attitudes. The key premise is that attitudes can be introspectively accessible even when their causal genesis is not.

Appraiser (blind)
The constitutive/causal distinction as response to confabulation is already prominent in the literature; this restates rather than advances that move.

Nisbett-Wilson subjects confabulate not about their beliefs but because they mistake trained response dispositions for belief-based actions. When the stockings experiment subject says 'I chose these because of quality,' they're not misreporting a belief but wrongly categorizing a non-doxastic disposition as doxastic. Genuine attitudes are constituted by their role in practical reasoning and linguistic behavior; dispositions shaped by priming or implicit bias lack this rational integration. The key premise is that the attitude/disposition boundary is not given transparently, and interpretive work is needed to classify our own mental states into kinds, but once correctly classified as attitudinal, those states are authoritative because they're partly constituted by rational self-conception.

Restricting authority to properly attitudinal states is a standard defensive move; the attitude/disposition boundary claim doesn't add enough novelty.

Interpretivists like Carruthers claim we know our minds through interpretation, not access. The move to 'access to interpretive dispositions' feels like relabeling rather than resolving the tension between access and interpretation.

Current debates treat 'attitudes' monolithically, but Nisbett-Wilson style confabulation studies target immediate reasons for actions and reactions—occurrent, conscious episodes. Standing beliefs and intentions, however, are individuated by patterns over time, and here interpretive methods actually give subjects an advantage: they have access to more data points, experience the phenomenology of deliberation from the inside, and can observe their own patterns of inference in a way that episodic snapshots miss. The interpretive turn threatens first-person authority only if we misconceive attitudes as episodic mental states rather than dispositional patterns. What subjects confabulate about is their occurrent reasoning; what they can know through interpretation is their standing commitments. The key premise is that attitudes are fundamentally dispositional and that interpretive access to one's own pattern-generating mechanisms (even if not introspectively transparent) is richer than external behavioral interpretation allows.

The debate assumes interpretation either preserves authority (somehow) or undermines it. When I interpret myself as believing P, this very act of endorsement can crystallize an inchoate dispositional state into a determinate belief. The key premise is that many of our attitudes exist in a superposed or indeterminate state until self-ascription forces a collapse. Nisbett and Wilson show we confabulate about reasons and causes, but this gets wrongly generalized to all self-knowledge. Draw a principled distinction between authority over one's commitments (what I stand for, what I endorse) versus authority over one's causal-explanatory profile (what actually drives my behavior). The Moran-style agentialist is right that I determine what I believe through deliberation about what to believe, but wrong to think this deliberative stance gives me causal-historical knowledge. The interpretivist is right that causal self-knowledge is inferential, but wrong to extend this to normative self-knowledge. The key premise is that 'belief' in the committal sense and 'belief' in the causal-dispositional sense are genuinely distinct kinds, and first-person authority attaches only to the former. This explains why confabulation studies undermine some self-knowledge claims without undermining the asymmetry Bar-On and Moran identify.

The commitment/etiology distinction has been made before; this application to confabulation is competent but not novel.

Carruthers and Gopnik assume self-interpretation and other-interpretation use the same evidence symmetrically. But consider forming an intention right now. When you self-ascribe 'I intend to φ,' you're interpreting evidence that exists only up to this moment, and the intention itself shapes future evidence. When I ascribe an intention to you, I can use evidence from after your self-ascription to test it. This temporal asymmetry means self-interpretation is hostage to future confirmation in a way other-interpretation isn't. The confabulation literature actually supports this: subjects confabulate precisely when asked to explain actions before completing them. This shows self-interpretation can't simply be other-interpretation turned inward, because the evidential base has a fundamentally different temporal structure.

The temporal-direction claim is confused—other-interpreters also interpret past evidence, and self-interpretation can use prospective evidence; the asymmetry doesn't hold as stated.
